**Surah Ya-Sin**
Eighty-three verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ya Sin﴾ ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ya Sin﴾ ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom﴾. We have already discussed, in general terms, the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-tahajjī) at the beginning of Surah al-'Ankabūt, and we mentioned that in every surah that Allah opened with disjointed letters, the letters were followed by a mention of the Remembrance (al-Dhikr), the Book (al-Kitāb) or the Qur'an. Here we will mention some discussions:

**The first discussion:** There are matters in the mention of these letters at the beginnings of the surahs which indicate that they are not devoid of wisdom, but human knowledge does not reach their specific wisdom. So we say: what is the general wisdom in them? As for the evidence that they contain something indicating wisdom, it is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned half of the letters, which are fourteen letters, and this is half of twenty-eight letters, and these are all the letters found in the language of the Arabs, according to our statement that the hamzah is an alif that is vocalised. Then Allah, exalted is He, divided the letters into three categories: nine letters from the alif to the dhāl, nine other letters at the end of the letters from the fā' to the yā', and ten from the middle, from the rā' to the ghayn. From the first category He mentioned two letters, which are the alif and the ḥā', and He left out seven. From the other category He left out two letters, which are the fā' and the wāw, and He mentioned seven. He did not leave out from the first category, from the letters of the throat and chest, except one letter which He did not mention, which is the khā'. And He did not mention from the other category, from the letters of the lips, except one letter which He did not leave out, which is the mīm. From the ten middle letters, He mentioned one and left out one: He mentioned the rā' and left out the zāy; He mentioned the sīn and left out the shīn; He mentioned the ṣād and left out the ḍād; He mentioned the ṭā' and left out the ẓā'; He mentioned the 'ayn and left out the ghayn. This is not something that occurs by coincidence, but is a deliberate arrangement, and therefore it is for a wisdom. As for the fact that their specific meaning is not known, this is evident. Suppose that someone claims to know something about them: what would he say about the fact that some surahs begin with one letter, such as the surahs of Nūn, Qāf and Ṣād;

some with two letters, such as the surahs of Ḥā' Mīm, Yā' Sīn, Ṭā' Sīn and Ṭā' Hā';

some with three letters, such as the surahs of Alif Lām Mīm, Ṭā' Sīn Mīm and Alif Lām Rā';

some with four letters, such as the two surahs of Alif Lām Mīm Rā' and Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād;

and some with five letters, such as the two surahs of Ḥā' Mīm 'Ayn Sīn Qāf and Kāf Hā' Yā' 'Ayn Ṣād.

Suppose someone says: this is an indication that speech is either a particle (ḥarf), or a verb (fi'l), or a noun (ism). The particle often comes as a single letter, like the wāw of conjunction, the fā' of sequence, the hamzah of interrogation, the kāf of comparison, the bā' of attachment, and others.

It comes as two letters, like man for partitive, aw for option, am for the medial interrogative, an for the conditional, and others.

The noun, the verb and the particle come as three letters, like ilā and 'alā as particles, and ilā and 'alā as nouns; and alā yā'lū and 'alā ya'lū as verbs. The noun and the verb come as four letters, and the noun alone comes as three, four and five letters, like fujl, sujl and jirdaḥl. So what has come in the Qur'an is an indication that the composition of the Arabic language is from these letters in these ways. Then what would this speaker say about the restriction of some surahs to a single letter and others to more than that? No one knows the full secret except Allah and whomever Allah has informed of it.

When you know this, we say: know that worship (ʿibādah) is of three kinds: heart-based (qalbiyyah), tongue-based (lisāniyyah) and bodily (jārihiyyah). Each of these has two types: a type whose meaning and reality are understood, and a type that is not understood. As for the heart-based worship, although it is further from doubt and ignorance, there are in it things whose evidence is not known by reason, and it is obligatory to believe in them and accept them on the basis of revelation (samʿ), such as the bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), which is thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword, over which the believer and the certain one pass like a flash of lightning; and the scale by which deeds are weighed, which have no weight in the eyes of the observer; and the modes of Paradise and Hell. The existence of these things is not known by rational proof; what is known by reason is their possibility, while their occurrence is known with certainty through revelation. Among them are things that are known, such as monotheism (tawḥīd), prophethood (nubuwwah), the power of Allah and the truthfulness of the Messenger.

Likewise, in bodily worship, there are things whose meaning is known and things that are not known, such as the measures of the niṣāb (the minimum thresholds for zakāt) and the number of rak'ahs. We have already mentioned the wisdom in this, which is that when the servant performs what he has been commanded without knowing its benefit, he is performing pure worship, unlike when he knows the benefit, for then he may perform it for the benefit, even if he does not believe. This is like when a master says to his servant: "Move these stones from here," without informing him of the purpose of moving them, and he moves them; but if he said: "Move them, for beneath them is a treasure which is yours," he would move them even if he did not believe. When this is known, likewise in tongue-based, verbal worship, it must be that there is among it what its meaning is not understood, so that when the servant speaks it, it is known from him that he intends nothing but submission to the command of the Worshipped One, the Commander and Forbidder. Thus, when he says ﴿Ha Mim﴾, ﴿Ya Sin﴾, ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾, ﴿Ta Sin﴾, it is known that he did not mention that for a meaning he understands or that is made understood to him; rather, he pronounces it in fulfilment of what he has been commanded.

**The second discussion:** It has been said regarding Yā' Sīn specifically that it is a phrase which is a vocative (nidā'), meaning "O human being" (yā insān). Its explanation is that the diminutive of insān is unaysīn, so it is as if he removed the first part of it and took the last part and said ﴿Yā Sin﴾, meaning "O Unaysīn." On this view, it is possible that the address is to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and this is indicated by His saying after it: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾.

**The third discussion:** Yā' Sīn has been read as follows: with a ḍammah (ḍamm) as a nominative (marfū') on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, which is the word "this," as if he said: "This is Yā' Sīn"; or with a ḍammah on the basis of addressing a singular (nidā' al-mufrad), or on the basis that it is indeclinable (mabnī) like ḥaythu. It has been read with a naṣb (accusative) on the meaning "recite Yā' Sīn," or with a fatḥah like ayna and kayfa, or with a kasrah like jīr, due to the sukūn of the yā' and the kasrah of the letter before it. It is not permissible to say it is in the genitive (majrūr), because omitting (idmār) the genitive particle is not permissible, and there is no apparent oath particle in it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom﴾, it means "possessing wisdom," like the phrase "a pleasing life," meaning "possessing pleasure"; or it means that it speaks with wisdom, so it is like a living thing that speaks.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 36, verse 3:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ is the object of an oath, and concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The disbelievers denied that Muhammad was a messenger, and claims are established by proof, not by oath. So what is the wisdom in swearing? We say that there are several explanations.

The first: The Arabs used to avoid false oaths (*yamin fajira*, "a false oath"). They used to say that a false oath brings about the ruin of the world. The Prophet ﷺ confirmed this by saying: "A false oath leaves the dwellings desolate." Then they used to say that the Prophet ﷺ would be afflicted with punishment from their gods, which were the stars. The Prophet ﷺ would swear by the command of God, by the sending down of His speech to him, and by various other things, yet no punishment befell him. Rather, each day he grew higher in rank and more secure in position. This would lead to the belief that he was not a liar.

The second: When two debaters engage in speech, and one of them overcomes the other by advancing his argument and silences him, the one who is refuted says: "You established this by the strength of your disputation, while you know well the weakness of your position, and you know that the matter is not as you say, even if you present the form of a proof and I am unable to refute it." This frequently occurs between debaters. At this point, the one who has been silenced cannot bring another proof, because the silenced one would say about the other proof what he said about the first, and so he finds nothing but the oath. He says: "By God, I am not being obstinate, and the matter is as I have described. Had I known otherwise, I would have returned to it." Here the oath becomes necessary. Likewise, when the Prophet ﷺ presented the proofs, and the disbelievers said: ﴿This is only a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers worshipped﴾ (Saba': 43), and ﴿Those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "This is nothing but evident magic"﴾ (Saba': 43), it became necessary to hold fast to oaths, since proof was of no benefit.

The third: This is not merely an oath, but rather a proof that has come in the form of an oath. The Qur'an is a miracle, and the proof that he is a messenger is the miracle, and the Qur'an is such. If it is said: "Why was it not presented in the form of a proof? What is the wisdom in presenting the proof in the form of an oath?" We reply: The proof, when presented in the form of an oath, may not be attended to by the listener, so his heart does not accept it. But when it begins with the form of an oath, and an oath is not made, especially by the Most High, concerning a great matter, then great matters draw people's attention to listen to it. Thus, by the form of an oath, bodies stretch out toward it, and because it is a conclusive proof, the heart absorbs it, so it reaches the hearing and benefits the heart.

**The second issue:** The Qur'an being wisdom in their eyes is due to Muhammad being a messenger, so they may say: "This is not an oath." We reply: The answer to this is in two respects.

The first: That the Qur'an being a miracle is clear. If they deny it, it is said to them: "Then bring a surah like it."

The second: A rational person does not trust another's oath unless he swears by something whose greatness is believed in. So if the disbeliever swears by Muhammad, we do not believe him as we would believe him if he swore by the cross or the idol. And if he swore by our true religion, he would not be trusted in the same way as he would be trusted if he swore by his false religion. It is known that the Prophet ﷺ and his companions glorify the Qur'an, so his swearing by it is what makes them trust him.

Allah's saying: ﴿upon a straight path﴾ is a predicate following a predicate; that is, you are upon a straight path. The straight (mustaqim) is the nearest of the ways leading to the goal and the religion. Likewise, he turned toward Allah the Exalted and turned away from others, and the goal is Allah. The one who turns toward the goal is nearer to Him than the one who turns away from Him and deviates from Him. No one's understanding goes to the idea that His saying "Indeed you are upon a straight path" distinguishes him from others, just as one says "Muhammad is chosen among mankind," because all the messengers are upon a straight path. Rather, the intended meaning is to explain that the Prophet ﷺ is upon the straight path upon which the messengers were. His saying ﴿upon a straight path﴾ contains a subtle meaning from which the corruption of the Mubahiyya (antinomians) is known, those who say: the one bound by the law (mukallaf) becomes one who has arrived at the Truth, so no obligation remains upon him. This is because Allah has made clear that the messengers, as long as they were in this world, were travelling, journeying, guided, and walking along the straight path. So how about that ignorant, incapable one?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 36, verse 6:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Revelation of the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾. It is read in the genitive (bi'l-jarr), on the basis that it is a substitute (badal) for "the Qur'an", as if he had said: (By the Qur'an, the Wise, the revelation of the Almighty, the Most Merciful, that you are indeed among the messengers, to warn). It is also read in the accusative (bi'l-nasb), and in this there are two possibilities:

The first: that it is a verbal noun (masdar) whose verb is implied, as if he had said: "It was sent down as a revelation of the Almighty, the Most Merciful, so that you may warn", and its estimated meaning is: "The Qur'an, or the Wise Book, was sent down."

The second: that it is an object (maf'ul) of an implied verb, as if he had said: (By the Wise Qur'an, I mean the revelation of the Almighty, the Most Merciful, that you are indeed among the messengers, to warn). This is what al-Zamakhshari chose.

It is also read in the nominative (bi'l-raf'), on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of an implied subject (mubtada'), as if he had said: "This is the revelation of the Almighty, the Most Merciful, so that you may warn." It may bear another possibility on this reading, namely that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is (li-tundhira, "so that you may warn"), as if he had said: "The revelation of the Almighty is for warning." His saying: ﴿the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾ indicates that when a king sends a messenger, the people to whom he is sent will either oppose the sender and humiliate the messenger, in which case the king cannot take vengeance on them except if he is almighty (ʿazīz); or they will fear the sender and honour the messenger, in which case the king shows mercy to them. Or we may say: the messenger, in his mission, has with him a prohibition against certain things and a permission regarding certain things; the prohibition affirms might (ʿizza), and the permission indicates mercy (raḥma).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾.

Its explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿So that you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you﴾ (al-Qasas: 46). It has also been said that the intended meaning is affirmation (al-ithbat), and this is on two bases:

The first: "so that you may warn a people whose forefathers were warned," so that (ma) is verbal (maṣdariyya).

The second: that it is relative (mawsula); its meaning: "so that you may warn a people, those whose forefathers were warned, so they are heedless." According to our view that (ma) is negating (nafiya), its explanation is clear, for whoever whose forefathers were not warned, and the warning is far from him, he is heedless. According to our view that it is for affirmation, it is likewise, because its meaning is: "so that you may warn them with the warning of their forefathers, for they are heedless." Regarding this there are issues:

First issue: How can the two explanations be understood, when one requires that their forefathers were not warned, and the other requires that they were warned, and between them there is contradiction? We say: according to our view that (ma) is negating, its meaning is "whose forefathers were not warned", and the warning of their earliest forefathers does not contradict that the earlier of their forefathers were warned while the later of them were not warned.

Second issue: His saying: ﴿so that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾ requires that the Prophet ﷺ was not commanded to warn the Jews, because their forefathers were warned. We say: this is not so. As for our view that (ma) is for affirmation and not for negation, it is evident; and as for our view that it is negating, it is likewise, and we have explained this in His saying: ﴿Nay, it is the truth from your Lord, so that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you﴾ [al-Sajda: 3]. We said there that the intended meaning is that their forefathers were warned after their misguidance and after the sending of those who preceded. For when God sends a messenger, as long as there remains among the people someone who explains that prophet's religion and commands it, the messenger is not sent in most matters; but when no one remains among them who explains it, and all go astray, the covenant grows distant, and disbelief spreads, He sends another messenger confirming the religion of him who came before, or laying down another law. Thus the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾ is: those whose forefathers were not warned after they had strayed from the path of the earlier messenger. The Jews and Christians are included in this, because their nearer forefathers were not warned after they had gone astray. This is evidence that the Prophet ﷺ was sent with the truth to all creation.

Third issue: His saying: ﴿so they are heedless﴾ is evidence that sending a messenger occurs only in a state of heedlessness. As for if they come to have knowledge of what God has sent down, such that among them there is someone who conveys to them a law and they oppose him, then destruction is justly due to them; and this would not be punishment before God sends a messenger. Likewise, whoever opposes matters that do not require the explanation of the messengers deserves destruction without a sending. This is not a statement according to the Mu'tazila doctrine of rational goodness and badness (al-tahsin wa'l-taqbih al-'aqli); rather its meaning is that if God, the Exalted, had created in a people knowledge of the obligation of things and they abandoned it, they would not be heedless, and so their punishment does not depend upon the sending of messengers.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Certainly the Word has come into effect against most of them, so they do not believe﴾.

When He explained that the sending or the revelation is for warning, He indicated that the Prophet ﷺ does not bear the guidance that necessitates being guided; rather, upon him is only the warning, and many of those warned will not believe. Regarding His statement, exalted is He, ﴿the Word has come into effect﴾, there are several aspects:

The first, which is the well-known view, is that the intended "Word" is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I speak: "I will certainly fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you"﴾ [Sad: 85].

The second is that its meaning is: it had already been decreed in His knowledge that this one would believe and that this one would not believe. So He said concerning some: "he will not believe," and said concerning others: "he will believe." Thus ﴿the Word has come into effect﴾, meaning it came to exist and was established in such a way that it cannot be changed.

The third is that it may be said: the intended meaning is that the Word which Allah spoke through the tongue of the Messengers, concerning monotheism and other matters, has come into effect and its proof has become clear; so most of them do not believe after that. This is because one who hesitates to hear the evidence during the period of reflection is hoped to believe once the proof becomes clear to him. When it is established and confirmed, and most of them still do not believe, it becomes evident that they will not believe, since the time for hoping for faith has passed. Also, because they did not believe when the Word came into effect and persisted, so if they wanted something clearer than the proof, it would be direct witnessing (al-iyan), and at the time of direct witnessing, faith is of no benefit.

As for His statement, ﴿against most of them﴾, according to this aspect its meaning is that those to whom the call and the proof did not reach are few; so the Word has come into effect against most of those in whom faith was not found. As for the first and second aspects, it is clear, for most of the disbelievers died in disbelief and did not believe.

There is also an aspect, which is that it may be said: the word of the immediate punishment has come into effect against most of them, so they do not believe, and this is close to the first.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles on their necks, and they reach up to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾

When He had explained that they do not believe, He explained that this is from God. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾. In this there are several interpretations (wujuh):

The first: the intended meaning is that We have made them restrained, not spending in the way of God, as He said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ (al-Isra' 29).

The second: the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and his two companions from the Makhzum clan, when "Abu Jahl swore that he would crush the head of Muhammad. He saw him prostrating, so he took a rock and raised it to drop it on his head, but it stuck to his hand, and his hand to his neck."

The third, which is the strongest and most fitting with what preceded, is that this is a metaphor (kinaya) for God's preventing them from being guided. Concerning it there are several issues:

First issue: Are the first two interpretations connected with what came before? We say: The first interpretation has a connection, namely that His saying ﴿so they do not believe﴾ includes that they do not pray, as He said: ﴿And God would not let your faith (iman) go to waste﴾ (al-Baqarah 143), meaning your prayer (salat), according to some exegetes. Zakat is related to prayer as we have explained, so it is as if He said: they do not pray and do not give zakat. As for the second interpretation, the connection is subtle: when He said: ﴿Certainly the word has come to pass upon most of them﴾, and we mentioned that the intended meaning of it is the proof (burhan), He said after that: "Rather, they witnessed and saw what is close to necessity, when his hand stuck to his neck and he was prevented from releasing the stone, and he is compelled to faith but did not believe," so He knew that he will not believe at all. The explanation is the third interpretation.

Second issue: To what does ﴿fa-hiya﴾ refer? We say: there are two views:

One: it refers to the hands, though they are not mentioned, but they are understood, since the one who is shackled has his hands gathered together in the shackle to his neck.

Second: and this is what al-Zamakhshari chose, it refers to the shackles. The meaning: We have placed on their necks shackles, heavy and thick, such that they reach the chins, so the one shackled cannot lower his head with them.

Third issue: How is the prevention from faith understood from the shackle on the neck, so that it becomes a metaphor? We say: The shackled one whose shackle has reached his chin, and who remains raising his head, cannot see the path that is at his feet. He then mentioned that before them is a barrier and behind them a barrier, so he cannot be capable of following the way or seeing it. It was mentioned earlier that the one sent is upon a straight path, so this one whom the Prophet guides to the intellectual straight path is made prevented, like the shackled one who is made prevented from seeing the sensory path. It may also bear another meaning, namely that it is said: shackles on the necks are an expression for non-submission, for the one who submits is described as having placed his head upon the line and his neck humbled, whereas the one on whose neck is a thick shackle reaching the chin does not lower his head nor move it in the manner of one who affirms. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿muqmahun﴾, for the muqmah is the one who raises his head in aversion; it is said: a camel is qamih when it raises its head and does not drink water nor lowers it to drink. Faith is like pure water by which there is life, and it is as if He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles on their necks, and they reach up to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised﴾, not submitting their necks to the command of God.

On this basis, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and covered them so they cannot see﴾ [36:9]

completes the meaning of God's making them shackled [36:8]. For His saying, ﴿We have placed before them a barrier﴾, indicates that they do not follow the path of right guidance. It is as if He said: they do not see the truth so as to submit to it, because of the barrier, and they do not submit to you so as to see the truth and submit to it, because of the shackle and the faith that brings about certainty.

Either by following the Messenger first, so that the realities become clear to them afterward, or by the matters becoming manifest first and then following the Messenger second. They do not follow the Messenger first, because they are shackled, so the truth does not become manifest to them from the Messenger second. And the truth does not become manifest to them first, because they are caught in the barrier, so they do not follow the Messenger second.

There is another aspect to this, which is to say: the obstruction is either within the self or outside of it, and they have both obstructions from faith. Within the self is the shackle, and from outside is the barrier. Their gaze does not fall upon themselves, so they do not see the signs that are within themselves, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾ (Fussilat: 53). This is because the one with raised head (al-muqmah) does not see himself, and his gaze does not fall on his hands. Their gaze also does not fall upon the horizons, because those between the two barriers do not see the horizons, so the signs that are on the horizons do not become clear to them. On this basis, His saying: ﴿Indeed We have placed shackles on their necks﴾ and ﴿We have placed before them﴾ indicates their failure to be guided by the signs of God within the selves and on the horizons.

Concerning the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have placed before them a barrier﴾, there are several issues:

[Page 41]

The first issue: mentioning the barrier before them has an evident benefit, since they are travelers in this world and should follow the straight path, and ﴿a barrier before them﴾ means they cannot travel. As for the barrier behind them, what is its benefit? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects.

The first: a human being has innate guidance (hidayah fitriyyah), and the disbeliever may abandon it, and rational guidance (hidayah nazariyyah), and the disbeliever has not attained it. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿We have placed before them a barrier﴾, so they do not follow the way of guidance that is rational, ﴿and We have placed behind them a barrier﴾, so they do not return to the natural guidance that is innate.

The second: a human being's origin is from God and his destiny is to Him. The blindness of the disbeliever does not see what lies before him of the return to God, nor what lies behind him of entering existence by the creation of God.

The third: when a traveler has no choice but to take a road, if the road ahead of him is blocked, he loses his destination, but he can turn back. But if the road behind him and ahead of him are both blocked, the place where he is becomes no place to stay, since it is deadly. So His saying: ﴿We have placed before them a barrier and behind them﴾ indicates their destruction.

The second issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and covered them﴾, with the letter fa' (so/then), requires that the covering have a connection to the barrier, and that the covering follow from the placing of the barrier. How is that? We say: that is from two aspects:

One of them: that this is an explanation of matters that follow one another, where some of them are a cause for others. It is as if He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed We have placed shackles on their necks﴾, so they do not see themselves because of their raised heads, ﴿and We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier﴾, so they do not see what is on the horizons. Then it is possible that they could see the sky and what is on their right and left, so after all this He said: ﴿And over their eyes is a covering﴾ (al-Baqarah: 7), so they see nothing at all.

The second of them: this is an explanation that the barrier is close to them, to the extent that it becomes like a covering over their eyes. For whoever has a barrier placed behind him and before him, adjoining him, such that between them there is a space adjoining both, his eye remains on the surface of the barrier, so he sees nothing. As for what is other than the barrier, it is due to the screen, and as for the surface of the barrier itself, it is because the condition for visibility is that the object not be very close to the eye.

The third issue: He mentioned the two barriers, before them and behind, and did not mention the right and the left. What is the wisdom in this? We say: as for our view that it indicates the innate and rational guidance, it is evident. As for other than that, we say that by what has been mentioned there is generality and prevention from following the straight paths, because if they intend to travel toward the right side or the left side, they become oriented toward something and turned away from something, so what they face becomes what is before them, and God places the barrier there, preventing them from traveling. Thus, wherever the disbeliever turns, God places a barrier before him.

Another aspect, better than what we have mentioned: when we explained that the placing of the barrier became a cause of covering, the barrier was adjacent to him, and he is adjacent to the two barriers, so he has no ability to move to the right or the left. Therefore there is no need for a barrier on the right or on the left. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We covered them, so they cannot see﴾, may mean what we have mentioned, that they do not see anything. It may also mean that the disbeliever is blocked, and the path of truth is closed to him, and he does not see the barrier nor know the obstruction, so he thinks he is on the straight path and not astray.

Then He, may He be exalted, made clear that warning does not benefit them, given what God has done to them of shackling, barrier, covering and blindness, by His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ (Ya-Sin: 10). That is, warning and its absence are equal with respect to their faith, since it does not exist in them under either circumstance. If it is said: if warning and its absence are the same, then why warning? We say: we have answered in other places that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It is the same for them﴾ and did not say: ﴿It is the same for you﴾. So warning in relation to the Prophet (ﷺ) is like not warning, because one of them releases him from responsibility, and is a cause of increase in his nobility in this world and his happiness in the next. As for their situation, it is the same, since the Prophet's (ﷺ) warning is so that they may depart from what they are upon and attain the reward of warning, even if they do not benefit from it, because of the perdition written for them in the abode of settlement.

On this basis, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and covered them so they cannot see﴾ [36:9]

completes the meaning of God's making them shackled [36:8]. For His saying, ﴿We have placed before them a barrier﴾, indicates that they do not follow the path of right guidance. It is as if He said: they do not see the truth so as to submit to it, because of the barrier, and they do not submit to you so as to see the truth and submit to it, because of the shackle and the faith that brings about certainty.

Either by following the Messenger first, so that the realities become clear to them afterward, or by the matters becoming manifest first and then following the Messenger second. They do not follow the Messenger first, because they are shackled, so the truth does not become manifest to them from the Messenger second. And the truth does not become manifest to them first, because they are caught in the barrier, so they do not follow the Messenger second.

There is another aspect to this, which is to say: the obstruction is either within the self or outside of it, and they have both obstructions from faith. Within the self is the shackle, and from outside is the barrier. Their gaze does not fall upon themselves, so they do not see the signs that are within themselves, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾ (Fussilat: 53). On this basis, His saying: ﴿Indeed We have placed shackles on their necks﴾ and ﴿We have placed before them﴾ indicates their failure to be guided by the signs of God within the selves and on the horizons.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful in the unseen. So give them good news of forgiveness and a generous reward.﴾ The sequence is clear. In the exegesis (tafsir) there are several issues.

The first issue: He said earlier, ﴿that you may warn﴾ (al-Sajdah: 3), and that implies general warning, as we have explained. Here He said, ﴿You can only warn﴾, which implies restriction. How can the two be reconciled? We say there are several ways.

The first: His words ﴿that you may warn﴾ (al-Sajdah: 3) mean warning in any case, whether it is beneficial or not. His words ﴿You can only warn﴾ mean that beneficial warning applies only to those who follow the Reminder and fear God.

The second: When God said that sending messengers and sending down revelation, and warning or not warning, are equal with regard to the people of obstinacy, He told His Prophet: your warning is not useless in every respect. So warn in general terms. You can only warn with that general warning those who follow the Reminder. It is as if He is saying: O Muhammad, by your warning you guide, though you do not know whom you guide. So warn the black and the red, while your real aim is those who follow your warning and benefit from your reminder.

The third: We say that His words ﴿that you may warn﴾ refer to the initial stage. When you have warned, exerted yourself, and conveyed the message, and some mock, turn away, grow arrogant, and withdraw, then turn away after that. ﴿You can only warn﴾ those who have followed you.

The fourth, which is close to the third: You warn everyone about the fundamentals, but you warn about the branches, such as neglecting prayer and zakat, only those who follow the Reminder and believe.

The second issue: His words ﴿who follows the Reminder﴾ may have several meanings.

The first, which is the well-known one: who follows the Qur'an.

The second: who follows what is in the Qur'an of verses. This is supported by His words, ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ (Sad: 1), since He did not make the Qur'an identical with the Reminder.

The third: who follows the proof, for it is a reminder that perfects the natural disposition (fitrah). In every case the meaning is: you can only warn the scholars who fear. This is like His words, ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ (Fatir: 28), and His words, ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (al-Ankabut: 9). So His words ﴿follows the Reminder﴾ mean believes, and His words ﴿fears the Most Merciful﴾ mean does righteous deeds. This meaning is confirmed by His words, ﴿give them good news of forgiveness and a generous reward﴾, because we have mentioned repeatedly that forgiveness is the reward of faith, so every believer is forgiven, while the generous reward is the reward of action, as He said: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and generous provision﴾ (Saba': 4). Explaining the Reminder as the Qur'an is supported by the definite article in "the Reminder," and the Qur'an was already mentioned in His words, ﴿By the wise Qur'an﴾. As for His words ﴿fears the Most Merciful﴾, there is a subtle point in it: mercy produces reliance and hope. So He said, even though He is the Most Merciful and the Most Compassionate, the intelligent person should not abandon fear, for whoever's blessings come more through His mercy, fear of Him is more complete, lest He cut off the continuous blessings. The completion of this subtle point is that among God's names are two that belong to Him alone: Allah and al-Rahman, as He said, ﴿Say: call upon Allah, or call upon al-Rahman﴾ (al-Isra': 110). Some of the imams even said that they are both proper names. Once you know this, Allah is a name that indicates awe, and al-Rahman indicates tenderness. In one place He said, ﴿hoping for Allah﴾, and here He said, ﴿fears the Most Merciful﴾, meaning: although He is possessed of awe, do not cut off your hope in Him, and although He is possessed of mercy, do not feel secure from Him.

His words ﴿in the unseen﴾ mean by evidence, even if one has not reached the level of what is seen and witnessed, for when one reaches that level, fear no longer has any benefit. The well-known view is that the unseen means what is hidden from us, namely the conditions of the Resurrection. It has also been said that the Oneness of God is included in it.

[Page 43]

His words ﴿so give them good news﴾ indicate the second of the two matters of prophethood, for the Prophet ﷺ is a bringer of good news and a warner. He mentioned that he was sent to warn, and that beneficial warning comes with following the Reminder. So He said: give good news just as you warned and benefited. His words ﴿of forgiveness﴾ are indefinite, meaning a forgiveness that is wide and covers from all sides, so that no trace of the self's effects is seen on the person, and the lights of the pure spirit appear upon him. ﴿And a generous reward﴾ means a reward possessing generosity. We have already discussed the meaning of "generous" in His words, ﴿and generous provision﴾ (Saba': 4), and in His words, ﴿a generous provision﴾ (al-Ahzab: 31).

[Page 44]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces, and We have enumerated all things in a clear register.﴾

On the order (of the verses), there are several explanations.

First: When God explained the Message (al-risalah), which is one of the three foundations (al-usul al-thalathah) by which a person becomes a believer and a Muslim, He mentioned another foundation, which is the Resurrection (al-hashr).

Second: When God mentioned warning and glad tidings with His words, ﴿so give him good news of forgiveness﴾, and this was not fully manifest in this world, He said: if it is not seen in this world, then God brings the dead to life and recompenses the warners and recompenses the bearers of glad tidings.

Third: When God mentioned the fear of the Most Merciful in the unseen (khashyat al-Rahman bil-ghayb), He mentioned what confirms it, which is the bringing of the dead to life. In the interpretation, there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿Indeed, We⁠﴾ (inna nahnu) may have two possibilities:

One: that it is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar), like the saying of the speaker:

*I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is (my) poetry.*

Such a statement is made when one has great fame, because the one who is not known is asked, "Who are you?" and he answers, "I am the son of so-and-so," and so he is recognized. But the one who is famous, when asked, "Who are you?" says, "I am," meaning: there is no identifier for me more manifest than myself. So He said: "Indeed, We (nahnu)" are known by the attributes of perfection, and when We are made known by Ourselves, then do not deny Our power to bring the dead to life.

Two: that the predicate is ﴿We bring to life⁠﴾ (nuhyi), as if He had said: "Indeed, We bring the dead to life," and ﴿We⁠﴾ (nahnu) is for emphasis. The first is preferable.

The second issue: (inna nahnu) contains an indication of Divine Oneness (al-tawhid), because sharing (al-ishtirak) requires distinction by other than the self. For example, if Zayd shares his name with another, and he were to say, "I am Zayd," the complete identification would not be achieved, because the listener may say, "Which Zayd?" and he answers, "The son of Amr." But if there were another Zayd whose father is also Amr, then his saying "the son of Amr" would not suffice. So when God said, "Indeed, We⁠﴾ (inna nahnu), meaning: there is no one other than Us who shares with Us, so that we would have to say, "We are such-and-such" in order to be distinguished. At that point, the three foundations are all mentioned: the Message, the Oneness (of God), and the Resurrection.

The third issue: His words, ﴿and We record what they have sent forward⁠﴾ (wa naktubu ma qaddamu), contain several explanations:

One: the intended meaning is "what they sent forward and what they left behind" (ma qaddamu wa akhkharu), and He suffices by mentioning one of them, as in His words, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat⁠﴾ (Al-Nahl: 81), where the intended meaning also includes the cold.

Two: the meaning is the deeds they sent forward in advance, whether righteous or corrupt. This is like His words, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forward⁠﴾ (Al-Rum: 36), meaning: because of what they brought into existence before others and caused to exist.

Three: "We record their intentions (niyyat), for they precede the deeds," and "their traces" means their deeds, according to this explanation.

The fourth issue: "and their traces" (wa athararahum) has several explanations:

The first: "their traces" means their footsteps. A group of his Companions lived far from the mosques, so they wished to move closer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, God records your steps and rewards you for them, so remain in your houses."

The second: they are the good traditions (sunan hasanah), such as written books, built bridges, and continuous endowments (habais), and the evil traditions (sunan sayyi'ah), such as the continuous oppressions established by a tyrant, misleading books, and instruments of amusement and instruments of prohibited things that remain in use. This is in the meaning of his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever establishes a good tradition, he has its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it, without any reduction from the reward of the doer. And whoever establishes an evil tradition, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it." So "what they sent forward" is their actions, and "their traces" are the actions of those who give thanks. So give them good news (fa-bashshirhum) where they are held accountable for them and rewarded for them.

The third: what we mentioned, that "the traces" are the deeds and "what they sent forward" are the intentions, since the intention precedes the deed.

The fifth issue: The recording is before the bringing to life. So why did He place the mention in this order, saying "We bring to life and We record," and did not say, "We record what they sent forward and bring them to life"? We say: the recording magnifies the matter of bringing to life, because if bringing to life were not for the reckoning, it would not be magnified; and if recording in itself were not a bringing to life and a returning, it would have no effect at all. So bringing to life is what is considered, and recording is an emphasis that magnifies its matter. Therefore bringing to life was placed first. Also, because when He said, ﴿Indeed, We⁠﴾, this conveys majesty and sovereignty, and bringing to life is a great matter that belongs exclusively to God, while recording is less than that. So He joined to the definition (of Divine majesty) the great matter, and mentioned what magnifies that great matter.

His words, ﴿and We have enumerated all things in a clear register⁠﴾ (wa kulla shay'in ahsaynahu fi imamin mubin), may have several meanings:

One: this is an explanation that what they sent forward and their traces is a matter written upon them that cannot be changed, for the pen has dried with what is to be. So when He said, ﴿and We record what they sent forward⁠﴾, He clarified that before that there is another writing: God wrote upon them that they would do such and such, and then when they do it, it is written upon them that they did it.

Two: this is a confirmation of the meaning of His words, ﴿and We record⁠﴾, because one who writes something on sheets and throws them away may not find them, as if he had not written. So He said: We record and We preserve that in a clear register. This is like His words, ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets⁠﴾ (Ta-Ha: 52).

Three: this is a generalization after specification, as if God records what they sent forward and their traces, and the recording is not limited to that; rather, every thing is enumerated in a clear register. This indicates that none of the sayings or actions escapes or is lost to the knowledge of God. This is like His words, ﴿And everything they did is in the Zubur﴾ and ﴿every small and great thing is inscribed⁠﴾ (Al-Qamar: 52), meaning: what is in the Zubur is not confined to what they did; rather, everything they did is written.

His words, ﴿We have enumerated it⁠﴾ (ahsaynahu), are more eloquent than "We wrote it," because one who writes something scattered needs to gather its count; so He said: it is enumerated in it. The Book is called an imam (a leader or guide) because the angels follow it, so whatever is written in it of a term, sustenance, bringing to life, and causing death, they follow. It has also been said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The word imam has come in plural form in His words, ﴿On the day We will call every people with their imam⁠﴾ (Al-Isra': 71), meaning with their leaders. Accordingly, imam, when singular, is like kitab (book) and hijab (veil); and when plural, it is like jibal (mountains) and hibal (ropes). The mubin (clear) is one who makes matters manifest, because it makes manifest to the angels what they do and to people what is done to them. It is also the Distinguisher, who separates between the conditions of creation, so that it places one group in Paradise and another group in the Blaze.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And present to them the example of the people of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾

On this there are two views, and the arrangement is clear under both views.

The first view is that the meaning is: present a parable on their behalf.

The second is that the meaning is: present, for your own sake, the people of the town as a parable for them, that is, liken them in your own mind to the people of the town.

On the first view, we say: when God said, ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ (46:9), and said, ﴿so that you may warn﴾ (32:3), He said: Say to them: ﴿I am not an innovation among the messengers﴾ (46:9). Rather, a little before me, messengers came to the people of the town, and they warned them with what I have warned you about, mentioned monotheism, warned of the Resurrection, and gave good news of the bliss of the abode of permanence.

On the second view, we say: when God Almighty said that warning does not benefit those whom God has led astray and whom He has decreed will not believe, He said to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿So do not grieve, and present to yourself and to your people a parable﴾, that is, liken them in your own mind to a parable in which three messengers came to them and they did not believe, and the messengers endured killing and harm. You came to them alone, and your people are more numerous than the people of the three. They came to a single town, but you were sent to the whole world.

In the interpretation there are several issues.

The first issue: What is the meaning of the saying "he struck a parable" (ḍaraba mathalan)? And of His words, ﴿and present﴾ (wa-ḍrib), given that in the language ḍarb (striking) means either the touching of one body against another with force, or travelling when it is followed by the particle fī, as in His words: ﴿And when you travel in the land﴾ (4:101)? We say: His words "he struck a parable" mean: "he made a parable", because ḍarb is a term for a kind (nawʿ). It is said: "These things are of one kind (ḍarb wāḥid)", that is, consider this and that to be of one kind.

The second issue: "the people of the town" means: present to them a parable like the people of the town. So the parable is omitted and "the people" is placed in its position in i'rab (grammatical case), as in His words: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (12:82). This is the view of al-Zamakhshari in his Kashshaf. It is possible to say that there is no need for an elided element; rather the meaning is: make the people of the town a parable for them, or liken the people of the town to them.

The third issue: "when the messengers came to it." The word idh (when) is in the accusative because it is in apposition (badal) to "the people of the town", as if He had said: "Present to them" at the time the messengers came, and liken that time to the time of your own coming. This too is the view of al-Zamakhshari. According to our view, that this parable is struck for the very person of Muhammad (ﷺ) as consolation, it is possible to say that idh is an adverbial accusative (ẓarf) governed by the verb "present" (iḍrib), meaning: make the striking take place at the time when they came and it occurred in it. The town was Antioch, and the messengers were from the people of Jesus, and they were the nearest messengers sent to a people before the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). They were three, as God Most High has made clear.

His words ﴿when We sent﴾ (idh arsalnā) may bear two meanings:

One is that "when We sent" is in apposition to "when they came to it", as if He had said: present to them a parable, when We sent to the people of the town two.

The second, which is the more correct and the clearer, is that idh is an adverbial accusative and the verb governed by it is "came to it", meaning: the messengers came to it at the time when We sent them to it. That is, their coming was not on their own initiative; rather they came because they were commanded to. In this there is a subtle point: the account says that the messengers were sent by Jesus, peace be upon him, who dispatched them to Antioch. God Most High says: the sending by Jesus, peace be upon him, is Our sending, and the messenger of a messenger of God by God's permission is a messenger of God. So let it not occur to you, O Muhammad, that those people were the messenger of a messenger while you are the messenger of God. Their denial is like your denial, and thus the consolation is complete through His words ﴿when We sent﴾.

This supports a legal question: that the agent of an agent (wakīl al-wakīl), acting with the permission of the principal (muwakkil), is the agent of the principal, not the agent of the agent, so that he is not dismissed by the dismissal of the first agent, but he is dismissed when the first principal dismisses him. And on our view, that God's words ﴿and present to them a parable﴾ concern the striking of a parable for the sake of Muhammad (ﷺ), this is evident.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 36, verses 14–16:

And His saying: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them both﴾

There is a profound wisdom in the sending of two, namely that they were sent on behalf of ʿIsa (Jesus) by the permission of God. It was incumbent upon them to convey the matter to ʿIsa and to bring what God had commanded. God knows everything and has no need of a witness who testifies before Him, whereas ʿIsa is a human being, so God commanded him to send two, so that their word against their people would be a complete proof before ʿIsa.

And His saying: ﴿So We strengthened [them] with a third﴾, meaning, We strengthened. It is also read fa-ʿazzaznā bi-thālithin (with the letter zāy lightened), from ʿazza, meaning to overpower; as if He said: "We overpowered and subdued with a third." The first reading is more evident and more well-known. The object is omitted where He did not say "fa-ʿazzaznāhumā" (We strengthened them both), for a subtle meaning: the purpose of sending them was the support of the truth, not their own support, and all of them strengthen the firm religion with the clear proof. And in this there are issues:

The first issue: The Prophet ﷺ sent his messengers to the regions and was content with one, whereas ʿIsa (peace be upon him) sent two. We say: the Prophet sent them to establish the branches (furuʿ) of the law, which is less than the foundations (usul), so he was content with one, for the report of a single narrator is accepted in the branches. As for these two, they were sent with the foundations, and He made for them a miracle that gives certainty; otherwise sending two would not have sufficed, nor three.

The second issue: God said to Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿We will strengthen your arm﴾ (al-Qasas: 35), and there He mentioned the object, though here He did not mention it, even though the purpose there too was the support of the truth. We say: Musa (peace be upon him) was superior to Harun, and Harun was sent with him at his request, when he said: ﴿So send him with me﴾ (al-Qasas: 34). So Harun was sent to confirm Musa in what he says and to carry out what he commands. As for these two, each one is independent and speaks the truth. So there the purpose was strengthening Musa and sending one who would be a companion to him, namely Harun; whereas here the purpose is strengthening the truth. Thus the difference becomes clear.

Then God explained what took place between them and against them, similar to what took place between Muhammad ﷺ and his people. So they said: ﴿Indeed, we are sent to you﴾, as He said: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 252). He explained what the people said by His saying: ﴿They said: You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing﴾. They made their being human like them a proof of the absence of sending. This is a general statement of the polytheists who said concerning Muhammad: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him?﴾ (Sad: 8). They took it as a proof only on the basis that they did not believe in God's choice, but said of Him that He is an essential cause (mujib bi-l-dhat), and that since they are equal in humanity, preference is impossible. God answered their statement with His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ (al-Anʿam: 124), and with His saying: ﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills﴾ (al-Shura: 13), and other verses.

As for His saying: ﴿nor has the Most Merciful sent down anything﴾, it may bear two meanings:

The first: that it completes what they had mentioned, so that the whole is one single doubt. Its explanation is that they said: "You are human; you did not descend from God, and God did not send down to you anyone. How then have you become messengers of God?"

The second: that this is another independent doubt. Its explanation is that when they said: "You are human like us, so your preference over us is not permissible," they mentioned the doubt from the side of looking at the messengers. Then they said another doubt from the side of the Sender, namely that He, exalted is He, does not send down anything into this world, for His action in the higher world, and for the higher things to act upon the lower things, according to their doctrine, [is the case]. So God has not sent down any of things into this world, so how has He sent down to you? His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ is an indication of refutation of them, for since God is the Merciful of this world, and sending is a mercy, how would He not send down His mercy while He is the Merciful? Thus He said: they said, "The Most Merciful has sent down nothing," and how would the Most Merciful, being merciful, not send down anything? He is the complete mercy.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿You are only lying﴾, meaning: you are only liars.

﴿They said: Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. This is an indication that, by mere denial, they did not grow weary and did not abandon [the matter], but repeated that to them, restated the saying against them, and affirmed it with an oath. And ﴿They said: Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾, and they emphasized it with the lām (of emphasis), because "God knows" functions as an oath, since whoever says "God knows" about what is not the case has attributed ignorance to God, and that is a cause of punishment, just as breaking an oath is its cause. In His saying ﴿Our Lord knows﴾ there is an indication of refutation of them when they said: "You are human." For since God knows that they are indeed sent, it is like His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ (al-Anʿam: 124), meaning, He is knowing of affairs and capable, so He chose us by His knowledge for His message.

When they said, ﴿And upon us is only the conveyance﴾, that required them to reflect on their own affair, since they did not ask them for any wage and did not seek leadership. Their concern was only conveyance and remembrance, and that moves the intelligent person to reflect. The word ﴿al-mubin﴾ (the clear) admits several meanings:

The first: the conveyance that makes the truth clear from falsehood, meaning the one that distinguishes by means of the miracle and the proof.

The second: the conveyance that manifests what We sent for everyone, meaning it is not enough that we convey the message to one person or two.

The third: the conveyance that manifests the truth by every possible means. When that is complete and they still do not accept, then destruction is due upon them.

Their reply after this was that they ﴿said: Indeed we consider you a bad omen﴾. That was because when the Messengers displayed excessive effort in conveying, excess in denial appeared from them. So when the envoys said, ﴿Indeed we are sent to you﴾, they said, ﴿You are only liars﴾. When the Messengers confirmed their statement with an oath, saying, ﴿Our Lord knows﴾, they confirmed their own statement with the claim of bad omen. It is as if they said at first: you are liars, and at second: you have become persistent in lying, swearing and adjuring to it. And [there is] the hadith: "A false oath leaves the abodes desolate." So they said: we consider you a bad omen a second time. In the first case [they had said] "as you have left", so in the second case we will not leave you, because the bad omen has overtaken us through you. Thus they said: ﴿If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment will surely touch you from us﴾. The phrase ﴿we will surely stone you﴾ admits two aspects:

The first: we will revile you, using ﴿rajm﴾ (stoning) in the sense of speech. In this case the phrase ﴿and a painful punishment will touch you﴾ is a progression, as if they said: and he will not be content with reviling, but that will lead to beating and physical pain.

The second: that the intended meaning is stoning with stones. In that case the phrase ﴿and it will touch you﴾ is an explanation of the stoning, meaning: the stoning will not be a little stoning, where we stone you with one stone or two, but we will continue it upon you until death, and that is a painful punishment. The intended meaning would be ﴿we will surely stone you and it will surely touch you﴾, that because of the stoning there is a painful punishment from us. We have mentioned concerning ﴿al-alim﴾ (painful) that it means ﴿al-mu'lim﴾ (causing pain), and that the form ﴿fa'il﴾ in the sense of ﴿mufil﴾ is rare. It may be said that it is of the same type as His saying, ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (al-Haqqah 21), meaning one possessing pleasure, so the painful punishment is one possessing pain. In that case ﴿fa'il﴾ is in the sense of ﴿fa'il﴾ (active), which is common.

Then the Messengers replied to them by saying: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, meaning your ill omen is with you, and that is disbelief.

Then they said: ﴿Even if you are reminded?﴾ as an answer to their statement ﴿we will surely stone you﴾, meaning: will you do that to us, even if you are reminded, that is, the matter has been made clear to you by the miracle and the proof? ﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed the limits﴾, in that you make the one by whom blessing is sought like the one by whom ill omen is taken, and you intend to cause pain to one who is owed honour. Or ﴿musrifun﴾ (exceeding limits) means that you disbelieve, then persist after the truth has become manifest through the miracle and the proof. The disbeliever is a wrongdoer, so when the proof is established against him and the way is made clear to him, and he persists, he becomes a transgressor. The transgressor is one who goes beyond the limit to the point of reaching the opposite. They were like that in many matters: as for seeking blessing and ill omen, this is known; and likewise in causing pain and in honouring. As for disbelief, it is because the obligation is to follow the proof; if no proof is found for it, then at least one should not be certain of its opposite, yet they were certain of disbelief after the proof for faith.

If it is said: ﴿Nay﴾ here is for idrab (a grammatical term meaning a turning away from or retraction of what precedes), then what is the matter that is turned away from? We say: it may be said that His saying, ﴿Even if you are reminded?﴾, is directed at their denial and their attribution of lying to the Messengers through their saying, ﴿You are only liars﴾. It is as if they said: are we liars even if we bring the proof? Nay, ﴿you are a people who exceed the limits﴾. It may also be said: are we ill-omened even if we bring a demonstration of the soundness of what we are upon? Nay, ﴿you are a people who exceed the limits﴾. It may also be said: are we deserving of stoning and pain even if we demonstrate the soundness of what we brought? Nay, ﴿you are a people who exceed the limits﴾.

As for the narrative, it is well known: that Jesus, peace be upon him, sent two men to Antioch, and they called to monotheism and displayed the miracle of healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead. The king imprisoned them. Then he sent Shamʿun after them, and he came to the king without abandoning the message, and he brought himself close to the king through good management. Then he said to him: I hear that in the prison there are two men who claim a wondrous matter. Would they not come so that we may hear their words? The king said: Yes. So they were brought, and they stated their true claim. Shamʿun said to them: Do you have a proof? They said: Yes, so they healed the blind and the leper and raised the dead. Shamʿun said: O king, if you wish to overcome them, then tell the gods that you worship to do something of that kind. The king said: You are not unaware that they do not see, do not hear, are not able, and do not know. Shamʿun said: Then the truth has become manifest on their side. The king and a people believed, and others disbelieved, and the victory was for the deniers.

Then He said: ﴿And upon us is only the clear conveyance﴾. This is a consolation for themselves, meaning: we have discharged what was incumbent upon us, and it is an urging upon them to reflect. The first: the conveyance that makes the truth clear from falsehood, meaning the one that distinguishes by means of the miracle and the proof.

The second: the conveyance that manifests what We sent for everyone, meaning it is not enough that we convey the message to one person or two.

The third: the conveyance that manifests the truth by every possible means. When that is complete and they still do not accept, then destruction is due upon them.

Their reply after this was that they ﴿said: Indeed we consider you a bad omen﴾. That was because when the Messengers displayed excessive effort in conveying, excess in denial appeared from them. So when the envoys said, ﴿Indeed we are sent to you﴾, they said, ﴿You are only liars﴾. When the Messengers confirmed their statement with an oath, saying, ﴿Our Lord knows﴾, they confirmed their own statement with the claim of bad omen. It is as if they said at first: you are liars, and at second: you have become persistent in lying, swearing and adjuring to it. And [there is] the hadith: "A false oath leaves the abodes desolate." So they said: we consider you a bad omen a second time. In the first case [they had said] "as you have left", so in the second case we will not leave you, because the bad omen has overtaken us through you. The first: we will revile you, using ﴿rajm﴾ (stoning) in the sense of speech. In this case the phrase ﴿and a painful punishment will touch you﴾ is a progression, as if they said: and he will not be content with reviling, but that will lead to beating and physical pain.

The second: that the intended meaning is stoning with stones. In that case the phrase ﴿and it will touch you﴾ is an explanation of the stoning, meaning: the stoning will not be a little stoning, where we stone you with one stone or two, but we will continue it upon you until death, and that is a painful punishment. The intended meaning would be ﴿we will surely stone you and it will surely touch you﴾, that because of the stoning there is a painful punishment from us. It may be said that it is of the same type as His saying, ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (al-Haqqah 21), meaning one possessing pleasure, so the painful punishment is one possessing pain. In that case ﴿fa'il﴾ is in the sense of ﴿fa'il﴾ (active), which is common.

Then the Messengers replied to them by saying: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, meaning your ill omen is with you, and that is disbelief.

Or ﴿musrifun﴾ (exceeding limits) means that you disbelieve, then persist after the truth has become manifest through the miracle and the proof. The disbeliever is a wrongdoer, so when the proof is established against him and the way is made clear to him, and he persists, he becomes a transgressor. The transgressor is one who goes beyond the limit to the point of reaching the opposite. They were like that in many matters: as for seeking blessing and ill omen, this is known; and likewise in causing pain and in honouring. As for disbelief, it is because the obligation is to follow the proof; if no proof is found for it, then at least one should not be certain of its opposite, yet they were certain of disbelief after the proof for faith.

If it is said: ﴿Nay﴾ here is for idrab (a grammatical term meaning a turning away from or retraction of what precedes), then what is the matter that is turned away from? We say: it may be said that His saying, ﴿Even if you are reminded?﴾, is directed at their denial and their attribution of lying to the Messengers through their saying, ﴿You are only liars﴾. It may also be said: are we ill-omened even if we bring a demonstration of the soundness of what we are upon? Nay, ﴿you are a people who exceed the limits﴾. It may also be said: are we deserving of stoning and pain even if we demonstrate the soundness of what we brought? Nay, ﴿you are a people who exceed the limits﴾.

Then he said to him: I hear that in the prison there are two men who claim a wondrous matter. Would they not come so that we may hear their words? The king said: Yes. So they were brought, and they stated their true claim. Shamʿun said to them: Do you have a proof? They said: Yes, so they healed the blind and the leper and raised the dead. Shamʿun said: O king, if you wish to overcome them, then tell the gods that you worship to do something of that kind. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man, running. He said: "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾

There are two views regarding its benefit and its connection to what precedes it:

The first: it shows that they (the messengers) delivered the clear message, since the man who ran to them believed in them. On this view, the phrase ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾ carries outstanding eloquence, because when ﴿a man came from the farthest part of the city﴾ and had believed, it indicates that their warning and their proclamation had reached the farthest part of the city.

The second: when the parable was given to Muhammad (ﷺ) as consolation for his heart, after finishing the mention of the messengers, Allah mentioned the effort of the believers in confirming their messengers and their patience over what they suffered, and the arrival of the complete reward to them, so that this would be a consolation to the hearts of the companions of Muhammad, just as the mention of the messengers is a consolation to the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ). In the tafsir (exegesis of the Qur'an) there are the following issues:

The first issue: the words ﴿a man﴾ are indefinite, although he was well known and recognized by Allah. There are two benefits in this indefiniteness:

The first: it is to magnify his status, meaning he was a man complete in manliness.

The second: it serves to show the truth on the part of the messengers, since a man from among men believed in them, a man with no prior acquaintance with them, so it cannot be said that they had colluded. This man was Habib al-Najjar (Habib the carpenter), who used to carve idols. He believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) before his existence, since he became one of the scholars of the Book of Allah, and he saw in it the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his mission.

The second issue: the words ﴿running﴾ are an insight and guidance for the believers, so that they would exert their utmost effort in giving sincere advice. We have already mentioned the benefit of the words ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾, which is that he conveyed the message to such an extent that it reached those in ﴿the farthest part of the city﴾.

Page 49

The city was Antioch. It was once large and extensive, and it is now smaller than that, yet it remains large. Allah's words ﴿He said: "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ contain subtle meanings:

The first: in his words ﴿O my people﴾, there is an indication of compassion and tender concern for them, since addressing them as ﴿my people﴾ shows that he wants nothing for them but good. This is like the statement of the believer of the family of Pharaoh: "O my people, follow me." If it is asked: this man said "follow the messengers," while that one said "follow me"; what is the difference? We say: this man came to them, and at the start of his coming he advised them, and they had not seen his conduct, so he said: "Follow these who have shown you the proof and made the way clear to you." As for the believer of the family of Pharaoh, he was among them and had followed Moses and advised them repeatedly, so he said: "Follow me in believing in Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, and know that if it were not good, I would not have chosen it for myself, and you know that I have chosen it." It would not have been fitting for the man who came from the farthest part of the city to say: "You know that I follow them."

The second: he combined the display of sincere advice with the display of his faith. His words ﴿follow﴾ are advice, and his words ﴿the messengers﴾ show that he himself had believed.

The third: he put the display of sincere advice before the display of faith, because he was running in giving advice. As for faith, he had believed before. His words ﴿a man running﴾ indicate that he was intent on giving sincere advice. And what is mentioned in his narrative is that he was being killed while saying: "O Allah, guide my people."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Follow those who ask you no reward, and who are rightly guided.﴾ This is in the utmost beauty, and that is because when He said ﴿Follow the messengers,﴾ it was as if they had denied being messengers, so he descended a degree and said: There is no doubt that people in this world are travelling a path and seeking uprightness, and when a guide who indicates the way is present, it is obligatory to follow him. Refraining from following is only good in one of two cases: either the guide is excessive in demanding a wage, or else when one does not rely on his guidance and his knowledge of the way. But these people do not ask for a wage, and they are rightly guided, knowing the straight path that leads to the truth. So suppose they are not guiding messengers; are they not rightly guided? Then follow them.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾ When He said ﴿and they are rightly guided,﴾ He made clear the manifestness of their guidance, in that they are called from worshipping lifeless matter to worshipping the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and from worshipping what does not benefit to worshipping the One from whom every benefit comes.

There are subtleties in this:

The first: His saying ﴿mā liya﴾ (what is with me), meaning: what prevents me on my side? It is an indication that the matter on the part of the one worshipped is manifest and free of obscurity; whoever refrains from worshipping Him has an obstacle on his own side, and there is no obstacle on my side, so I worship Him without doubt. In turning from addressing the people to the state of his own self there is another wisdom.

A second subtlety: had he said, "What is with you that you do not worship the One who originated you," it would not have had the clarity of his saying ﴿mā liya﴾, because when he said ﴿mā liya,﴾ and no one is hidden from the state of his own self, everyone knew that he does not seek the cause and its explanation from anyone, since he is best informed about the state of his own self; so he is explaining the absence of an obstacle. But had he said "mā lakum," it could have been understood that he was seeking an explanation of the cause, on the basis that someone other than himself knows his state better. If it is said: God said, ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ (Nuh: 13), we say: the speaker there was not one being called, but rather a caller; whereas here the man is one being called to faith, so he said ﴿And why should I not worship﴾ when it was demanded of me.

The third: His saying ﴿the One who originated me﴾ is an indication of the existence of the requirement (muqtaḍā), for His saying ﴿mā liya﴾ indicates the absence of an obstacle.

Page 50
And when there is no obstacle, the act does not come into existence unless the requirement exists. So His saying ﴿the One who originated me﴾ points to the requirement, for the Creator at the beginning is the Owner, and the Owner is owed honour and veneration by the owned; and He is the Benefactor by bringing into existence, and the Benefactor is owed thanks for His favour by the one benefited.

The fourth: he placed the explanation of the absence of an obstacle before the explanation of the existence of the requirement, although the preferable order is to mention the requirement where the requirement exists and there is no obstacle, so that it comes into being. This is because the requirement, by its obviousness, needed no explanation at all, so at least one should begin with what is more in need of explanation, due to the need for it.

The fifth: he chose from the signs his own origination, because when he said ﴿And why should I not worship,﴾ attributing the worship to his own self, he chose what is closer to making worship obligatory upon himself. The explanation of this is that the creator of ʿAmr is owed worship from Zayd, because whoever created ʿAmr must be of perfect power, all-encompassing knowledge, and necessary existence, and He deserves worship from every responsible person; but the obligation of worship upon Zayd through the creation of Zayd is more evident in its obligation.

Know that the well-known meaning of His saying ﴿faṭaranī﴾ is "created me" in origination and innovation; the rarer interpretation is that it means "made me upon the natural disposition (fiṭrah)," as God the Exalted said: ﴿the natural disposition of God upon which He created mankind﴾ (al-Rum: 30). On this view, His saying ﴿And why should I not worship﴾ means: no obstacle exists in me, so I remain upon the natural disposition of my Lord; the natural disposition suffices in testimony and worship. If it is said: on this view the meaning of faṭr differs in His saying ﴿Originator of the heavens﴾ (al-An'am: 14), we say: it has been said that "Originator of the heavens" is from faṭr meaning splitting, so the objection stands; or we say the meaning is one in both: as if He said, "He created the responsible person upon his natural disposition and created the heavens upon their natural disposition." The first interpretation is more apparent.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ indicates fear and hope, as He said: ﴿Call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾, because whoever is the destination of return is feared and hoped for. There is also in it a subtle meaning, which is that the worshipper is of three categories, which we have mentioned repeatedly.

The first: a worshipper who worships God because He is a god and owner, whether or not He bestows favour afterward, like the slave who is obliged to serve his master whether the master treats him well or badly.

The second: a worshipper who worships God for the blessing that reaches him.

The third: a worshipper who worships God out of fear.

An example of the first: one who serves the generous.

An example of the second: one who serves the tyrant. The speaker placed himself in the higher category, saying: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾ He is my owner; I worship Him so that I may look to what He will give me, and so that I may look to His not punishing me; and He placed them below that, saying: ﴿and to Him you will be returned,﴾ meaning: your fear of Him and your hope in Him, so how do you not worship Him? For this reason he did not say "and to Him I will return," as he said "originated me," because he had become a worshipper of the first category; so his return to God is only for honour, and the cause of his worship is not that but something else.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Follow those who ask you no reward, and who are rightly guided.﴾ This is in the utmost beauty, and that is because when He said ﴿Follow the messengers,﴾ it was as if they had denied being messengers, so he descended a degree and said: There is no doubt that people in this world are travelling a path and seeking uprightness, and when a guide who indicates the way is present, it is obligatory to follow him.
