But these people do not ask for a wage, and they are rightly guided, knowing the straight path that leads to the truth. So suppose they are not guiding messengers; are they not rightly guided? Then follow them.

Then God the Exalted said: "Shall I take other gods besides Him?" (Q. 36:23), in order to complete the monotheism (tawhid), for tawhid lies between denial of God (ta'til) and associating partners with Him (ishrak). He said: "And why should I not worship..." pointing to the existence of the God; and He said: "Shall I take besides Him..." pointing to the negation of anything other than Him, so that the meaning of "There is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah) is realised.

In the verse there are also subtleties (lata'if):

The first: its mention in the form of a question carries the sense of the matter being clear. For whoever reports about something, saying for example, "I will not take," the listener may properly say to him, "Why do you not take?" and ask him for the reason. But when he says, "Shall I take?" his speech implies that he is independent of explaining the reason that would be demanded of him when reporting. It is as if he were saying: "I consulted you, so guide me," and the one consulted reflects. So it is as if he were saying: "Reflect on the matter and you will understand without my informing you."

The second: His saying "besides Him" (min dunihi). This is a subtle and wonderful point, and its explanation is that when He had made clear that he worships God by saying "He who created me" (Q. 36:22), He made clear that whatever is besides Him may not be worshipped. For if one were to change God, it would become obligatory to worship everything that shares with the worshipped one that has been taken as other than God, because all of them are needy, dependent and created. So if he had said, "I will not take gods," it would have been said to him: "That differs if you take a god other than the One who created you, and it will necessarily bind you by reason to take gods without limit. And if your god is your Lord and your Creator, then it is not permissible for you to take gods."

The third: His saying "Shall I take?" is an indication that other than Him is not a god, because what is taken cannot be a god. For this reason God the Exalted said: "He has taken neither a consort nor a son" (Q. 72:3), and He said: "Praise be to God, who has not taken a son" (Q. 17:111), because God the Exalted cannot have a son in reality, and it is not permissible. The Christians only said that God adopted Jesus and named him a son, so He said: "and has not taken a son" (Q. 25:2). It is not said that God the Exalted said regarding Himself: "So take Him as a Trustee" (Q. 73:9), where He said: "Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but He, so take Him as a Trustee" (Q. 73:9). We say: that is a renewed matter, because a person at the beginning of the affair is weak in patience and feeble in strength, so it is not permissible for him to abandon the means of this world and say, "I rely upon God." It is not good for any one of us to undertake nothing at all, leaving his children in the distress of need and not supplying their maintenance to his family, sitting in a mosque while his heart is attached to the gifts of Zayd and 'Amr. But when his heart grows strong through worship and he forgets himself, let alone others, and turns to the worship of his Lord with his whole heart, abandoning the world and its means, and entrusts his affair to God, then he is at that point among the righteous and the good. So God said to His Messenger: You know that all affairs are in the hand of God, you have known God with the knowledge that is His due, and you are certain that the East and the West and what is in them and what occurs between them are by the command of God, and that there is no god to be sought for the fulfilment of needs but Him. So take Him as a Trustee, and entrust all your affairs to Him, for you have risen above the rank of one who is commanded to earn lawful livelihood, though previously you used to trade in what is lawful. The meaning of His saying "so take Him as a Trustee" (Q. 73:9) is: in all your affairs.

And His saying "your intercession will not avail me" (la tughni 'anni) admits two interpretations:

One: that it be in the manner of a description, as if He had said: "Shall I take gods that do not avail when the Merciful intends harm for me?"

Two: that it be a fresh statement, as if He had said: "I will not take besides Him gods."

Then God the Exalted said: "If the Merciful intends me some harm, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me" (Q. 36:23). Regarding this there are issues:

First issue: He said, "If the Merciful intends me harm" (in yuridni al-Rahman bi-durr) (Q. 39:38), and He did not say, "If God intends harm for me." We say: when a verb is transitive to one object, it is transitive to two objects by means of a preposition, as the intransitive verb takes a preposition in their saying: "dhahaba bihi" (he took him away) and "kharaja bihi" (he brought him out). Then the eloquent speaker makes the object without a preposition that which is more fitting for the action to fall upon, and makes the other object one without a preposition. So if someone says, for example, "How is the condition of so-and-so?", he says, "The king has singled him out with honour and favour." But if he says, "How is the king's honour?", he says, "He has singled it out for Zayd," so he makes the one asked about an object without a preposition, because it is what is intended. Knowing this, what is intended in our present matter is the explanation that the servant is under God's control, Who turns him as He wills in hardship and ease, and harm is not the intended subject of the explanation. How could it be, when the speaker is a believer who hopes for mercy and favour on the basis of his faith, relying on God's promise? This is confirmed by his earlier saying, "He who created me" (Q. 36:22), where he made himself the object of the act of creation; so likewise he made himself the object of the will. The mention of harm came as a consequence. The same applies to His saying: "If God intends me harm" (Q. 39:38): the intended point is to explain that it will be as God wills, and harm in particular is not the thing intended by the mention. This is confirmed by what preceded, where God said: "Is not God sufficient for His servant?" (Q. 39:36), meaning that he is under His will. What we have mentioned is further supported by considering His saying: "Say: Who is it that will protect you from God if He intends you evil?" (Q. 33:17), where the structure differs and the object without a preposition is "evil", which is like "harm", whereas the object with a preposition is the one held responsible. This is because the intended point is the mention of harm for the sake of warning, and their being its locus. How not, when they were disbelievers who deserved punishment for their disbelief? So He made harm the intended subject of mention to deter them. If it is said: God has also mentioned mercy, where He said, "or if He intends you mercy" (Q. 33:17), we say that He mentioned mercy only to complete the matter by a dividing, exhaustive classification. Likewise, if you reflect on His saying: "They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say: Who then can avail you anything against God if He intends you harm, or intends you benefit?" (Q. 48:11), the speech is also with the disbelievers, and the mention of benefit came as a consequence of confining the matter by division. This is indicated by His saying: "Nay, God is ever Aware of what you do" (Q. 48:11), for that is for the purpose of warning. This is like His saying: "And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in manifest error" (Q. 34:24), where the intended meaning is: I am upon guidance and you are in error. Had he said it that way, someone would have objected, so he used the division. Similarly here the intended point is that harm falls upon you, and to forestall the objection he mentioned both harm and benefit.

Second issue: here he said, "If the Merciful" and in Az-Zumar he said, "If God intends me" (Q. 39:38). What is the wisdom in choosing the past tense form there and the present form here, and in mentioning the one who intends by the name al-Rahman here and by the name Allah there? We say: as for the past and the future, the particle "in" in the conditional makes the past become future. This is because what was mentioned here before was in the future form in His saying "Shall I take?" and "why should I not worship?", whereas what was mentioned there before was in the past form in His saying "Have you considered?" (Q. 53:19). Likewise in His saying: "If God touches you with harm" (Q. 10:107), because what precedes it was mentioned in the future form, namely "whoever is turned away from it" (Q. 6:16) and "I fear, if I disobey" (Q. 6:15). The wisdom in this is that the disbelievers used to threaten the Prophet ﷺ with harm from their gods reaching him. So it is as if he said: the threat has come from you, and this is what has already preceded from you. Here, however, it is the beginning of a speech issuing from the believer, for the affirmation; and the answer: it was not possible for such a thing to come from them, so the two matters differ. As for his saying there, "If God intends me" (Q. 39:38), we say: we have mentioned that the two names peculiar to the Necessary Existent are Allah and al-Rahman, as He said: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman" (Q. 17:110). Allah is for awe and majesty, and al-Rahman is for tenderness and mercy. There God was described with might and retribution in His saying: "Is not God the Mighty, Possessor of retribution?" (Q. 39:37), and He mentioned what indicates majesty in His saying: "If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth" (Q. 31:25), mentioning the name that indicates majesty. Here He mentioned what indicates mercy, in His saying "He who created me", for that is a blessing which is the condition of all other blessings. So He said, "If the Merciful intends me harm." Then He said: "their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me," in the order in which rational beings act. For whoever wishes to repel harm from a person harmed by someone first seeks to repel it in the best manner, so he intercedes first; and if that is accepted, well and good, and if not, he repels it by force. So He said: "their intercession will avail me nothing," and they have no power to rescue me in any way whatsoever. In these verses it has been shown that God the Exalted is worthy of worship in every respect: if one considers His side, He is the Originator, the Lord and Owner who deserves worship whether or not He afterwards does good; if one considers His beneficence, He is the Merciful; and if one considers fear, He is the one who repels harm. It has also been shown that other than Him is not fit to be worshipped in any respect, for the least of its ranks is to be prepared for it on a day of calamity; and other than God repels nothing except when God wills, and if He wills, there is no need for a repeller.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error﴾. That is, if I did so, I would be in clear error. The word *al-mubīn* (مُبِينٌ) is of the *mufʿil* form (مُفْعِلٌ) with the meaning of the *faʿīl* form (فَعِيلٍ), just as the reverse occurs: *faʿīl* with the meaning of *mufʿil*, as in His saying *alīm* (أَلِيمٌ), meaning *mu'lim* (مُؤْلِمٌ), painful. It is also possible to say: *ḍalāl mubīn* means that the matter is evident to the observer. The first explanation is the correct one.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾. Regarding the addressee in His saying ﴿your Lord﴾, there are several views:

First: the addressees are the messengers. The exegetes (*mufassirūn*) said: the people advanced toward him, intending to kill him, so he turned to the messengers and said: "Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to my words and bear witness for me."

Second: the addressees are the disbelievers. It is as if, when he had advised them and it did not benefit them, he said: "So I have believed, so listen to me."

Third: "your Lord" addresses whoever is listening, O listeners, "so listen to me," in a general sense, just as we said regarding the preacher when he says: "O poor wretch, how much your hopes are, and how little your deeds are," meaning by it every listener who hears him.

Regarding His saying ﴿so listen to me﴾ there are benefits:

The first: it is the speech of one who is deliberate and reflective, since he said ﴿so listen to me﴾. Indeed, the speaker, when he knows that his words have a group of listeners, reflects.

The second: that the intended hearing is the hearing that means acceptance. The speaker says: "I advised him and he heard my words," meaning he accepted them. If you ask: why did he say earlier ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me﴾, and here said ﴿I have believed in your Lord﴾, and did not say "I have believed in my Lord"? We say: our position is that the address is to the messengers, which is an evident matter, because when he said "I have believed in your Lord," it became clear to the messengers that he had accepted their words and believed in the Lord to whom they had called him. Had he said "in my Lord," they might have said: every disbeliever says "I have a lord, and I believe in my lord." As for our position that the address is to the disbelievers, then there is in it an explanation of tawḥīd (affirmation of God's oneness), because when he said ﴿I worship He who originated me﴾ and then said ﴿I have believed in your Lord﴾, it was understood that he was saying: "My lord and your lord are one; He who originated me is precisely your lord." This is unlike if he had said "I have believed in my Lord," for then the disbeliever would say: "I too have believed in my lord." A similar example is His saying, exalted: ﴿Allah is our Lord and your Lord﴾. (al-Shura: 15)

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It was said: "Enter Paradise."﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

It is as if he had heard from the messengers that he was among those who would enter Paradise, believed them, was certain of it, and knew it, so he said: "Would that my people knew, as I have known, so that they would believe as I have believed."

The intended meaning is not speech according to one view; rather it is action, that is, He does it at that moment without delay or postponement. Likewise the Exalted's words: ﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water"﴾ [Hūd: 44] can be understood as making the earth swallow its water.

Regarding the Exalted's words ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ there are several views:

The first: *mā* is interrogative, as if he had said: "Would that my people knew with what my Lord has forgiven me, so that they would busy themselves with it." This view is weak; otherwise the better form would be for *mā* to lose its *alif*, as in *bi-ma*, *fi-ma*, *'amma*, and *lima*.

[Page 54]

The second: *mā* is relative (*khabariyya*), as if he had said: "Would that my people knew of that which my Lord has forgiven me."

The third: *mā* is verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyya*), as if he had said: "Would that my people knew of my Lord's forgiveness of me." The other two views are the preferred ones.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾. We have mentioned that faith and righteous deeds necessitate two things: forgiveness and honor, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿Those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and generous provision﴾ (Sabā': 4). This man was among the righteous believers. The honored person is the opposite of the humiliated; humiliation is through need, and honor is through self-sufficiency. So God makes the righteous independent of everyone and meets all his needs Himself.

Then, when the Exalted had described his condition, He described the condition of those among his people who stayed behind and opposed him, by His words: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down [any].﴾ This is an indication of their destruction after him, swiftly and in the easiest manner, for He did not need to send an army to destroy them. There are several issues regarding this:

First issue: He said here ﴿We sent down﴾, attributing the verb to Himself, while regarding the condition of the believer He said ﴿It was said: "Enter Paradise"﴾, attributing the saying to an unmentioned agent. This is because punishment falls under the category of awe, so He used the language of exaltation. As for ﴿Enter Paradise﴾, He said ﴿it was said﴾ so that he would be like one congratulated by the words of the angels, since every angel and every righteous person who sees him says to him: "Enter Paradise, abiding therein forever." The Qur'an frequently includes the words ﴿It was said: "Enter"﴾ (al-Zumar: 72), indicating that the entry will be an entry with honor, just as the bridegroom enters the adorned house before the eyes of the witnesses, and everyone congratulates him.

Second issue: Why did He attribute the people to him (the believer), even though the messengers are more worthy of having a people for them? For the single person may have a people, who are his family and companions, while the messenger, by virtue of being sent, has all creation and all those to whom he was sent as his people. We answer with two points:

The first: to show the difference between two persons from one tribe, one of whom was honored to the utmost degree because of faith, and the other humiliated to the utmost degree because of disbelief. This man is of their people by lineage.

The second: that the punishment was specific to the relatives of that [man], for the others among the messengers' people who believed in them were not struck by the punishment.

Third issue: He restricted the non-sending down to what came after him, while God also did not send down an army against them before him. So what is the benefit of the restriction? We answer: their deserving of punishment came after him, when they persisted and became arrogant. So He made clear that the nature of the destruction was not by an army.

Fourth issue: He said ﴿from the heaven﴾, though He did not descend to them, nor did He send an army to them from the earth. So what is the benefit of the qualification? We answer: the answer to this is from two points:

The first: the intended meaning may be: "We did not send down an army upon them by a command from the heaven," so that it is general.

The second: the punishment descended upon them from the heaven, so He made clear that what descended was not an army with majesty for them; rather it was a single cry that extinguished their fire and ruined their dwellings.

Fifth issue: ﴿nor were We ever going to send down [any]﴾. What is the benefit of this, since His words ﴿We did not send down﴾ imply that He would not be among those who send down? We answer: His words ﴿nor were We ever going to﴾ mean: it was not fitting for Us to send down [an army], because the matter would be completed without that. So We did not send down, and We had no need to send down [an army]. Or we say: ﴿We did not send down, nor were We ever going to send down﴾ an army in such an event, [nor] in any other event. If it is said: "How then did God send down armies on the day of Badr and at other times, when He said: ﴿and sent down armies you did not see﴾ (al-Tawbah: 26)?" We answer: that is in exaltation of Muhammad (ﷺ). Otherwise, the stirring of a single feather from the wing of an angel would have been sufficient to uproot them, and the messengers of 'Īsā (peace be upon him) were not of the rank of Muhammad (ﷺ).

[Page 55]

Then God explained what it was by His words: ﴿It was not but a single cry﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its original form is "if there was not anything but a single cry," so the original would have been to mention the noun, but the Exalted made the verb feminine because of the explanatory predicate that follows it, which is "the cry" (*al-ṣayḥa*).

His words ﴿single﴾ emphasize that the matter is easy in the sight of God.

His words ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾ indicate the swiftness of the destruction, for their extinction came from the cry and did not lag behind its time. Describing them as "extinguished" is most eloquent, because the living thing has innate heat (*al-ḥarāra al-gharīziyya*), and whenever the heat is greater, the irascible faculty (*al-quwwa al-ghaḍabiyya*) and the concupiscent faculty (*al-quwwa al-shahwāniyya*) are more complete. They were of this kind: as for anger, they killed a believer who was advising them; as for desire, they endured the everlasting punishment for the sake of enjoying fleeting pleasures. Thus they were like a kindled fire, and because they were tyrannical and arrogant, like fire and whatever is created from it. Hence He said ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾.

There is another view: that the four elements (*al-'anāṣir al-arba'a*) may leave their natural disposition which God created them upon, and one element may become another by the will of God. Stones become water, water becomes stones; likewise water becomes air through boiling and heating, and air becomes water through cold. But this happens customarily over a period of time. As for air becoming fire, and fire becoming air through ignition and extinction, this happens in the swiftest time. So He said "extinguished" with reference to it. Thus the extinction of fire in swiftness is like the snuffing out of a lamp or a flame.

Otherwise, the stirring of a single feather from the wing of an angel would have been sufficient to uproot them, and the messengers of 'Īsā (peace be upon him) were not of the rank of Muhammad (ﷺ).

So God makes the righteous independent of everyone and meets all his needs Himself.

There are several issues regarding this:

This is because punishment falls under the category of awe, so He used the language of exaltation. As for ﴿Enter Paradise﴾, He said ﴿it was said﴾ so that he would be like one congratulated by the words of the angels, since every angel and every righteous person who sees him says to him: "Enter Paradise, abiding therein forever." The Qur'an frequently includes the words ﴿It was said: "Enter"﴾ (al-Zumar: 72), indicating that the entry will be an entry with honor, just as the bridegroom enters the adorned house before the eyes of the witnesses, and everyone congratulates him.

Second issue: Why did He attribute the people to him (the believer), even though the messengers are more worthy of having a people for them? For the single person may have a people, who are his family and companions, while the messenger, by virtue of being sent, has all creation and all those to whom he was sent as his people. We answer with two points:

The first: to show the difference between two persons from one tribe, one of whom was honored to the utmost degree because of faith, and the other humiliated to the utmost degree because of disbelief. This man is of their people by lineage.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ That is, this is the time of regret; so come, O regret. The indefinite form (ḥasrah) is for emphasis on multiplicity. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: the alif and lam in "al-ʿibād" (the servants) may carry two meanings:

One of them: it is for the known (al-maʿhūd), namely those whom the Blast (al-ṣayḥah) seized. So, "Alas for those!"

The second: it denotes the genus (taʿrīf al-jins), the genus of disbelievers who denied.

The second issue: who is the one regretting? We say there are several views:

The first: there is in reality no one regretting at all, since the purpose is to explain that this is the time of calling for regret, when remorse becomes certain upon the arrival of the punishment.

Here there is a linguistic point: the object may be dropped entirely when the aim does not relate to it. It is said: "So-and-so gives and withholds," and there is no thing given, since the intended meaning is that he has the power to withhold and to give. Dropping the object is common, while dropping the subject, as in our case, is rare. The reason for it is what we have mentioned: mention of the one regretting is not intended; rather, the intended meaning is that regret is realized at that time.

The second: the one who says "Alas for the ... !" is Allah, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify the matter and to make it dreadful. In that case it is like the expressions that occur concerning Allah, such as laughing, forgetting, mocking, wondering and wishing. Or we say: the meaning of our saying "Alas!" and "Alas for regret!" is not that the speaker is regretful or remorseful; rather, the meaning is that He informs of the occurrence of remorse. There is no need for a figurative usage in explaining that He, exalted is He, said "Alas!"; rather, He informs of it in its literal sense, except in the case of remorse, since calling (nidāʾ) is figurative and the intended meaning is informing.

The third: those among the Muslims and the angels who are filled with longing and sorrow. Do you not see what is related about Ḥabīb, that at the time of his killing he was saying: "O Allah, guide my people," and after they had killed him and he had been admitted to Paradise, he said: "Would that my people knew"? So it is permissible for a Muslim to feel sorrow for a disbeliever and to grieve for him and over him.

The third issue: "Yā ḥasratan" has been read with tanwīn, and "Yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" with idafah without the word ʿalā. It was also read "Yā ḥasratan ʿalā" with the hāʾ, treating the connected reading as if it were a pause.

The fourth issue: who is meant by "al-ʿibād" (the servants)? We say there are several views:

One of them: the three messengers. It is as if the disbelievers say at the appearance of the punishment: "Alas for them! Would that they had been present in our affair, so that we might believe in them."

The second: they are the people of Ḥabīb.

The third: everyone who disbelieved, persisted and was arrogant. According to the first view, the use of "servants" for believers is as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Ḥijr: 42) and His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ (al-Zumar: 53). According to the second view, the use of "servants" for disbelievers is as such. A distinction is made between the word "ʿabd" in absolute form and what is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, for attribution to the noble confers nobility upon the thing attributed: you say "the House of Allah" and it carries a nobility that "the house" does not carry. On this basis, His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ (al-Furqān: 63) is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants﴾, and likewise: ﴿servants of Allah﴾ (al-Insān: 6).

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the cause of the regret by His saying: ﴿And no messenger came to them except that they used to mock him﴾. This is the cause of remorse. That is because whoever is visited by a king from the desert, who introduces himself to him and asks of him a simple matter, but he denies him and does not respond to what he calls him to, then he stands before him while he is on his throne of kingship and informs him that he is that king, will have a remorse beyond which there is no increase. Likewise, the messengers are kings and greater than them, by the honour Allah gave them and by making them His deputies, as He said: ﴿If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 31). They came and introduced themselves, and they had no apparent greatness to the senses. Then on the Day of Resurrection, or at the appearance of the punishment, their greatness before Allah became manifest to them. What they called to was a simple matter whose benefit returns to them, namely the worship of Allah, and they did not ask any wage for it. At that point there is intense remorse. And how could it not be, when they persisted in turning away, to the point that they harmed, mocked, belittled and disdained them?

As for His saying: ﴿there came to them﴾, the pronoun may refer to the people of Ḥabīb, meaning: there did not come to them any messenger from the three messengers ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾, according to our view that the regret is for them. It may also refer to the persisting disbelievers.

Then, when Allah, exalted is He, had explained the condition of the earlier ones, He said to those present: ﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ That is, those who remain do not see what befell those who came before them. It may also be said that those about whom He said "Alas!" are those about whom He said "Did they not see?" The meaning is that every destroyed people before them were a people who denied and were destroyed, going back to the people of Noah and before him.

His saying: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ is, in meaning, a substitute for His saying: ﴿how many We destroyed﴾. That is because the meaning of "how many We destroyed" is: did they not see the multitude of Our destructions? And the meaning of "did they not see the many who were destroyed, that they to them do not return" is then a substitution of the kind of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl), since His saying "that they to them do not return" describes a state of those destroyed, meaning they were destroyed in such a way that there is no return for them to them. This is like your saying: "Have you not seen Zayd, his discipline?" On this basis, His saying ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ has two meanings:

One of them: they were destroyed with a destruction that leaves no return for them to those in the world.

The second: they do not return to them, meaning the remaining ones do not return to the destroyed ones by lineage or by birth. The meaning is that We destroyed them and cut off their offspring. There is no doubt that destruction accompanied by the cutting off of offspring is more complete and more comprehensive. The first meaning is more famous in transmission, and the second is more evident in reason.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, all of them, when brought together, will be present before Us﴾. When He explained the destruction, He explained that whoever Allah destroyed is not left alone; rather, after it there is gathering, reckoning, detention and punishment. Had whoever was destroyed been left, death would have been a rest, and how well the poet said:

"Had we, when we die, been left alone, death would be rest for every living thing;
But when we die, we are raised, and after that we are questioned about every thing."

Regarding His saying ﴿And indeed, all of them﴾, the "in" has two possible readings:

One: it is the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), the lam in "lammā" distinguishes it from the negating "in," and "mā" is an additional element emphasizing the meaning. The reading then is with lightening of "lammā."

The second: it is a negating particle, and "lammā" means "illā" (except). Sībawayh said: it is said, "I implore you by Allah, lammā you did such-and-such," meaning "illā you did such-and-such." The reading then is with the doubling in "lammā." What supports this is what is transmitted, that Ubayy recited: "wa mā kullun illā jamīʿun" (and not all of them except are gathered). In Sībawayh's statement that "lammā" means "illā," there is an appropriate meaning: "lammā" is as though two negating particles were combined, namely "lam" and "mā," so the negation is emphasized. For this reason it is said in answer to one who says "He has done it," "lammā yafʿal" (not yet), and in answer to one who says "He did it," "lam yafʿal" (he did not). And "illā" is as though it were two negating particles, "in" and "lā," so one of them is used in place of the other. Al-Zamakhsharī said: If someone asks: "kull" and "jamīʿ" have the same meaning, so how is "jamīʿ" made the predicate of "kull," when the lam has entered upon it, since the implied construction is: "wa in kullun la-jamīʿun"? We say: the meaning of "jamīʿ" is "gathered," and the meaning of "kull" is "every individual," such that no one is excluded from the judgment. So the meaning becomes: every individual gathered together with the other, joined to it. It is also possible to say that "muḥḍarūn" (present) is in the sense of what he mentioned. That is because if he had said "wa in jamīʿun la-jamīʿun muḥḍarūn," it would have been a correct statement, and the answer he mentioned would not arise. Rather, the correct view is that "muḥḍarūn" functions like an adjective for "jamīʿ," so it is as though he said: "jamīʿun jamīʿun muḥḍarūn," just as one says "al-rajulu rajulun ʿālimun" (the man is a man, a scholar) and "al-nabiyyu nabiyyun mursalun" (the prophet is a prophet, sent). The "wa" in "wa in kullun" is for conjoining narration to narration, as though he says: "I have explained to you what I mentioned, and I will explain that every one of them is present before Us." Likewise is the "wa" in His saying, exalted is He:

The second: it denotes the genus (taʿrīf al-jins), the genus of disbelievers who denied.

The first: there is in reality no one regretting at all, since the purpose is to explain that this is the time of calling for regret, when remorse becomes certain upon the arrival of the punishment.

Here there is a linguistic point: the object may be dropped entirely when the aim does not relate to it. It is said: "So-and-so gives and withholds," and there is no thing given, since the intended meaning is that he has the power to withhold and to give. Dropping the object is common, while dropping the subject, as in our case, is rare. The reason for it is what we have mentioned: mention of the one regretting is not intended; rather, the intended meaning is that regret is realized at that time.

The second: the one who says "Alas for the ... !" is Allah, by way of metaphor (istiʿārah), to magnify the matter and to make it dreadful. In that case it is like the expressions that occur concerning Allah, such as laughing, forgetting, mocking, wondering and wishing. Or we say: the meaning of our saying "Alas!" and "Alas for regret!" is not that the speaker is regretful or remorseful; rather, the meaning is that He informs of the occurrence of remorse. There is no need for a figurative usage in explaining that He, exalted is He, said "Alas!"; rather, He informs of it in its literal sense, except in the case of remorse, since calling (nidāʾ) is figurative and the intended meaning is informing.

The third: those among the Muslims and the angels who are filled with longing and sorrow. Do you not see what is related about Ḥabīb, that at the time of his killing he was saying: "O Allah, guide my people," and after they had killed him and he had been admitted to Paradise, he said: "Would that my people knew"? So it is permissible for a Muslim to feel sorrow for a disbeliever and to grieve for him and over him.

The third issue: "Yā ḥasratan" has been read with tanwīn, and "Yā ḥasrata al-ʿibād" with idafah without the word ʿalā. It was also read "Yā ḥasratan ʿalā" with the hāʾ, treating the connected reading as if it were a pause.

The fourth issue: who is meant by "al-ʿibād" (the servants)? We say there are several views:

One of them: the three messengers. It is as if the disbelievers say at the appearance of the punishment: "Alas for them! Would that they had been present in our affair, so that we might believe in them."

The second: they are the people of Ḥabīb.

The third: everyone who disbelieved, persisted and was arrogant. According to the first view, the use of "servants" for believers is as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Ḥijr: 42) and His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾ (al-Zumar: 53). According to the second view, the use of "servants" for disbelievers is as such. A distinction is made between the word "ʿabd" in absolute form and what is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, for attribution to the noble confers nobility upon the thing attributed: you say "the House of Allah" and it carries a nobility that "the house" does not carry. On this basis, His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ (al-Furqān: 63) is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants﴾, and likewise: ﴿servants of Allah﴾ (al-Insān: 6).

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the cause of the regret by His saying: ﴿And no messenger came to them except that they used to mock him﴾. This is the cause of remorse. That is because whoever is visited by a king from the desert, who introduces himself to him and asks of him a simple matter, but he denies him and does not respond to what he calls him to, then he stands before him while he is on his throne of kingship and informs him that he is that king, will have a remorse beyond which there is no increase. Likewise, the messengers are kings and greater than them, by the honour Allah gave them and by making them His deputies, as He said: ﴿If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 31). They came and introduced themselves, and they had no apparent greatness to the senses. Then on the Day of Resurrection, or at the appearance of the punishment, their greatness before Allah became manifest to them. What they called to was a simple matter whose benefit returns to them, namely the worship of Allah, and they did not ask any wage for it. At that point there is intense remorse. And how could it not be, when they persisted in turning away, to the point that they harmed, mocked, belittled and disdained them?

As for His saying: ﴿there came to them﴾, the pronoun may refer to the people of Ḥabīb, meaning: there did not come to them any messenger from the three messengers ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾, according to our view that the regret is for them. It may also refer to the persisting disbelievers.

Then, when Allah, exalted is He, had explained the condition of the earlier ones, He said to those present: ﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ That is, those who remain do not see what befell those who came before them. It may also be said that those about whom He said "Alas!" are those about whom He said "Did they not see?" The meaning is that every destroyed people before them were a people who denied and were destroyed, going back to the people of Noah and before him.

His saying: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ is, in meaning, a substitute for His saying: ﴿how many We destroyed﴾. That is because the meaning of "how many We destroyed" is: did they not see the multitude of Our destructions? And the meaning of "did they not see the many who were destroyed, that they to them do not return" is then a substitution of the kind of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl), since His saying "that they to them do not return" describes a state of those destroyed, meaning they were destroyed in such a way that there is no return for them to them. This is like your saying: "Have you not seen Zayd, his discipline?" On this basis, His saying ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ has two meanings:

One of them: they were destroyed with a destruction that leaves no return for them to those in the world.

The second: they do not return to them, meaning the remaining ones do not return to the destroyed ones by lineage or by birth. The meaning is that We destroyed them and cut off their offspring. There is no doubt that destruction accompanied by the cutting off of offspring is more complete and more comprehensive. The first meaning is more famous in transmission, and the second is more evident in reason.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, all of them, when brought together, will be present before Us﴾. When He explained the destruction, He explained that whoever Allah destroyed is not left alone; rather, after it there is gathering, reckoning, detention and punishment. Had whoever was destroyed been left, death would have been a rest, and how well the poet said:

"Had we, when we die, been left alone, death would be rest for every living thing;
But when we die, we are raised, and after that we are questioned about every thing."

Regarding His saying ﴿And indeed, all of them﴾, the "in" has two possible readings:

One: it is the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), the lam in "lammā" distinguishes it from the negating "in," and "mā" is an additional element emphasizing the meaning. The reading then is with lightening of "lammā."

The second: it is a negating particle, and "lammā" means "illā" (except). Sībawayh said: it is said, "I implore you by Allah, lammā you did such-and-such," meaning "illā you did such-and-such." The reading then is with the doubling in "lammā." What supports this is what is transmitted, that Ubayy recited: "wa mā kullun illā jamīʿun" (and not all of them except are gathered). In Sībawayh's statement that "lammā" means "illā," there is an appropriate meaning: "lammā" is as though two negating particles were combined, namely "lam" and "mā," so the negation is emphasized. For this reason it is said in answer to one who says "He has done it," "lammā yafʿal" (not yet), and in answer to one who says "He did it," "lam yafʿal" (he did not). And "illā" is as though it were two negating particles, "in" and "lā," so one of them is used in place of the other. [Page 58]

It is as if he says: "And I also say: a sign for them is the dead earth." On this verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** What is the connection of this verse to what came before? We say it is related to what precedes it in two respects.

The first: when He said, ﴿And all of them will surely be brought before Us﴾, this was an allusion to the Gathering (al-hashr). So He mentioned what proves its possibility, to put an end to their denial, their deeming it unlikely, their persistence, and their obstinacy. He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life﴾, meaning: in this way We will bring the dead to life.

The second: when He mentioned the situation of the messengers and the destruction of those who denied them, and since their concern was tawhid (the oneness of God), He mentioned what points to it. He began with the earth, because it is their place, from which they are never separated in motion or in rest.

**Second issue:** The earth is a sign in an absolute sense, so why did He restrict it to them by saying ﴿a sign for them﴾? We say: a sign is enumerated and recounted for one who does not know the thing in the most eloquent way. As for one who knows a thing through direct sight, no proof is cited to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) and the sincere servants of God knew God before the earth and the heaven, so the earth was not what made Him known to them. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ (Fussilat: 53). And He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient regarding your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾ (Fussilat: 53), meaning: your Lord is sufficient as one who makes you know. Through Him you came to know everything, so He is a witness for you over everything. As for these people, the truth became clear to them through the horizons and themselves. Likewise, here the earth is a sign for them.

**Third issue:** If we say that the sign is mentioned to prove the possibility of bringing the dead to life, then His saying ﴿We have brought it to life﴾ is sufficient, and there is no need for His saying ﴿and We brought forth from it grain﴾ or other things. If we say that it is for proving the existence and oneness of God, then there is no benefit in His saying ﴿the dead earth, We have brought it to life﴾, because the earth itself is an evident proof and a dazzling demonstration. Then, suppose it is not sufficient; His saying ﴿the dead, We have brought it to life﴾ is sufficient for tawhid, so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and We brought forth from it grain﴾?

It has a benefit with respect to explaining the bringing to life of the dead. When He brought the earth to life and brought forth grain from it, that was a complete life, because the earth that is green but does not produce crops or bring forth grain is below what it produces in terms of life. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, said: "The One who brought the earth to life in a complete way, making it produce crops, will bring the dead to life in a complete way, such that they perceive matters."

As for its relation to tawhid: in it there is an enumeration of blessings. It is as if He says: "A sign for them is the earth, for it is their place and their cradle, in which is their movement and their settling, and the essential matter on which their existence and their possibility depend. Whether it was dead or not, it is a place for them, which they cannot do without, and that is a blessing. Then its being brought to life, so that it turns green, is a second blessing, for it becomes more beautiful and pure. Then bringing grain out of it is a third blessing, for their sustenance comes into their place; God could have made their provision in the sky or in the air, and they would not have had certainty. Then He made the gardens in it a fourth blessing, because the earth produces grain every year, whereas trees from which fruits are taken come into existence after grain. Then We caused springs to gush forth in it so that they would have reliance on what is obtained; had its water come from the sky, it would have been obtained, but one would not know where it is planted, where the rain falls, or where the drops descend." All of this is beneficial in relation to explaining the bringing to life of the dead, because His saying ﴿and We brought forth from it grain﴾ is like an indication of the necessary matter without which one cannot do.

His saying ﴿and We made in it gardens﴾ is like a matter one needs, which, if absent, does not make a person self-sufficient, yet he remains in a disturbed state. His saying ﴿and We caused to gush forth in it springs﴾ is an indication of adornment, which, if absent, does not make a person lacking and does not leave him in the distress of need, but he would not be in the best condition. The condition of a person with grain is like that of a poor man who has what fills his need in some respects, but does not remove his need in every respect. With fruits, his condition is considered like that of one who is content with flowing springs on which a person relies and by which he strengthens his heart, like the wealthy one who has stored up provision for years. So God, mighty and majestic, says: "Just as We did with the dead land, so We do with the dead in the earth: We bring them to life and give them what they cannot do without for their survival and formation, of the limbs they need and their faculties, like the eye and the faculty of sight, the ear and the faculty of hearing, and others. We add to them what is an adornment, like complete reason and comprehensive perception." So it is as if He said: "We bring the dead to life in a complete way, just as We brought the earth to life in a complete way."

**Fourth issue:** Regarding the mention of grain He said ﴿from it they eat﴾, and regarding trees and fruits He said ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾. This is because grain is a necessary sustenance, so He said ﴿from it they eat﴾, meaning: they are its eaters. As for fruits, they are not like that. It is as if He, may He be exalted, said: "If We had not brought them forth, they would remain without eating, so We brought them forth so that they might eat them."

**Fifth issue:** He singled out the date palm and grapes for mention among all other fruits, because the most delicious food is sweetness, and it is most complete in them. Also, dates and grapes are both sustenance and fruit, which the others are not. And also, they are more beneficial, for they are carried from land to distant places. If it is said: God mentioned pomegranates and olives in the Cattle (al-An'am), and fresh fodder (al-qadb), olives, and figs in other places, we say: in al-An'am and elsewhere, the intent is the mention of fruits and produce. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby﴾ (Fatir: 27), and His saying: ﴿Let man look at his food﴾ (Abasa: 24)? So He covered the kinds by mention. Here, however, the intent is to mention the attributes of the earth, so He chose from them the most delicious and most beneficial. We have mentioned in the surah of al-An'am what yields benefits from it, and from it one knows the benefit of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾ (al-Rahman: 68).

**Sixth issue:** In the places where God mentioned fruits, He did not mention the date through the word for its tree, which is the palm (al-nakhla), nor did He mention the grape through the word for its tree; rather He mentioned it by the words "grape" (inab) and "grapes" (a'nab), and did not mention the vine (karm). This is because the tree of the grape, in relation to its fruit, is lowly and of little benefit, whereas the palm, in relation to its fruit, is great, of high worth, and of much use: many vessels are made from it, its bark is used, and it has a resemblance to animals. So He chose from it what is most wondrous. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We caused to gush forth in it springs﴾ is a great sign, because the earth's parts, by the customary order, do not rise, yet we see the sources of rivers and springs in elevated places, and that is a proof of power and choice. Those who hold to the doctrine of natures (al-tab'iyya) said: the mountains are like constructed domes, and vapors rise to them just as they rise to the ceilings of bathhouses, and drops of water form there and then gather. If they are not strong, still waters are produced, like wells, and flow in channels; if they are strong, they split the earth and come out as flowing rivers, and they gather so that great rivers are formed, fed by rainwater and snow. We say: the particularity of some mountains with springs is a clear proof of choice, and what they have stated is a forced and far-fetched claim. Rather, the truth is that God, may He be exalted, created water in elevated places and guided it into rivers and channels, or water rose from lower places to high places by the command of God, and flowed through valleys to the regions whose people God has favored.
