The Prophet (ﷺ) and the sincere servants of God knew God before the earth and the heaven, so the earth was not what made Him known to them. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ (Fussilat: 53). And He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient regarding your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾ (Fussilat: 53), meaning: your Lord is sufficient as one who makes you know. Through Him you came to know everything, so He is a witness for you over everything. As for these people, the truth became clear to them through the horizons and themselves. Likewise, here the earth is a sign for them.

**Third issue:** If we say that the sign is mentioned to prove the possibility of bringing the dead to life, then His saying ﴿We have brought it to life﴾ is sufficient, and there is no need for His saying ﴿and We brought forth from it grain﴾ or other things. If we say that it is for proving the existence and oneness of God, then there is no benefit in His saying ﴿the dead earth, We have brought it to life﴾, because the earth itself is an evident proof and a dazzling demonstration. Then, suppose it is not sufficient; His saying ﴿the dead, We have brought it to life﴾ is sufficient for tawhid, so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and We brought forth from it grain﴾?

It has a benefit with respect to explaining the bringing to life of the dead. When He brought the earth to life and brought forth grain from it, that was a complete life, because the earth that is green but does not produce crops or bring forth grain is below what it produces in terms of life. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, said: "The One who brought the earth to life in a complete way, making it produce crops, will bring the dead to life in a complete way, such that they perceive matters."

As for its relation to tawhid: in it there is an enumeration of blessings. It is as if He says: "A sign for them is the earth, for it is their place and their cradle, in which is their movement and their settling, and the essential matter on which their existence and their possibility depend. Whether it was dead or not, it is a place for them, which they cannot do without, and that is a blessing. Then its being brought to life, so that it turns green, is a second blessing, for it becomes more beautiful and pure. Then bringing grain out of it is a third blessing, for their sustenance comes into their place; God could have made their provision in the sky or in the air, and they would not have had certainty. Then He made the gardens in it a fourth blessing, because the earth produces grain every year, whereas trees from which fruits are taken come into existence after grain. Then We caused springs to gush forth in it so that they would have reliance on what is obtained; had its water come from the sky, it would have been obtained, but one would not know where it is planted, where the rain falls, or where the drops descend." All of this is beneficial in relation to explaining the bringing to life of the dead, because His saying ﴿and We brought forth from it grain﴾ is like an indication of the necessary matter without which one cannot do.

His saying ﴿and We made in it gardens﴾ is like a matter one needs, which, if absent, does not make a person self-sufficient, yet he remains in a disturbed state. His saying ﴿and We caused to gush forth in it springs﴾ is an indication of adornment, which, if absent, does not make a person lacking and does not leave him in the distress of need, but he would not be in the best condition. The condition of a person with grain is like that of a poor man who has what fills his need in some respects, but does not remove his need in every respect. With fruits, his condition is considered like that of one who is content with flowing springs on which a person relies and by which he strengthens his heart, like the wealthy one who has stored up provision for years. So God, mighty and majestic, says: "Just as We did with the dead land, so We do with the dead in the earth: We bring them to life and give them what they cannot do without for their survival and formation, of the limbs they need and their faculties, like the eye and the faculty of sight, the ear and the faculty of hearing, and others. We add to them what is an adornment, like complete reason and comprehensive perception." So it is as if He said: "We bring the dead to life in a complete way, just as We brought the earth to life in a complete way."

**Fourth issue:** Regarding the mention of grain He said ﴿from it they eat﴾, and regarding trees and fruits He said ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾. This is because grain is a necessary sustenance, so He said ﴿from it they eat﴾, meaning: they are its eaters. As for fruits, they are not like that. It is as if He, may He be exalted, said: "If We had not brought them forth, they would remain without eating, so We brought them forth so that they might eat them."

**Fifth issue:** He singled out the date palm and grapes for mention among all other fruits, because the most delicious food is sweetness, and it is most complete in them. Also, dates and grapes are both sustenance and fruit, which the others are not. And also, they are more beneficial, for they are carried from land to distant places. If it is said: God mentioned pomegranates and olives in the Cattle (al-An'am), and fresh fodder (al-qadb), olives, and figs in other places, we say: in al-An'am and elsewhere, the intent is the mention of fruits and produce. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby﴾ (Fatir: 27), and His saying: ﴿Let man look at his food﴾ (Abasa: 24)? So He covered the kinds by mention. Here, however, the intent is to mention the attributes of the earth, so He chose from them the most delicious and most beneficial. We have mentioned in the surah of al-An'am what yields benefits from it, and from it one knows the benefit of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾ (al-Rahman: 68).

**Sixth issue:** In the places where God mentioned fruits, He did not mention the date through the word for its tree, which is the palm (al-nakhla), nor did He mention the grape through the word for its tree; rather He mentioned it by the words "grape" (inab) and "grapes" (a'nab), and did not mention the vine (karm). This is because the tree of the grape, in relation to its fruit, is lowly and of little benefit, whereas the palm, in relation to its fruit, is great, of high worth, and of much use: many vessels are made from it, its bark is used, and it has a resemblance to animals. So He chose from it what is most wondrous. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We caused to gush forth in it springs﴾ is a great sign, because the earth's parts, by the customary order, do not rise, yet we see the sources of rivers and springs in elevated places, and that is a proof of power and choice. Those who hold to the doctrine of natures (al-tab'iyya) said: the mountains are like constructed domes, and vapors rise to them just as they rise to the ceilings of bathhouses, and drops of water form there and then gather. If they are not strong, still waters are produced, like wells, and flow in channels; if they are strong, they split the earth and come out as flowing rivers, and they gather so that great rivers are formed, fed by rainwater and snow. We say: the particularity of some mountains with springs is a clear proof of choice, and what they have stated is a forced and far-fetched claim. Rather, the truth is that God, may He be exalted, created water in elevated places and guided it into rivers and channels, or water rose from lower places to high places by the command of God, and flowed through valleys to the regions whose people God has favored.

[Page 60 of the original]

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That they may eat of its fruit and of what their hands have made. Will they not then be thankful?﴾ The arrangement is evident, and it also becomes apparent in the exegesis.

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Why did He delay the reminder of benefit, with His words ﴿That they may eat﴾, until after mentioning the fruits, so that He said ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth therein﴾? And why did He say about the grain, ﴿from it they eat﴾, right after mentioning the grain, but not say ﴿That they may eat﴾ right after mentioning the palm trees and grapes? We say: Grain is a staple food, and its existence is completed by rainwater. For this reason, most lands are seen to have no trees or crops, and tilling does not cease there, relying on the water of the sky. This is a kindness from God, in that He made what man needs more widely available. As for fruits, they are not completed except by rivers, and trees do not bear fruit except after the existence of rivers. Therefore He delayed it.

The second issue: To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿its fruit﴾ refer? We say: The well-known view is that it refers to God, meaning ﴿that they may eat of the fruit of God﴾. In this there is a subtle point: fruits, after the existence of trees and the flowing of rivers, do not come into existence except by God, the Exalted, and if God had not created that, they would not have come into existence. So the fruit, after all that which the one who supposes is the cause of its existence, is nothing but by God, the Exalted, and His will. Therefore it is "its fruit." It may also refer to the palm trees, and He omitted the grapes because it is known that they are in the same ruling as the palm trees. It may also be said that it refers to what was mentioned, meaning "from the fruit of what We have mentioned." These two views were transmitted by al-Zamakhshari. There is another, stranger but closer, possibility: that what is meant by "fruit" is the benefits. One says, "the fruit of trade is profit," and one says, "the fruit of worship is reward." In that case the pronoun refers to the gushing forth indicated by His words ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth therein﴾, meaning "that they may eat of the benefits of that gushing forth." Its benefits are more numerous than the fruits; indeed, it includes what God, the Exalted, said: ﴿That We pour down water in abundance﴾ (Abasa: 25), up to His words: ﴿and cause grain to grow therein, and grapes and herbage, and olives and palm trees, and gardens of dense trees, and fruit and fodder﴾ (Abasa: 27–31). The gushing forth is closer in mention than the palm trees. And if it referred to God, He would have said "from Our fruit," as He said "And We made," and "And We caused to gush forth."

The third issue: What is the status of ما in His words ﴿and of what their hands have made﴾? Which kind of ما is it? We say: There are several views:

The first: it is a negation particle, as if He said: "and their hands did not make the gushing forth, rather God caused it to gush forth."

The second: it is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) meaning "that which." As if He said: "and that which their hands have made of plantings after the gushing forth, they also eat from it, and they eat from the fruit of God which He brought forth without any effort by people." So "that which their hands have made" is joined to what God created without any part of man in it.

The third: it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) according to the reading of one who reads "and what their hands have made" without a returning pronoun. Its meaning is: "that they may eat of its fruit and the work of their hands"; that is, they plant and God causes it to grow and creates its fruit, so they eat the combined result of the work of their hands and the creation of God. This view is not possible according to the reading of one who reads it with the pronoun.

The fourth issue: According to our view that ما is a relative pronoun, it may mean "and what their hands have made," that is, by trade. As if He mentioned the two kinds of what a person eats by them, which are agriculture and trade. Among plants, some are eaten without any work of the hands, like grapes and dates and others. Among them is what requires a craft to be done to it so that it can be eaten, like things that are not eaten except cooked, or like olives, which are not eaten except after preparation. Then, when He enumerated the blessings, He pointed to gratitude with His words ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾, and it was phrased in the form of a question, for the reasons we have explained regarding the benefits of interrogation in what preceded.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of what they do not know﴾. We have already mentioned that the word subhan (Glory be) is a proper noun indicating tasbih (glorification), and its implied meaning is: "Glorify with the glorification of Him who created all the pairs." The meaning of "sabbih" (glorify) is "nazzih" (declare free of imperfection). The connection of this verse with what precedes it is as follows: when God said ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾, and the thanks due to God is worship, and they had abandoned it and were not content with abandoning it, but worshipped other than Him and committed shirk, He said ﴿Glory be to Him who created the pairs﴾, whereas no other has created anything. Some say: when He clarified that they denied the signs and did not give thanks, He explained what the rational person should be like, saying ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾. Others say: when He clarified the signs, He said ﴿Glory be to Him who created﴾, declaring Him free of having any partner or being incapable of reviving the dead.

Page 61

There are several issues here:

The first issue: His saying ﴿all﴾ indicates that the actions of servants are created by God, because the zawj (pair) is the sinf (kind), and the actions of servants are kinds, and they have counterparts that fall under the genera of accidents. Thus they are part of the "all" concerning which God said that He created all the pairs. It cannot be said that ﴿of what the earth grows﴾ takes the speech out of generality, because whoever says "I gave Zayd all that I had" the statement is general if it is limited to that; but if he then says "of the garments," the speech does not remain general. We reply: that applies when "min" (of) is for specifying (bayan al-takhsis), but if it is for emphasizing the generality, then it does not. The proof is that whoever says "I gave him everything of the beasts, garments, slaves and maidservants" is understood to be enumerating the kinds to emphasize generality. This is supported by His saying in Ha Mim: ﴿And He who created all the pairs and made for you of the ships and cattle that you ride﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 12), without restriction.

The second issue: God mentioned three matters within which created things are contained. His saying ﴿of what the earth grows﴾ includes the apparent things in the earth such as plants and fruits; His saying ﴿and of themselves﴾ includes the psychological proofs; and His saying ﴿and of what they do not know﴾ includes what is in the regions of the heavens and the depths of the earths. This is evidence that He did not mention these for specification, as shown by the fact that He did not mention cattle, which God created, nor minerals; rather He mentioned these things to emphasize the meaning of generality, as we mentioned in the example.

The third issue: His saying ﴿and of what they do not know﴾ contains a subtle meaning, namely that God mentioned that all is created only to declare God free of any partner, for the created cannot be a partner of the Creator. But true monotheism is attained only by acknowledging that there is no god but God. God the Exalted said: know that what prevents association is in what you know and what you do not know, because creation is general and the preventer of partnership is creation. So do not associate with God anything of what you know, for you know that it is created, and of what you do not know, for it is all created before God, since all of it is possible.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾

When God had argued from the conditions of the earth, which is the universal place, He argued from the night and day, which is the universal time. The indication of place and time is appropriate, because substances cannot do without place, and accidents cannot do without time, since every accident exists in a time. A similar point is mentioned in His words: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ (Fussilat: 37). Then He said after it: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾ (Fussilat: 39), where He argued by time and place there too. However, the primary aim there is the establishment of Oneness, by His words: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun﴾ (Fussilat: 37), and then resurrection, by His words: ﴿Indeed He who revived it is the one who will revive the dead﴾ (Fussilat: 39). Here the primary aim is the establishment of resurrection, because the mention of resurrection is more frequent in this surah, as the examination of the surah shows, whereas the mention of Oneness is more frequent there, as evidenced by His words in it: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ (Fussilat: 9), and so on. The end of the two surahs clarifies the matter. There are several issues:

Page 62

The first issue: place repels from the People of the Sunnah the doubts of the philosophers, and time repels from them the doubts of the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists).

As for the explanation of the first: the philosopher says, "If the non-existence of the world preceded its existence, then at the assumption of the world's non-existence there would be a 'before,' and 'before' and 'after' are realized only through time. So before the world there would be time, and time is part of the world, and so it follows that a thing exists at the time of its non-existence." If they respond that above the outermost sphere there is neither void nor plenum, we say: before the existence of the world, neither instant nor time exists.

As for the explanation of the second: the anthropomorphist says, "It is not possible for an existent to exist except in a place, so God is in a place." We say: then you must say, "God is in a time," because just as imagination cannot say, "He exists and there is no place," it cannot say, "He was existing and there was no time." Every time is originated, and we have agreed that God, exalted is He, is eternal.

The second issue: If someone says, "If the intended purpose is argument from time, why did He choose the night, saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾?" We say: when He argued by place, which is the dark, namely the earth, and said: ﴿And a sign for them is the earth﴾ (Ya-Sin: 33), He argued by time, in which there is darkness, which is the night.

Another aspect: the night contains the stillness of people, the calm of sounds, and sleep, which is like death, and after it comes the rising of the sun, like the blowing of the Trumpet, so people move. He therefore mentioned death, just as He said of the earth: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. Thus He mentioned from the two times the one most resembling death, just as He mentioned from the two places the one most resembling death.

The third issue: What is the meaning of stripping the day from the night? We say: its meaning is distinguishing it from it. It is said: "the day has been stripped from the night" when the end of the day arrives and the beginning of the night enters, and "God stripped it from it, so it was stripped from it." When it is used without the word "from," as in "you stripped the day or the sun," its meaning is that it entered its end. If it is asked: "The night in itself is a sign, so what need is there for His words: ﴿We strip from it the day﴾?" We say: the benefits and excellences of a thing are made clear by its opposite. For this reason God never made the night alone a sign in any place without mentioning the sign of the day along with it. His words ﴿and behold, they are in darkness﴾ mean: they enter into darkness. "Idha" here is for sudden occurrence, meaning that nothing remains in their hands of a matter after it, and they must enter into it.

The Qur'an verse 38 (Ya-Sin): ﴿And the sun runs on to a stationary place for it. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

It is possible that the waw is coordinating with "the night", so the sense is: "And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day, and the sun runs, and the moon – We have determined it." So all of these together are one sign. His saying, ﴿And the sun runs﴾, points to the cause of the stripping of the day, for it runs to its stationary place, which is the time of sunset, and so the day is stripped away. The benefit of mentioning the cause is that when God said, "We strip from it the day," it was not unlikely that some of the ignorant would say, "The stripping of the day is not from God; the day is stripped away only by the setting of the sun." So God said, ﴿And the sun runs to a stationary place for it﴾, pointing to the blessing of the day after the night. It is as if, when He said, ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾, He mentioned that the sun runs and rises at the end of the night, so the day returns with its benefits.

As for His saying, ﴿to a stationary place (li-mustaqarr)﴾, the lam may be for time, as in His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun (li-duluk al-shams)﴾ (al-Isra: 78) and His saying, ﴿So divorce them at their waiting period (li-'iddatihinna)﴾ (al-Talaq: 1). The reason for using the lam for time is that the lam with a kasra in nouns is for establishing the sense of possession (idafa), but attributing an action to its cause is the best of attributions, because idafa is for defining the first term by the second, as in the phrase "the house of Zayd" (dar Zayd). Yet the action is known by its cause, so one says: "Trade for profit (ittajir li-l-ribh)" and "buy for food (ishtari li-l-akl)." When it is known that the lam is used for causation, we say: the time of a thing resembles the cause of a thing, because the time brings about the matter occurring in it, and matters are connected to their times, so one says: "He went out (kharaja li-'ashr min kadha)" and "Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun (li-duluk al-shams)," because time is a defining factor like a cause.

On this basis, its meaning is: the sun runs at the time of its being stationary, that is, whenever it remains stationary for a period, it is commanded to run, and so it runs. It is also possible that the lam means "to" (ila), that is, to its stationary place. Its explanation is that the lam is mentioned for time, and time has two ends, a beginning and an end. One says: "I traveled from Friday to Thursday (min yawm al-jumu'a ila yawm al-khamis)," so the use of what is used for one of its two ends is permitted because of the connection between them. This is supported by the reading of one who recited: ﴿And the sun runs to a stationary place for it﴾ (wa-l-shamsu tajri ila mustaqarr lahā). On this basis, there are several views regarding that stationary place:

The first: the Day of Resurrection, when it comes to rest and no movement remains for it.

The second: the Sunnah (the sunset, or the end of the sun's course).

The third: the night, that is, it runs until the night.

The fourth: that the stationary place is not in reference to time but to place, and in that case there are several views:

The first: it is the furthest point of its rising in summer and the furthest point of its descent in winter; that is, it runs until it reaches that place, then it returns.

The second: it is the furthest of its risings, for each day it has a rising point, for six months, then it returns to those arches (al-muqantarat). This is the view mentioned earlier regarding the height, for the difference in risings is due to the difference in height.

The third: it is its arrival at its house at the beginning.

The fourth: it is the circle upon which its movement is based, where it does not deviate from the zodiac belt (mintaqat al-buruj) as the sun passes through it, and we will mention it.

It is also possible to say: ﴿to a stationary place for it﴾ means: it runs in the manner of its stationary place.

The astronomers (ahl al-hay'a) said: the sun is in an orbit, and the orbit revolves and thereby turns the sun, so the sun runs in the manner of its stationary place. The philosophers (al-falasifa) said: it runs to its stationary place, meaning toward a matter which, if it found it, would make it come to rest, and this is the extraction of the possible configurations, which is extremely weak. God answered this with His saying: ﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: it is not by its own will, but that is by the will of God, His decree, His management, and His subjugation of it.

If it is said: You have enumerated many views but have not mentioned the preferred one; what is your preferred view? We say: The preferred view is that what is meant by the stationary place is the location, that is, it runs in order to reach its stationary place, which is the furthest of its rising and descent, for this includes the risings and the settings, and the course which does not differ, and the time, which is the year and the night, so it is more complete in benefit.

His saying, ﴿That﴾ (dhalika), may refer to the running of the sun, meaning: that running is the decree of God; and it may refer to the stationary place, meaning: the stationary place is the decree of God. "Al-'Aziz" is the Dominant, and He, with perfect power, prevails. "Al-'Alim" is the one of perfect knowledge, that is, the One who was able to make it run in the most beneficial manner, and knew what was most beneficial, so He made it run accordingly. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: the sun, for six months, each day passes over the zenith of a thing which it did not pass over the day before at that zenith. Had God decreed that it pass over a single zenith, the land that lay under its path would burn, and the mass would remain dominant over the other places. So God decreed for it a distance, so that the moistures would gather in the interior of the earth and in the trees during winter; then He decreed its nearness gradually, so that the plants and fruits might emerge from the earth and the tree, ripen and dry; then it moves away so that the face of the earth and the branches of the trees do not burn.

The second: God decreed for it a rising each day and a setting each night, lest the strengths and the eyes grow weary through staying awake and fatigue, and lest the world fall into ruin through abandoning cultivation because of perpetual darkness.

The third: He made its course slower than the course of the moon and faster than the course of Saturn, because it is of perfect light. Had it been slow in its course, it would have remained for a long time at the zenith of one thing and burned it; and had it been very swift, it would not have had a lingering period sufficient to ripen fruits in a single place.

[Page 63]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the moon—We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old date-stalk.﴾

Page 64

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is necessary to supply a word that completes the meaning of the sentence, because the moon did not make itself into phases. So the meaning is: We determined its course as phases. Based on what he mentioned, it is possible to say that the intended meaning is: "And the moon, We have made it possessing phases (*dhā manāzil*)," because "possessor of a thing" is close to the thing itself. This is why the saying of the speaker is permitted: "a pleasing life" (*ʿīshatun rāḍiyatun*), since the possessor of a thing is like one who is established by the thing, so they used the adjectival form.

His words ﴿until it returns like the old date-stalk﴾: that is, it returns in its thinness to its former state that it had before. The *ʿurjūn* (the dried stalk of a date cluster), from *al-inʿirāj* (curving), is said of the stalk of a date cluster: *ʿurjūn*. And *qadīm* means that which has been long in time. It has been said: whatever has remained for a year is *qadīm*. The correct view is that this specific measure is not a condition for applying the term *qadīm* to it; rather, custom is what is taken into account. So one does not say of a city built one or two years ago that it is an ancient building or that it is ancient. Yet some things are called *qadīm* even if they have not existed for a year. This is why it is permitted to say "an ancient house" (*bayt qadīm*) and "an ancient building" (*binā' qadīm*). But it is not permitted to say of the world (*ʿālam*) that it is *qadīm*, because antiquity in a house and a building is established by the passage of time and the years passing over it. Applying the term *qadīm* to the world is not customary except among those who believe that it has no beginning and nothing precedes it.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Neither may the sun overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; and each is travelling in an orbit.﴾

This is an indication that each of the things mentioned was created in accordance with wisdom. The sun was not suited to a speed of motion by which it would overtake the moon; otherwise there would be summer and winter in a single month, and the fruits would not ripen.

As for His words: ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day⦆. It has been said in its interpretation that the authority of the night, which is the moon, does not outstrip the sun, which is the authority of the day.

It has also been said: its meaning is "nor does the night outstrip the day", i.e., the night does not enter the time of the day.

The second view is far-fetched, because that would be clarifying the obvious. The first view is correct if what is intended is what I have explained, namely that the meaning of His words ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ is that when the moon is on the eastern horizon during the nights of conjunction-opposition (ayyam al-istiqbal), the sun is opposite it on the western horizon. Then at sunset the moon rises, and at sunrise the moon sets, as though they had a single motion, although the sun lags behind the moon by a noticeable amount each night, as perceived by the senses. So if the moon had a single motion by which it outstrips the sun and the sun does not overtake it, and the sun had a single motion by which it lags behind the moon and does not overtake the moon, then the moon and the sun would remain for a long period in one place, because the sun's motion is one degree each day. Therefore God Most High placed in all the stars another motion, other than the motion of the month and the year, namely the daily revolution. By this revolution no star outstrips another star at all, because whenever one star rises, its counterpart sets, and whenever a star advances to the position where another star is, relative to us, that star advances. By this motion the sun is not outstripped. Thus it becomes clear that the authority of the night does not outstrip the authority of the day. So what is meant by "night" is the moon and what is meant by "day" is the sun. His words ﴿Neither may the sun overtake the moon﴾ indicate its slow motion, which completes the revolution in a year. His words ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ indicate its daily motion, by which it returns from the east to the east again in a day and a night. On this basis, there are several issues:

Issue One: What is the wisdom in using "night" and intending its authority, which is the moon? And what would happen if He had said "nor does the moon outstrip the sun"? We say: If He had said "nor does the moon outstrip the sun", it would not have been understood that the indication is to the daily motion, and contradiction would have been suspected, for if the sun does not overtake the moon, it is apparently faster. And if He had said "nor is the moon outstripping", it would be thought that the moon does not outstrip, and so it is not faster. Therefore He said "the night and the day", so that it would be known that the indication is to the motion by which the revolution is completed in the period of a day and a night, and so that all the stars have, or are subject to, rising and setting in the night and the day.

Issue Two: What is the benefit of His words ﴿Neither may the sun overtake﴾ in verbal form, and His words ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ in the form of the active participle? Why did He not say "nor does the night outstrip" or "overtaking the moon"? We say: The primary motion that belongs to the sun, by which the moon is not overtaken, is specific to the sun, so He made it as though it proceeded from it, and it was mentioned in verbal form, because the verbal form is not applied to something from which the action does not proceed. Thus one does not say "he sews" if sewing does not proceed from him.

The second motion is not specific to any one star; rather all share in it, by reason of the motion of the sphere. So that is not a sphere belonging to a particular star. The motion is therefore not as if it proceeded from it, and He used the active participle, because it does not necessarily imply the proceeding of the action. One says "So-and-so is a tailor" even if he is not actually sewing at the time.

If it is said: His words ﴿He covers the night over the day, seeking it swiftly﴾ (al-A'raf: 54) indicate otherwise than what you have mentioned, for if the day seeks the night then the night is ahead of it, and you have said that His words ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ mean what you mentioned, so the night would be outstripping and not outstripping.

We say: We have mentioned that what is meant by "night" here is the authority of the night, which is the moon, and it does not outstrip the sun by the swift daily motion. What is meant by "night" there is the night itself, and each one, since it follows the other, is as though seeking it. If it is asked: why did He say here "outstrips the day" while there He said "seeking it", and did not say "pursuing it"? We say: That is because of what we have explained, that what is meant in this surah by "night" is the star of the night, and in this motion it is as if it had no motion and did not outstrip, and it is not of its nature to be outstripping; whereas what is meant there is the night and the day themselves, which are two periods of time, and time has no rest, so it is sought swiftly, since pursuit proceeds from it. His words ﴿and each is travelling in an orbit﴾ confirm what we have mentioned, namely that for all of them there is rising and setting in a day and a night, none of them outstrips another with respect to this motion, and each motion is in an orbit belonging to it. And in this are several issues:

Issue One: The tanwin in His words "wa-kullun" (and each) is a substitute for the genitive construction, its meaning being "each one". The omission of the tanwin is due to the idafa, so that definiteness and indefiniteness do not combine in one word. When the word that is added to has been dropped verbally, the tanwin is returned to it verbally, while in meaning it remains defined by the idafa. If it is asked: does the matter differ when there is an explicit idafa and when it is omitted? We say: Yes, because the statement "each one of the people is so-and-so" does not lead understanding to anything other than them, so it restricts understanding to them. But when one says "each such-and-such" the understanding includes a generality greater than the generality with the explicit idafa. This is like "qablu" and "ba'du": when you say "do it before such-and-such", but when you omit the added word and say "do it before", the understanding is that the act is before everything.

If it is asked: is there a difference between our saying "kullun minhum", "kulluhum", and "kullun"? We say: Yes. With "kulluhum" you establish the matter as restricted to them; with "kullun minhum" you first establish the matter as general, then qualify it by specification, saying "minhum"; and with "kullun" you establish the matter as general and leave it so.

Issue Two: If "kullun" means "each one of them", and what is mentioned is the sun and the moon, how did He say "yasbahun" (they travel)? We say: The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: We have explained that His words "kullun" are for generality, so it is as though He informed about every star in the sky that wanders.

[page 66]

The second: The word "kull" may be treated as singular, considering that it is a singular word, not dual or plural, and it may be made plural because its meaning is plural. As for the dual, neither the word nor the meaning indicates it. So it is good for one to say "Zayd and 'Amr, kullun jā'a" or "kullun jā'ū", but one does not say "kullun jā'ā" with the dual.

The third: When He said "nor does the night outstrip the day", and what was meant was what is in the night of stars, He said "yasbahun".

* * *

Issue Three: What is the falak? We say: It is a rotating body, or a rotating surface, or a circle, because the people of the language agreed that the spindle-whorl (falakat al-mighzal) was named falaka because of its roundness, and the falaka of the tent is the flat round piece of wood placed on the top of the pole so that the pole does not tear the tent, and it is a round flat surface. If it is said: then according to this the sky would be round. Most exegetes agreed that the sky is spread out, without edges, over mountains, and is like a level ceiling, and His words confirm this: ﴿and the raised roof﴾ (al-Tur: 5). We say: There is nothing in the texts that indicates decisively that the sky is spread out and not round, and sensory evidence has indicated that it is round, so it is necessary to adopt that.

As for the first, it is evident, because a domed ceiling does not cease to be a ceiling, and likewise its being over mountains.

As for the sensory evidence, there are several aspects:

The first: whoever travels far toward the south sees stars like Suhayl and others appear to him perpetually, so that one who observes sees them always, while Banat Na'sh and others remain perpetually hidden from him. If the sky were flat and level, all would be visible to all, unlike when it is round, for then part of it is concealed by the edges of the earth, and so it is not seen.

The second: when the sun is in conjunction with Aries, for example, after it sets there appears to us a star in the zodiac from Aries to Libra, then after a little while the star whose setting was after the setting of the sun is concealed, and the star whose rising was after the rising of the sun appears, and the reverse; this is a clear proof, and if it is examined it becomes certain.

The third: before its rising and after its setting, the sun's light appears and the atmosphere is somewhat illuminated before it rises; were it not that part of the sky is concealed by the earth, where the sun is located, its body would not be seen and its light would not spread as it does, but rather, when it returns to the sky, its body and light would appear together to everyone, since the sky would then be level and fully exposed to everyone.

The fourth: when the moon is eclipsed at an hour of the night on the eastern side, then if people in the west are asked about the time of the eclipse, they report an eclipse at an hour other than that hour, earlier than the hour in which the people of the east saw the eclipse. Yet the eclipse occurs at one time in all regions of the world, while the night differs. This indicates that night on the eastern side comes before night on the western side. The sun has set for the people of the east while it is still visible in the sky to the people of the west. Thus its concealment by the earth is known; had the sky been level, this would not be so.

The fifth: if the sky were spread out, the moon, when it is directly above our heads, would be nearer to us, and when it is on the horizon it would be farther from us, because the general (the horizon) is smaller than the diameter and the stake. Likewise with the sun and the stars: they should appear larger when nearer, and they do not.

If it is said:

[page 67]

It is possible that it is on the horizon on the surface of the sky, and when it is directly over our heads it is sunk into the sea of the sky, since tearing is possible in the sky. We say: There is no dispute about the possibility of a tear, but then the moon's motion would be in a circle, not along a straight line, and that is our point. Also we say: if that were so, the moon for the people of the east, at the middle of their day, would be larger in size, being near their heads, given its being placed on the lower surface of the sky, and for us in the sea of the sky. In sum, the proofs are many, and multiplying them befits the books of astronomy, whose purpose is to explain that science; the purpose of exegesis is not to explain that, but the portion we have presented suffices to show that it is a round sphere.

**The fourth issue:** This indicates that each star has an orbit (*falak*). What is your view on this? We say: as for the seven wandering bodies (*al-sab'a al-sayyara*), each has its own orbit. As for the other stars, it has been said that they all share one orbit. Let us mention a brief discussion on this topic from astronomy (*al-hay'a*, the science of celestial configuration), since it is necessary to begin with it because of the explanation of *falak*. We say: It has been said that the Moon has an orbit, because its motion is faster than the motion of the other six. Likewise, each star has an orbit, because their courses differ in speed, slowness and passage. Some of them pass through one circle and others through another circle. At some times one of them passes by another without eclipsing it, and at other times it eclipses it. So each star has an orbit.

Then the people of astronomy said: every orbit is a solid sphere. That is not necessary. Rather, what is necessary is that we say: for each orbit there is a sphere, a surface, or a circle that the star produces by its motion. God, exalted is He, is able to create the star within a sphere in which its existence is like that of a nail fixed in the thickness of a hollow sphere, and He turns the sphere so that the star rotates with the rotation of the sphere. According to the view of the astronomers, the motion of the wandering stars is in this manner.

Likewise, He is able to create a ring surrounded by four parallel surfaces, which are four parallel circles, like a millstone when we hollow it out and remove from its middle a hand-mill, leaving a ring surrounded by surfaces and circles as we have mentioned. The stars are in it, and it is an orbit. That ring turns and turns the star. Although motion in this manner is within God's power, none of those whose opinion is considered has held it.

Likewise, He is able to make the stars such that they cut through the sky, producing an imagined circle, just as if you imagine a fish in water on two sides, descending from one side and ascending to a place on the other side in a curve. This is what is understood from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each in an orbit they float﴾ (Yasin: 40). The apparent meaning is that the motion of the stars is in this manner. The astronomers rejected this and said: motion in this manner is not permissible, because the star has a body; when it cuts through the sky and moves, either the place of its rotation splits and rejoins, like water that the fish moves, or it does not split and does not rejoin, but there is an empty space in which the star rotates. But emptiness is impossible, and the sky does not accept splitting and rejoining. This is what they relied upon. We say: both are permissible.

As for emptiness, it is not needed here, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they float﴾ implies that it is by splitting and rejoining. As for the impossibility of splitting and rejoining, they have no proof for it. Their argument concerning the boundary that determines the directions is weak there. Then they said, as we have explained: the motions emerge, and by this we know the eclipses. If the stars had different motions, the eclipse would not necessarily occur at the time at which an eclipse or lunar eclipse is judged to occur. That is because we say: the Sun has two orbits. One of them has its centre at the centre of the world. The second has its centre above the centre of the world, like the whiteness of an egg between its yolk and its membrane. The Sun is a sphere in the eccentric orbit (*al-falak al-kharij al-markaz*), which turns once a year with its rotation. When it is placed on the upper side, it is far from the Earth, and it is said to be at the apogee (*al-awj*). When it is on the lower side, it is near the Earth, and it is at the perigee (*al-hadid*).

As for the Moon, it has one orbit that encompasses all its parts and orbits, and another orbit which is part of the first orbit, surrounding it like the upper skin of an onion. And a third orbit is within the lower orbit, as was the case with the eccentric orbit in the Sun's orbit. In the eccentric orbit there is a sphere the size of the body of the Sun, and in the sphere the Moon is fixed like a nail in a sphere in which it is immersed. The upper orbit is called *al-jawzahr*, the eccentric orbit is called *al-falak al-hamil* (the carrying orbit), and the lower orbit in which the carrying orbit is located is called *al-falak al-ma'il* (the inclined orbit). The sphere that is in the carrier is called *falak al-tadwir* (the epicyclic orbit). They said likewise regarding the five remaining wandering stars, except that the upper one which they called *al-jawzahr* they did not attribute to them. Thus they established twenty-four orbits: the highest orbit and the orbit of the zodiac (*falak al-buruj*). Saturn has three orbits: the *mumaththil* (the representing orbit), the carrier, and the epicyclic orbit. Jupiter has three, as Saturn does. Mars likewise has three. The Sun has two orbits: the *mumaththil* and the eccentric orbit, the centre-bearing one. Venus has three orbits, as the superior planets have. Mercury has four orbits: the three we mentioned for the superior planets, and another orbit which they call *al-mudir* (the directing orbit). The Moon has four orbits, and the fourth they call the *jawzahr* orbit. The *mudir* is not like the *jawzahr*, because the *mudir* does not encompass the orbits of Mercury, whereas the *jawzahr* does encompass them. Some of them added to the five, for each orbit, two other orbits, and made their epicycles composed of three orbits. They said: because of these bodies the motions of the stars differ, and there occur for them retrogression (*'urud*), retrograde motion (*ruju'*), stationary phase (*istiqama*), slowness and speed.

This is their discussion in a summary and abbreviated form. We say: it is not far from God's power to create the like of that. But as for it being necessary, we do not concede it. Their retrogression and stationary phase are by God's will, and likewise their latitude, longitude, slowness, speed, nearness and distance. This is the complete discussion.

**The fifth issue:** The astrologers (*al-munajjimun*) said: the stars are living beings, as evidence that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿they float﴾, and that is not applied except to a rational being. We say: if you mean the degree by which glorification (*tasbih*) is valid, then we say yes, for there is nothing among these things except that it glorifies God's praise. If you mean something other than that, then it is not established, and usage does not prove it, as in His saying, exalted is He, regarding the idols: ﴿Why do you not speak?﴾ (al-Saffat: 92) and His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not speak?﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 23).

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾. It has a connection with what preceded in two respects:

The first: when He bestowed favour by reviving the earth, which is the place of living creatures, He made clear that He did not limit Himself to this. Rather, He made for humanity a way that is taken from the sea for good, and they may traverse it or travel upon it just as they travel upon land. This is like His saying: ﴿And We carried them on the land and the sea﴾ (al-Isra: 70). This is supported by His saying: ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that which they ride﴾ (Ya-Sin: 42), if we interpret it as meaning camels, for they are like the ships of the deserts.

The second: when He explained the floating of the stars in their orbits (aflak), He mentioned something similar to it, namely the floating of the ship on the seas.

It also has a third aspect: the matters with which Allah has blessed His servants are of two kinds, some necessary and some beneficial. The first is for need, and the second is for adornment. The creation of the earth and its reviving is of the first kind, for it is the place without which humanity would not exist, and without its reviving humanity would not live. The night and the day in His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ are also of the first kind, for it is the time without which humanity would not have come into being; and the sun, the moon and their movement, were they not present, humanity would not live. Then, when He mentioned two signs of the first kind, He mentioned two signs of the second kind, which is adornment:

The first: the ships that run on the sea, by which what is used for adornment is extracted from the sea, as He said: ﴿And from each you eat tender flesh and extract ornaments which you wear, and you see the ships therein plowing [through the water]﴾ (Fatir: 12).

The second: the animals that are on land, which are like the ships on the sea, in His saying: ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that which they ride﴾ (Ya-Sin: 42). Indeed, animals are an adornment, as He said: ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ (al-Nahl: 8), and He said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture﴾ (al-Nahl: 6). Thus it is an argument against them by means of the necessary and the beneficial. It cannot be said that the beneficial is mentioned in His saying: ﴿gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾, for these are for adornment; because we say that this came as a consequence of the necessary, for when Allah created the earth productive to remove necessity, and sent down water upon it, it followed that by the power of Allah He would bring forth from it palm trees and grapevines. As for the ship, it is intended and not a consequence. Then, once the connection is known, there are linguistic and semantic discussions regarding the verses.

As for the linguistic ones, we mention them in issues:

First issue: The commentators said: "the dhurriyyah" (offspring) are the fathers, meaning: We carried your fathers in the ship. The alif and lam are for definiteness, i.e. the ship of Noah, which is mentioned in His saying: ﴿And construct the ship﴾ (Hud: 37), and it is known to the Arabs, so He said "the ship." This is the saying of some of them. But most of them hold that "dhurriyyah" is applied only to offspring, and on this basis the meaning must be explained. We say: "the ship" either means the specific ship that belonged to Noah, or it means the genus, as He said: ﴿And He made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 12), and He said: ﴿And you see the ships therein plowing﴾ (Fatir: 12), and He said: ﴿So when they board the ship﴾ (al-Ankabut: 65), and other uses of the definite article with "ship" to denote the genus. If the intended meaning is the ship of Noah, peace be upon him, then there are several views:

The first: that the meaning is: We carried your descendants until the Day of Resurrection in that ship; for without that there would have remained no progeny or posterity for the children of Adam. On this basis, His saying: ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ replaces His saying: "We carried them," as an indication of the completeness of the blessing; that is, the blessing was not limited to you, but extended to your descendants until the Day of Resurrection. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. It is possible in my view to say on this basis that He specified the offspring by mention only because those present were disbelievers, and there was no benefit in their existence. So He said: ﴿We carried their offspring﴾, meaning the carrying was not a carrying of them, but rather a carrying of what was in their loins of believers. This is like one who carries a box that has no value, but within it are jewels; if he is asked, "Why do you carry this box and toil in carrying it, when it cannot be sold for anything?" he says: "I am not carrying the box, but what is in it."

The second: that "dhurriyyah" here means the genus; its meaning is: We carried their kinds. This is because the offspring of an animal is of its own kind and species, and "dhurriyyah" is applied to the genus. Hence the Prophet ﷺ's prohibition of killing the "dharari" (ﷺ), that is, the women, is reported, because a woman, although a different category from a man, is of his kind and species. One says: "dharariyyuna," meaning "our likes." So His saying: ﴿that We carried their offspring﴾ means their likes; and their fathers are then included among them.

The third: that the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And a sign for them﴾ refers to "the servants," since He said: ﴿Alas for the servants﴾, and after that He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the earth﴾, and He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾, and He said: ﴿And a sign for them, that We carried their offspring﴾. Once this is known, it is as if He said: "And a sign for the servants: that We carried the offspring of the servants." It is not necessary that the pronoun in both places refer to specific individuals, as He said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (al-Nisa: 29), meaning one of them kills another. Similarly, when a people fight and all die in the fighting, one says: "These people killed themselves," so in both places the reference is to the people, not specific individuals; rather, the meaning is that some of them killed others. So likewise His saying: ﴿And a sign for them﴾ means a sign for each part of them: that We carried the offspring of some of them upon others, or the offspring of some of them.

As for if we say that the intended meaning is the genus of ships, this is more evident, because Noah's ship was not in their presence, and they did not know who was carried in it. But the genus of ships is apparent to everyone. His saying about Noah's ship: ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾ (al-Ankabut: 15) means by the existence of its kind and its likeness. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Do you not see that the ships run through the sea by the favour of Allah, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾ (Luqman: 31). So we say: His saying: ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ means the offspring of the servants, and He did not say "We carried them," because the settling of the earth is general to everyone who dwells upon it, so He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ up to His saying: ﴿from it they eat﴾, because eating is general. As for carrying in the ship, among people there are those who never ride it in their lives and are never carried in it; but the offspring of the servants must have that, for among them are those who need it and are carried in it.

Second issue: "the ship" (al-fulk) is sometimes used in the plural, as when He said: ﴿And you see the ships therein plowing﴾ (Fatir: 12), and at other times in the singular, as when He said: ﴿in the laden ship﴾. We say: there is a subtle point of fine linguistic knowledge here, namely that a word may have a vowel pattern like that of another word in form, while the two vowel patterns differ in meaning. An example is your saying: "sajada yasjudu sujudan" as a verbal noun, and "hum qawmun sujud" as the plural of "sajid." You may think they are one word with two meanings, but that is not so. Rather, "sujud" as a verbal noun has an original vowel, and if we say the verb is derived from the verbal noun, then the vowel of "sujud" as a plural is a changed vowel, since the plural is derived from the singular, and the derived form must undergo a change in vowel, letter, or both. So when we wished to derive a plural form from "sajid," we changed it and used the form "sujud." Thus "sujud" as a verbal noun and as a plural are not among the homonymous words that are coined with one vowel pattern for two meanings. Knowing this, we say: "al-fulk," when singular, is like "qufl" and "burd," and when plural, like "khushub," "murud," and others. If you say: "When you make it a plural, what is its singular?" We say: its singular may be "fulkah" or another form that has not been used, like the singular of "nisa'" (women), since it has not been used. The same applies to: ﴿imamin mubin﴾ and to His saying: ﴿a day when We shall call every people with their imam﴾ (al-Isra: 71), meaning with their imams. In ﴿imamin mubin﴾, "imam" is like "zimam" and "kitab"; and in ﴿every people with their imam﴾, "imam" is like "sihan," "kiram," and "ji'ab." This is among the subtle points of morphology.

As for the semantic ones, we mention them in issues:

First issue: Here He said: ﴿We carried their offspring﴾, bestowing favour upon them by carrying their offspring; and in another place He said: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing vessel﴾ (al-Haqqah: 11), bestowing favour upon them there by carrying themselves. We say: because whoever benefits what is connected to another has benefited that other; and whoever repels harm from what is connected to another has not repelled harm from that other, but has benefited him. An example: whoever does good to a person's child and gladdens him, that child's father is gladdened by his gladness; and if someone removes pain from a person's child, he has gladdened the father, though he has not in reality removed pain from the father. When the water rose, harm would befall them; so He said: "I have repelled harm from you," and had He said: "I have repelled harm from your children," the repelling of harm from them would not have been clearly expressed. Here He intended to express benefits, so He said: ﴿We carried their offspring﴾, because the benefit is achieved through the benefit to the offspring. This is shown by the fact that here He said: ﴿in the laden ship﴾, for the filling of the ship with goods conveys the benefit when it is mentioned; but the repelling of harm is not so, because the heavier the ship, the slower the escape, whereas there lies safety. So in that context He chose what indicates escape from harm, namely the running (jary), and here what indicates the completeness of benefit, namely the loading (shahn). If it is said: He said ﴿And We carried them on the land and the sea﴾ (al-Isra: 70) without saying "We carried their offspring," although the aim in both places is to express blessing, not to remove affliction, we say: when He said ﴿on the land and the sea﴾, it was general to creation, for no one is without being carried on land or sea; but carrying on the sea was not general, so He said, in effect: "If We did not carry you yourselves, We have carried those whose affairs concern you: your children, relatives, brothers and friends."

Second issue: His saying ﴿the laden﴾ conveys another benefit beyond what we mentioned, namely that the human being sinks in water and drowns. Therefore his being carried in the ship happens by the power of Allah. Yet some of the natural philosophers say: "The light does not sink in water, because the light seeks the direction above." So He said ﴿the laden ship﴾, which is heavier than the heavy things that sink; and despite this Allah carried the human being in it along with its weight. If they say that this is because a void is impossible, we say: we have mentioned the proofs indicating the possibility of a void in the rational books. Therefore, keeping the heavy above water is nothing but by the will of Allah.

Third issue: He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the earth﴾ and He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾, and He did not say: "And a sign for them is the ship, which We made such that it carries them." This is because their being carried in the ship is the wonder. As for the ship itself, it is no wonder, for it is like a house built of wood. But the earth itself is a wonder, and the night itself is a wonder, which no one has power over except Allah.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We created for them of the like of it that they ride.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: as regards the linguistic and semantic aspects. As for the language, His saying "for them" (lahum) may be taken as referring to the offspring, meaning: We carried their offspring, and We created for those who are carried what they ride. It may also be taken as referring to the servants to whom the statement "And a sign for them" (﴿وآيَةٌ لَهُمْ﴾) refers, and this is the correct view, because the apparent meaning is that pronouns refer to one single thing.

The second issue: (min) may carry two meanings.

The first: that it is a connecting particle (ṣila), its implied sense being: "And We created for them its like." This is the view of al-Akhfash. Sibawayh says that min is a connecting particle only in negation, as in: "Mā jā'anī min aḥad" (no one came to me), as in His saying: ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ (Qaf: 38).

The second: it is explanatory (mubayyina), as in His saying: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾ (Nuh: 4). It is as if, when He said "We created for them" (Ya-Sin: 42), and what was created was various things, He said "of the like of the ship" to clarify.

The third issue: the pronoun in ﴿its like﴾ refers, according to the majority, to the ship (al-fulk), and this is like His saying: ﴿And other kinds of similar ones﴾ (Sad: 58). On this basis, the more evident view is that the intended meaning is another ship that existed in their time. What supports this is that He said: ﴿And if We will, We drown them﴾, and if the intended meaning were the camels, as some exegetes have said, then His saying "And We created for them of the like of it that they ride" would be an interruption between two connected statements. It may also be said that the pronoun refers to something known but unmentioned, its implied sense being: "And We created for them of the like of what We have mentioned of the created things," in His saying: ﴿He created the pairs, all of them, of what the earth brings forth﴾.

This is like what they said concerning His saying: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾, that the pronoun refers to what we have mentioned, meaning: of the fruit of what we have mentioned. On this basis, His saying ﴿We created for them﴾ contains a subtle point: that every person has a mount of the animals to ride, but not everyone rides the ship. So He said concerning the ship: "We carried their offspring" (﴿حَمَلْنا ذُرِّيَّتَهم﴾), though We did not carry them ourselves. As for creation, it is general for them, and as for what they ride, there are two views:

The first: it is the ship like the ship of Noah.

The second: it is the camels, which are "the ships of the desert." If it is asked: if the intended meaning is Noah's ship, what is the connection of the discourse? We say: He reminded them of the condition of the people of Noah, and that the deniers perished while the believers succeeded; likewise, if they believe they will succeed, and if they deny they will perish.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if We will, We drown them﴾, indicating two benefits:

The first: that in a state of blessing one should not feel secure from the punishment of Allah.

The second: that this is an answer to an implied question, namely that the naturalist says: "The ship carries by the necessity of nature, and what is hollow does not sink." So He said: "It is not so; rather, if Allah wills, He drowns them, and that is not by the necessity of nature." And if his corrupt statement were valid, it would be possible for someone to say: "Do you not agree that some ships capsize and break, and some are pierced by a piercer so that they sink, and all of that is by the will of Allah? If Allah wills to drown them, He drowns them without any of these causes, as is the doctrine of the People of the Sunna, or by some of those causes, as you concede."

And His saying, ﴿Then there will be no one to cry out for them﴾, meaning, no helper who would protect them from drowning.

And His saying, ﴿nor will they be rescued﴾, when drowning overtakes them. This is because deliverance from punishment is either by averting the punishment from its root or by lifting it after it has befallen. So He said: "there is no one to cry out for them" that would avert it, and "nor will they be rescued" after they have fallen into it. This is like His saying: ﴿Their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they save me﴾.

In His saying, ﴿So there is no one to cry out for them, nor will they be rescued﴾, there is another benefit beyond restriction, namely that He said "no صَرِيخ (one to cry out for them)" and did not say "no مُنْقِذ (rescuer) for them." This is because one whose role is not to help does not begin to help for fear of being defeated and losing his dignity. Rather, one helps and rescues only the person whose role it is to rescue. So He said "there is no صَرِيخ for them." As for one whose role is not to rescue, if he sees someone dear to him in harm, he begins the rescue even though he does not trust himself to rescue and does not think it likely, and he only exerts his utmost effort. So He said ﴿nor will they be rescued﴾, and did not say "there is no مُنْقِذ for them."

Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except as a mercy from Us and as enjoyment for a time﴾. This indicates two matters:

First: the rescue is divided into two kinds, mercy and enjoyment. That is, for whom God knows will believe, God rescues him as a mercy; and for whom He knows will not believe, He lets him enjoy for a time and increase in sin.

Second: it clarifies that rescue does not yield permanence, but rather that cessation in this world is unavoidable. So God rescues him as a mercy and lets him enjoy for a time, then He causes him to die. Thus cessation is bound to occur.

The signs were meant to produce certainty and to make necessary the conviction of what God, exalted is He, had said, but they did not produce certainty in them. He said: then at least they should guard themselves against punishment, for whoever is informed of the occurrence of a punishment will guard against it, even if he is not certain of the truthfulness of the informant, as a precaution. So God, exalted is He, said: when the decisive proof is presented to them, they do not recognize it, and when it is said to them, "Fear," they do not fear. They are thus in the utmost ignorance and the extremity of heedlessness, unlike the scholars who follow demonstrative proof, and unlike the common people who base matters on the most cautious course. What we have mentioned is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾, with the particle of hope (la'alla), meaning: in your assumption. For whoever is unaware of the aspect of the demonstrative proof does not abandon the method of caution and precaution. The answer to His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear"﴾ is omitted, its meaning being: and when that is said to them, they do not fear, or they turn away. It was omitted because what follows it indicates it, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them﴾ [al-An'am: 4]. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what is before you and what is behind you﴾, there are several interpretations:

First: "What is before you" is the Hereafter, for they are facing toward it, and "what is behind you" is this world, for they are leaving it behind.

Second: "What is before you" refers to kinds of punishment such as drowning and burning and other things, indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry for them, nor are they rescued﴾. "What is behind you" is death, which pursues you; if you escape these things, there is no escape for you from it. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and enjoyment for a time﴾.

Third: "What is before you" is the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, for he is present with you, and "what is behind you" is the matter of the Resurrection, for if you guard against denying Muhammad ﷺ and denying the Resurrection, God will have mercy upon you. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾, even though mercy is obligatory, there are several interpretations for it, which we have mentioned repeatedly, and here we add another aspect: that when He said: ﴿Fear﴾, in the sense that if you do not reach certainty based on the proofs, then fear as a precaution, He said: ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾, meaning: the people of certainty will certainly be shown mercy, and the people of precaution are hoped to be shown mercy. The truth is what we have mentioned, in two aspects:

One of them: Fear, hoping for mercy, for God is not obligated to anything.

The second: that guarding oneself, considered in relation to Him, is a matter that gives rise to the expectation of mercy. If someone is certain of it on account of an external matter, that does not prevent hope. For when a king has in his heart to give one who serves him many times more than his wage, yet the service does not require that, it is valid for him to say: "Do such-and-such." And it is not unlikely that your wage reaches you in greater amount than what you deserve.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾
