Whoever denies some of them, denying all of them becomes easy for him.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 36, verses 47–49:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom Allah would have fed if He willed? You are not but in clear error."﴾

This indicates that they withhold everything that is due from the *mukallaf* (the person bound by religious obligations). That is because the *mukallaf* is obligated to exalt the side of Allah and to show compassion toward the creation of Allah. They abandoned the exaltation of Allah when it was said to them, "Fear Allah," and they did not fear Him. They abandoned compassion toward the creation of Allah when it was said to them, ﴿Spend,﴾ and they did not spend. In this there are subtleties:

The first: They were addressed with the lowest degrees of exaltation and compassion, and they did not bring any of it. The sincere servants of Allah were addressed with the lowest level and they brought the highest. We say this because they were commanded in matters of piety to guard against what is before them of punishment or the Hereafter, and what is behind them of death or punishment, and this is the minimum of guarding. As for the elect, they guard against changing the heart of the king against them even if he does not punish them, and guarding against punishment belongs only to the distant. So they did not guard against the disobedience of Allah, and they did not guard against the punishment of Allah. The sincere ones feared Allah and avoided opposing Him, whether or not He would punish them for it. As for compassion, they were told, ﴿Spend from what﴾ — that is, some of what belongs to Allah that is in your hands — and they did not spend. The sincere ones preferred others over themselves and gave away everything in their hands; indeed, they directed their very selves toward benefiting the servants of Allah and warding off harm from them.

The second: Just as in the matter of exaltation the benefit of exalting returns only to the one who exalts, since Allah is independent of their exaltation, likewise in the matter of compassion the benefit of compassion returns only to them. For whoever is not provided for by the wealthy man will not die except at his appointed term, and his provision must reach him; but the fortunate one is the one whom Allah has decreed that the provision should reach others through his hand.

The third: His saying ﴿from what He has provided you﴾ points to two matters:

The first: that withholding it is extremely ugly, for the most miserly of the miserly is the one who withholds the wealth of others.

The second: that the fear of poverty should not prevent you from this, for Allah has provided you, so when you spend, He will replace it for you again just as He provided you at first.

There are also issues in this:

The first issue: At His saying, "And when it is said to them, 'Spend,'" He omitted the response, and here He answered and gave more than the response. That is because if He had said, "And when it is said to them, 'Spend,' they say, 'Shall we feed one whom Allah would have fed if He willed?'" it would have been sufficient. So what is the benefit of His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe﴾ [al-Ankabut: 12]? We say: the disbelievers used to claim that feeding is among the praiseworthy qualities, and they boasted of it. They only intended by that statement to refute the believers. They said: "We feed the guests, believing that our deeds are praiseworthy, and were it not for our feeding, the guest's need would not be met. And you say that your God provides whom He wills, so why do you tell us to spend?" Since their aim was to refute the believers, not to refrain from feeding, Allah the Exalted said of them, ﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe,﴾ indicating the refutation. As for their saying, ﴿Guard against what is before you,﴾ they had no refutation of the believers, so they turned away, and Allah turned away from mentioning their turning away, since the knowledge of it is already established.

The second issue: What is the benefit of changing the wording in their reply, where they did not say, "Shall we spend on one whom Allah would have provided if He willed?" That is because they were commanded to spend in His saying, ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend,"﴾ so their reply should have been, "Shall we spend?" Why then did they say, [the Arabic: ] ﴿Shall we feed﴾? We say: In it is a demonstration of the extreme extent of their opposition. For when they were commanded to spend — and spending includes feeding and other things — they did not spend, nor did they spend even less than that, which is feeding, and they said, "We will not feed." This is like when a speaker says to another, "Give Zayd a dinar," and he replies, "I will not give him a dirham," whereas the matching response would be, "I will not give him a dinar." But exaggeration in this manner is more complete, so it is likewise here.

The third issue: Their statement was true, for if Allah willed, He would have fed him. So why did He mention it in the context of blame? We say: because their intent was to deny the power of Allah, or to deny the permissibility of commanding spending while Allah has power. Both are corrupt, and Allah clarified this in His saying, ﴿from what He has provided you,﴾ for it indicates His power and validates His command to give. For whoever has wealth in the hand of another and has wealth in his own treasuries is free to choose: if he wills, he gives from what is in his treasuries, and if he wills, he orders the one who has the wealth to give. And it is not permissible for one who has his wealth in your treasuries, which exceeds what is in my hand, to say, "Give him from it." His saying ﴿You are not but in clear error﴾ indicates their belief that they had silenced the believers with this statement, and that their command to spend, together with their claim of Allah's power, is manifestly corrupt, while their own belief is the corrupt one. In it there are linguistic and semantic discussions.

As for the linguistic: We say: ﴿in﴾ (*in*) may be used for negation in the sense of *ma* (*ma*), and the original use of *in* is for the conditional, while the original use of *ma* is for negation. But the two share some aspects, so they are close. *Ma* is used in the conditional, and *in* is used in negation. The shared aspect is that each of them is a particle composed of two close letters, for the hamza is close to the alif and the mim is close to the nun. The meaning that follows *ma* must be such that it may or may not be established. As for *ma*, this is clear. As for *in*, it is because when you say, "If Zayd comes to me, I will honor him," it must be that he does not presently come, so *in* is used in place of *ma*. And it is said, "*In* Zayd is standing," meaning: "*Ma* Zayd is standing [i.e., Zayd is not standing]." And *ma* is used in the conditional; you say, "*Ma* you do, I will do," and what indicates what we mentioned is that the negating *ma* is used where *in* is not used, for you say, "*Ma in* Zayd sat," making *in* a relative particle (*silah*), and you do not say, "*In* Zayd sat," meaning negation. And in the sense of the conditional, you say, "*Imma* you see," making *in* the root and *ma* the added particle. This shows us that *in* in the conditional is the root and *ma* is the addition, and *ma* in negation is the reverse.

The second inquiry: We have mentioned that His saying ﴿You are not but﴾ conveys what "You are in clear error" does not convey, because it entails restriction, that they are in nothing but error.

The third inquiry: Describing the error as "clear": we have mentioned its meaning, that because of its manifestness, it makes itself evident as error; that is, they are in an error that is not hidden from anyone, that it is error.

The fourth inquiry: We have mentioned that His saying ﴿in error﴾ indicates that they are immersed in it and sunk in it, and His saying in other places ﴿upon clear proof﴾ and ﴿upon guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] indicates that they are riding the middle of the straight path, able over it.

As for the semantic: They described the believers as being in clear error only because they supposed that the believer's speech is contradictory, and whoever's speech is contradictory is in extreme error. We say this because they said, ﴿Shall we feed one whom Allah would have fed if He willed?﴾, indicating that if Allah willed to feed them, He would feed them, so you cannot feed them, since that would be obtaining what is already obtained. And if Allah does not will to feed them, no one can feed them, because what Allah does not will cannot occur, so we have no power to feed; how then do you command us to feed? There is another aspect: they said, "Allah intends to starve them, so if we feed them, that would be an attempt to nullify the act of Allah, which is impermissible. And you say, 'Feed them.' This is error." And they were not in error except that they looked at the intended purpose and did not look at the demand and command. That is because when a master commands his servant with a command, it is not fitting for the servant to uncover the reason for the command and to seek knowledge of the purpose for which he was commanded. An example: when a king wants to ride out to attack his enemy in such a way that no one should know, and he says to his servant, "Bring the mount," then if the servant were to inquire and seek to uncover the purpose for which he rides, he would be accused of wanting to inform his enemy so that he would be cautious of him and expose his secret. So the proper manner in obedience is to follow the command, not to pursue the intended purpose. Thus, when Allah the Exalted says, ﴿Spend from what He has provided you,﴾ it is not permissible for them to say, "Why did Allah not feed them from what is in His treasuries?"

As for the semantic: They described the believers as being in clear error only because they supposed that the believer's speech is contradictory, and whoever's speech is contradictory is in extreme error. We say this because they said, ﴿Shall we feed one whom Allah would have fed if He willed?﴾, indicating that if Allah willed to feed them, He would feed them, so you cannot feed them, since that would be obtaining what is already obtained. And if Allah does not will to feed them, no one can feed them, because what Allah does not will cannot occur, so we have no power to feed; how then do you command us to feed? There is another aspect: they said, "Allah intends to starve them, so if we feed them, that would be an attempt to nullify the act of Allah, which is impermissible. And you say, 'Feed them.' This is error." And they were not in error except that they looked at the intended purpose and did not look at the demand and command. That is because when a master commands his servant with a command, it is not fitting for the servant to uncover the reason for the command and to seek knowledge of the purpose for which he was commanded. An example: when a king wants to ride out to attack his enemy in such a way that no one should know, and he says to his servant, "Bring the mount," then if the servant were to inquire and seek to uncover the purpose for which he rides, he would be accused of wanting to inform his enemy so that he would be cautious of him and expose his secret. So the proper manner in obedience is to follow the command, not to pursue the intended purpose. Thus, when Allah the Exalted says, ﴿Spend from what He has provided you,﴾ it is not permissible for them to say, "Why did Allah not feed them from what is in His treasuries?"

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 36, verses 47–49:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom Allah would have fed if He willed? You are not but in clear error."﴾

This indicates that they withhold everything that is due from the *mukallaf* (the person bound by religious obligations). That is because the *mukallaf* is obligated to exalt the side of Allah and to show compassion toward the creation of Allah. They abandoned the exaltation of Allah when it was said to them, "Fear Allah," and they did not fear Him. They abandoned compassion toward the creation of Allah when it was said to them, ﴿Spend,﴾ and they did not spend. In this there are subtleties:

The first: They were addressed with the lowest degrees of exaltation and compassion, and they did not bring any of it. The sincere servants of Allah were addressed with the lowest level and they brought the highest. We say this because they were commanded in matters of piety to guard against what is before them of punishment or the Hereafter, and what is behind them of death or punishment, and this is the minimum of guarding. As for the elect, they guard against changing the heart of the king against them even if he does not punish them, and guarding against punishment belongs only to the distant. So they did not guard against the disobedience of Allah, and they did not guard against the punishment of Allah. The sincere ones feared Allah and avoided opposing Him, whether or not He would punish them for it. As for compassion, they were told, ﴿Spend from what﴾ — that is, some of what belongs to Allah that is in your hands — and they did not spend. The sincere ones preferred others over themselves and gave away everything in their hands; indeed, they directed their very selves toward benefiting the servants of Allah and warding off harm from them.

The second: Just as in the matter of exaltation the benefit of exalting returns only to the one who exalts, since Allah is independent of their exaltation, likewise in the matter of compassion the benefit of compassion returns only to them. For whoever is not provided for by the wealthy man will not die except at his appointed term, and his provision must reach him; but the fortunate one is the one whom Allah has decreed that the provision should reach others through his hand.

The third: His saying ﴿from what He has provided you﴾ points to two matters:

The first: that withholding it is extremely ugly, for the most miserly of the miserly is the one who withholds the wealth of others.

The second: that the fear of poverty should not prevent you from this, for Allah has provided you, so when you spend, He will replace it for you again just as He provided you at first.

There are also issues in this:

The first issue: At His saying, "And when it is said to them, 'Spend,'" He omitted the response, and here He answered and gave more than the response. That is because if He had said, "And when it is said to them, 'Spend,' they say, 'Shall we feed one whom Allah would have fed if He willed?'" it would have been sufficient. So what is the benefit of His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe﴾ [al-Ankabut: 12]? We say: the disbelievers used to claim that feeding is among the praiseworthy qualities, and they boasted of it. They only intended by that statement to refute the believers. They said: "We feed the guests, believing that our deeds are praiseworthy, and were it not for our feeding, the guest's need would not be met. And you say that your God provides whom He wills, so why do you tell us to spend?" Since their aim was to refute the believers, not to refrain from feeding, Allah the Exalted said of them, ﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe,﴾ indicating the refutation. As for their saying, ﴿Guard against what is before you,﴾ they had no refutation of the believers, so they turned away, and Allah turned away from mentioning their turning away, since the knowledge of it is already established.

The second issue: What is the benefit of changing the wording in their reply, where they did not say, "Shall we spend on one whom Allah would have provided if He willed?" That is because they were commanded to spend in His saying, ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend,"﴾ so their reply should have been, "Shall we spend?" Why then did they say, [the Arabic: ] ﴿Shall we feed﴾? We say: In it is a demonstration of the extreme extent of their opposition. For when they were commanded to spend — and spending includes feeding and other things — they did not spend, nor did they spend even less than that, which is feeding, and they said, "We will not feed." This is like when a speaker says to another, "Give Zayd a dinar," and he replies, "I will not give him a dirham," whereas the matching response would be, "I will not give him a dinar." But exaggeration in this manner is more complete, so it is likewise here.

The third issue: Their statement was true, for if Allah willed, He would have fed him. So why did He mention it in the context of blame? We say: because their intent was to deny the power of Allah, or to deny the permissibility of commanding spending while Allah has power. Both are corrupt, and Allah clarified this in His saying, ﴿from what He has provided you,﴾ for it indicates His power and validates His command to give. For whoever has wealth in the hand of another and has wealth in his own treasuries is free to choose: if he wills, he gives from what is in his treasuries, and if he wills, he orders the one who has the wealth to give. And it is not permissible for one who has his wealth in your treasuries, which exceeds what is in my hand, to say, "Give him from it." His saying ﴿You are not but in clear error﴾ indicates their belief that they had silenced the believers with this statement, and that their command to spend, together with their claim of Allah's power, is manifestly corrupt, while their own belief is the corrupt one. In it there are linguistic and semantic discussions.

As for the linguistic: We say: ﴿in﴾ (*in*) may be used for negation in the sense of *ma* (*ma*), and the original use of *in* is for the conditional, while the original use of *ma* is for negation. But the two share some aspects, so they are close. *Ma* is used in the conditional, and *in* is used in negation. The shared aspect is that each of them is a particle composed of two close letters, for the hamza is close to the alif and the mim is close to the nun. The meaning that follows *ma* must be such that it may or may not be established. As for *ma*, this is clear. As for *in*, it is because when you say, "If Zayd comes to me, I will honor him," it must be that he does not presently come, so *in* is used in place of *ma*. And it is said, "*In* Zayd is standing," meaning: "*Ma* Zayd is standing [i.e., Zayd is not standing]." And *ma* is used in the conditional; you say, "*Ma* you do, I will do," and what indicates what we mentioned is that the negating *ma* is used where *in* is not used, for you say, "*Ma in* Zayd sat," making *in* a relative particle (*silah*), and you do not say, "*In* Zayd sat," meaning negation. And in the sense of the conditional, you say, "*Imma* you see," making *in* the root and *ma* the added particle. This shows us that *in* in the conditional is the root and *ma* is the addition, and *ma* in negation is the reverse.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾

This is a reference to what they believed: that the piety (taqwa) commanded in His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Be mindful of God"﴾ and the spending (infaq) mentioned in His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided"﴾ serve no purpose, because the promise has no reality. His words ﴿When is this promise﴾ mean: when will the promised thing occur? There are several issues here.

The first issue: ﴿in﴾ is a conditional particle, which requires an apodosis (jawab), but ﴿when (mata)﴾ is an interrogative (istifham) that cannot serve as an apodosis. So what is the answer? We say: in form it is an interrogative, but in meaning it is a denial. It is as if they said, "If you are truthful about the occurrence of the Resurrection, then tell us when it will happen."

The second issue: who is addressed in their words ﴿if you are truthful﴾? We say: the apparent meaning is that it is addressed to the prophets, because when they denied the message, they said, "If you, O claimants to the message, are truthful, then inform us when it will happen."

The third issue: there is no promise mentioned in this passage, so to what does the phrase ﴿this promise﴾ refer? We say: it refers to the promise contained in His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Be mindful of what is before you and what is behind you"﴾, namely the Hour's arrival. Or we say it is known even though it is not mentioned, because the prophets were constantly reminding them of the Hour, the reckoning, reward and punishment.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They await only a single blast﴾. That is, they await only the known blast. The indefinite form (tankir) is for magnification. If it is said: they were not awaiting it; rather, they were certain it would not come. We reply: "awaiting" here is an action, because they were doing what would bring about ruin for its doer, hastening punishment and bringing the Hour closer, were it not for God's decree, power and knowledge. They do not say [this] (in the sense of an actual statement). Or we say: since their saying "when" was not a genuine interrogative, He described their awaiting as non-genuine awaiting, because whoever says "when" is understood to be awaiting, and the speech is judged by its content.

Several features of the blast are mentioned here that indicate its terror and magnitude:

The first: the indefiniteness. It is said: "So-and-so has much wealth," or "He has a heart," meaning he is bold.

The second: ﴿single (wahida)﴾, meaning it needs no second.

The third: ﴿it will seize them (ta'khudhuhum)﴾, meaning it will encompass them with seizing and reach everyone in the east and west of the earth. There is no doubt that such a thing can only be great.

His words ﴿it will seize them while they are disputing (yakhissimun)﴾ and ﴿so they will not be able to make a bequest nor return to their families﴾ are among the things that magnify the matter. The usual blast, when it strikes someone heedless, makes him tremble, for one who is occupied with an important matter trembles at heart when a crier shouts at him. This is unlike one who awaits the blast. So when the blast is of the intensity and power we have described, and it strikes the heedless one who is occupied with his adversary, the trembling is complete and the fear is greatest.

It may be said that ﴿disputing (yakhissimun)﴾ refers to the resurrection: they say it will never happen at all, so they are heedless of it. This is unlike one who believes it will occur, so he prepares and awaits its happening, and he does not tremble. This is what is meant by His words ﴿And all who are in the heavens and on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills﴾ [az-Zumar: 68], referring to those who believed in its occurrence and prepared for it. We have illustrated this with the example of one who sees lightning and knows that thunder will follow, and one who does not see it and does not know; then when thunder rolls, you see the one who saw the lightning and knew standing firm, while the heedless and bewildered one is struck senseless.

Then He explained the severity of the seizing: it is such that it gives them no respite to make bequests. In this there are features that clarify the severity.

The first: ﴿they are not able﴾. The saying "So-and-so does not make a bequest in this state" is less forceful than saying "He is not able to make a bequest," because one who does not make a bequest may still be able to do so.

The second: the bequest, which is by speech. Speech is produced more quickly than action. So He said ﴿they will not be able﴾ to say a single word, so how could they do an action that requires a long time, such as discharging obligations and returning wrongful gains?

The third: choosing the bequest from among all words indicates that they have no power even over the most important words, for at the time of death the need for a bequest is most pressing.

The fourth: the indefiniteness in "bequest" is for generality, meaning they have no power to make any bequest at all, even one in a few words. Since a bequest can be accomplished by gesture, one who is unable to do that is unable to do anything else.

The fifth: His words ﴿nor return to their families﴾ explain the intensity of the need for a bequest, because one who hopes to reach his family may refrain from a bequest for lack of need. But one who is certain he will never reach his family must make a bequest. So if he is unable to do so while needing to, this shows the utmost severity.

There are two interpretations of His words ﴿nor return to their families﴾:

One: as we have mentioned, they are certain they will not be given time to gather with their families, and this makes the need for a bequest necessary.

The second: they will not return to their families, meaning they will die and have no return to the world. One who travels a journey, knowing he will not return from it or gather with his family again, makes a bequest.

Then He explained what follows the first blast, saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and behold, from the graves they will hasten toward their Lord﴾. That is, it will be blown into [once more], as He said elsewhere: ﴿Then it will be blown into again, and behold, they will be standing, looking﴾ [az-Zumar: 68]. There are several issues here:

The first issue: He said in one place ﴿Then it will be blown into again, and behold, they will be standing, looking﴾, and here He said ﴿and behold, from the graves they will hasten toward their Lord﴾. Standing is not the same as hastening, and the phrase ﴿and behold (fa-idha hum)﴾ in both places implies that they occur together. We reply: the answer to this has two aspects.

One: standing does not conflict with swift walking, since one who walks is standing, and it does not conflict with looking.

The second: swiftness means that matters come together, as if everything occurs in a single moment, like the saying of the poet:

"Attacking, retreating, advancing, turning back together,
like a boulder the flood rolled down from a height."

The second issue: how can the two blasts have effects on two opposite things, giving life and causing death? We reply: there is no effective agent other than God, and the blowing is a sign. Moreover, the terrifying sound shakes bodies. In the state of life, the parts of the living being were gathered, and the shaking disperses them. In the state of death, the parts were scattered, and the shaking brings them together. The result is that the two blasts produce a shaking and movement of the bodies: when they are joined, they scatter, and when they are separated, they gather.

The third issue: what is the precise meaning of ﴿idha﴾ used for suddenness? We reply: it is the ﴿idha﴾ of time, its meaning being: "The Horn is blown, and then, when it is blown, they hasten." But a thing may be a time-frame for another thing whose being a time-frame is already known. In speech, one knows it is a time-frame, but from observation no new knowledge arises. For example, one says, "When the sun rises, the air becomes bright," and so on. When one sees the air brightening at sunrise, no additional knowledge is gained. But if you say, "I went out, and behold, a lion was at the door," that moment was the time of the lion's being at the door, but it was not known. When he sees it, he knows it, and the knowledge that this moment was the time of its presence comes with a sense of surprise (mufajaah) upon perception. Therefore it is called ﴿idha﴾ of suddenness.

The fourth issue: where will the graves be at that time, when the blast has shaken the mountains? We reply: God will gather the parts of each individual in the place where he was buried, and he will emerge from that place, which is his grave.

The fifth issue: this is a context that mentions awe, and the disbeliever was mentioned previously. The word "Lord" indicates mercy. If He had said, instead of "their Lord," a word that indicates awe, would that be more fitting or not? We say: this word is the best it could be, because one who has done wrong and is compelled to turn toward one who has been good to him suffers greater pain and deeper regret than anyone else.

The sixth issue: the evildoer, when he turns toward the one who does good, advances one foot and holds back the other, while hastening (naslan) is rapidity of walking. How then can this be produced by them? We reply: ﴿they hasten﴾ not by their own choice. We have mentioned in the explanation of His words ﴿and behold, they are looking﴾ that He intended to show the perfection of His power and the execution of His will, since when the Horn is blown, there will be at that moment gathering, assembling, life, standing, and running all in a single time. So His words ﴿and behold, from the graves they will hasten toward their Lord﴾ mean that in a single time they will reach this degree, which is hastening, a state that does not occur except after stages.

How then can this be produced by them? We reply: ﴿they hasten﴾ not by their own choice. We have mentioned in the explanation of His words ﴿and behold, they are looking﴾ that He intended to show the perfection of His power and the execution of His will, since when the Horn is blown, there will be at that moment gathering, assembling, life, standing, and running all in a single time. So His words ﴿and behold, from the graves they will hasten toward their Lord﴾ mean that in a single time they will reach this degree, which is hastening, a state that does not occur except after stages.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our resting place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."﴾

That is, when they are resurrected they say this, because His saying ﴿And the Horn is blown﴾ indicates that they have been resurrected. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: If someone says, "Had Allah said, 'So when they will be from the graves to their Lord, they will hasten' [36:51], and they said, 'Woe to us!', would it not have been more fitting?" We say: God forbid. That is because His saying ﴿So when they will be from the graves to their Lord, they will hasten﴾, as we have mentioned, is an indication that He, exalted is He, in the briefest time, gathers their parts, joins them, brings them to life and sets them in motion, such that their hastening occurs at the time of the blowing. Yet that requires gathering and joining. So if He had said "they will say," it would have been like the state of "to hasten," meaning, they will hasten saying, "Woe to us!" But that is not the case, for their saying "Woe to us!" comes before they hasten. He mentioned the hastening only for the benefits we have mentioned.

The second issue: If someone says, "We know the meaning of the vocative in such phrases as 'Alas for regret!' (ya hasratan), 'Alas for my regret!' (ya hasratana) and 'Woe to us!' (ya wailana), but what is the difference between their saying and God's saying, when He said, ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [36:30] without any attached pronoun, whereas they said, 'Alas for our regret!', 'Alas for our regret!' and 'Woe to us!'?" We say: Since the speaker was the one addressed, no one had knowledge except of his own state or of the state of one near to him, so each one was preoccupied with himself, and each one would say, "Alas for our regret!" and "Woe to us!" Thus His saying ﴿They said, "Woe to us!"﴾ means each one said, "Woe to me!" As for when Allah said it, He said it in a general manner, because His knowledge encompasses their states.

The third issue: What is the connection of ﴿Who has raised us up from our resting place?﴾ to their saying ﴿Woe to us!﴾? We say: When they were resurrected they remembered what they used to hear from the messengers, so they said, ﴿Woe to us! Who has raised us up?﴾ Did Allah raise us up with the promised resurrection, or were we sleeping and He woke us? This is like a person who has been promised that an enemy he cannot withstand will come to him, and then sees a terrifying man approaching him, and trembles within himself and says, "Is this that, or not?" What indicates what we have mentioned is their saying ﴿from our resting place﴾, where they called the graves a place of rest, indicating that they doubted whether they had been sleeping and were woken, or had been dead, and the dominant assumption in their minds was resurrection, so they combined both matters. They said, ﴿Who has raised us up?﴾ indicating their assumption that it was the promised resurrection, and they said, ﴿from our resting place﴾ indicating their imagining the possibility of awakening.

The fourth issue: What does ﴿this﴾ (hadha) refer to? We say: There are two views:

One of them: it refers to the resting place, as if they said, "Who has raised us up from our resting place, this?" so it would be an attribute of the resting place, as one says, "This speech of mine is true."

The second: ﴿this﴾ refers to the resurrection, meaning: this resurrection is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth concerning it.

The fifth issue: If "this" is an attribute of the resting place, how is His saying ﴿what the Most Merciful promised and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ valid? We say: "What the Most Merciful promised" would be the subject of a sentence whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being "what the Most Merciful promised is true, and the messengers spoke the truth." Or it may be said: "what the Most Merciful promised and what the messengers spoke truly of is true," and the first is more evident because of the fewness of the implied elements. Or it may be said: "What the Most Merciful promised" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being "it is what the Most Merciful promised of the resurrection, not an awakening from sleep, and the messengers spoke the truth in what they told you."

The sixth issue: If we say "this" refers to the resting place or to the resurrection, where is the answer to the question posed by their saying ﴿Who has raised us up?﴾? We say: Since their purpose in saying ﴿Who has raised us up?﴾ was to obtain knowledge that it was a resurrection or an awakening, the answer was given by His saying: this is a resurrection the Most Merciful promised, not an awakening. This is like a frightened person who says to another, "What do you say? Will so-and-so kill me?" and the other says, "Do not fear," and remains silent, knowing that his purpose is to remove terror from him, and by this the answer is achieved.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Not was it but a single Cry, and behold, they are all brought before Us.﴾

That is, the Blast was nothing but a single Cry. What indicates the Blast is His saying: ﴿And the Horn is blown.﴾ It may also be said: if the event was [the Cry], and "Cry" is read in the nominative, then "kāna" is the complete verb (al-tāmmah), meaning: nothing occurred except a single Cry. But feminine agreement is permissible by consideration of the apparent noun. The one who reads with the nominative may argue that His saying ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1] is a feminine form for the purpose of awe and emphasis. This is indicated by His saying ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 2], for it is for emphasis. Thus here, He said ﴿If it was but a single Cry﴾, feminine in the sense of awe-inspiring emphasis. For this reason, all the names of the Day of Gathering come in the feminine, such as al-Qiyamah (the Resurrection), al-Qari'ah (the Striking Calamity), al-Haqqah (the Inevitable), al-Tammah (the Overwhelming), al-Sakhkhah (the Deafening Blast), and others. Then He explained what will happen on that Day with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾

Page 80

His saying ﴿no soul will be wronged﴾ is so that the believer may feel secure, and ﴿you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ is so that the criminal disbeliever may despair. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: What is the benefit of addressing the criminal in indicating his despair with His saying ﴿you will not be recompensed﴾, while omitting the address in indicating the believer's security from punishment with His saying ﴿no soul will be wronged﴾, and He did not say "you, O believers, will not be wronged"? We say: because His saying ﴿no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ conveys generality, and it is so, for it will never be wronged. ﴿You will not be recompensed﴾ is specific to the disbeliever, for God recompenses the believer even if he has not done [good], since God has a special grace for the believer and a general justice, and this carries good tidings.

The second issue: What requires the mention of the particle of consequence (fa')? We say: when He said ﴿brought before Us﴾, meaning gathered, and gathering is for judgment and reckoning, it is as if He, exalted, said: when they are gathered, they are gathered only for judgment with justice, so there is no injustice at the time of gathering for justice. Thus the absence of injustice became consequent upon the bringing forth for justice. For this reason, one says to a ruler or judge: "You sat for justice, so do not oppress," meaning that this requires that and entails it.

The third issue: "They will not be recompensed for the very deeds they did," but rather "they will be recompensed with what they did" or "according to what they did." His saying ﴿you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ indicates that the recompense is with the very deed. It cannot be said that "jazā" transitively takes [its object] directly and with bi-: one says "jazaytuhu khayran" and "jazaytuhu bi-khayr." For that is not of this type, because when you say "jazaytuhu bi-khayr," the good is not your object; rather the bi- denotes correspondence and causation, as if you say: I repaid him a recompense because of what he did. We say the answer to this is from two aspects:

One of them: that this is an indication, by way of emphasis, of the absence of excess, because a thing does not exceed its very self. So we say: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they will be recompensed only with what they used to do﴾ [al-A'raf: 147] is, in equivalence, as if it were the very thing they did. It is said: "So-and-so answers me letter for letter," meaning he leaves nothing out. This necessitates great despair.

The second: that "mā" does not refer to a particular, but is for the category, its implied sense being: "you will not be recompensed except for the kind of deed," meaning: if it was good, then good; and if it was evil, then evil. Thus you will be recompensed for what you do, of evil and good. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

﴿Then He described the state of the righteous and said:﴾ ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, reclining on couches in shade.﴾ ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for.﴾

His words ﴿in busyness﴾ may have several meanings.

The first: they are occupied, away from the terror of that Day, by taking what Allah has given them of reward, so they have no news of punishment or reckoning. His words ﴿joyful﴾ complete the description of their safety. If He had said only "in busyness," it could be taken to mean they are engaged in great reflection on the Day and its terrors, as one who suffers a great trial and is then told of a loss in his property says, "I am busy with something more important than this." So He said ﴿joyful﴾, meaning they are occupied with pleasure and delight, not with woe and destruction.

The second: this is a description of their state, and it does not mean they are occupied away from something. Rather, the meaning is that they are engaged in an activity, and then He explained that their activity is not burdensome but pleasurable and beloved.

The third: they are busy with what they had not expected. In the world they imagined things and said, "When we enter the Garden we will seek only this and that," but they then see what had not occurred to them, and they become occupied with it.

[Page 81]

There are other meanings besides these, but they are weak:

The first: it has been said that it means the deflowering of virgins. This is what we mentioned in the third meaning: a person may, at the present time, prefer the caressing of maidens, and so he says, "In the Garden I will enjoy them," but then Allah may give him what occupies him away from them.

The second: it has been said that it means the playing of lutes. This is of the kind we mentioned, and it is a conjecture.

The third: that it means mutual visiting.

The fourth: that it means the hospitality of Allah. This is close to what we have said, because the hospitality of Allah is with the most delightful that is possible, and then that will occupy them from what they imagined in their worldly life.

His words ﴿joyful﴾ are the predicate of ﴿indeed﴾, and ﴿in busyness﴾ specifies what their joy is in. One says, "Zayd is coming upon his work and sitting in his house," so the prepositional phrase is not the predicate. If you put "sitting" in the accusative, then the prepositional phrase would be the predicate.

Likewise, if He had said ﴿in busyness joyful﴾ (in the accusative), its meaning would be: the companions of the Garden are busy, joyful, as a circumstantial state. It was also read in the accusative. The word "fākih" means one who is delighted and enjoys luxury, and from it comes "fākiha" (fruit), because it is not in abundance except for pleasure, and so it is not eaten to ward off the pain of hunger. There is a subtle meaning in this: by His words ﴿in busyness﴾ He indicated their freedom from pain, so there is no pain for them. Then by His words ﴿joyful﴾ He showed their finding of pleasure. One who is free from pain may not find pleasure, so He explained that they are in the most complete state.

Then He explained the perfection by His words ﴿they and their spouses﴾. This is because one who is in pleasure may have it spoiled by his reflection on the state of someone whose affair concerns him, so He said ﴿they and their spouses﴾ as well, so that no attachment of the heart remains for them. As for those among their relatives and brothers who are in the Fire, they are busy away from them, and there is no pain for them from them, and they do not desire their presence.

The word ﴿spouses﴾ may have two meanings.

The first: their likenesses in goodness and their equals in faith, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿of its kind, pairs﴾ [Sad 38:58].

The second: "spouses" are those understood as the wife of a woman and the wife of a man, as in His words: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:30], and His words: ﴿and leave wives behind﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:234]. Here the intended meaning is not likenesses.

His words ﴿in shade﴾: "zilāl" is the plural of "zill", and "zulal" is the plural of "zullah". What is meant is protection from the place of pain. One who sits under a shelter does not fear rain or the heat of the sun, and so he is prepared to ward off pain. Likewise, they have from the shade of Allah what protects them from evils, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿No weariness touches us therein, nor does fatigue touch us therein﴾ [Fatir 35:35], and He said: ﴿they see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾ [al-Insan 76:13], indicating the absence of pains. There is also a subtle point here: the state of the one under obligation, its disorder either comes from the busyness in which he is, even if he is in a high place, like one who sits in the heat of the sun in a pleasure garden, or it comes from the place, even if the busyness is desired, like playing with maidens in an exposed place; or it comes from food, like one who strolls in a garden when food is lacking; or it comes from the loss of the beloved. To this the people of the heart (the Sufis) point in the conditions of listening (sama', the listening to devotional music), by their saying: "the time, the place, and the companions." So He, exalted is He, said ﴿in busyness joyful﴾, indicating that they are not in fatigue. He said ﴿they and their spouses﴾, indicating the absence of desolate loneliness. He said ﴿in shade, on couches, reclining﴾, indicating the place. He said ﴿for them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for﴾, indicating the removal of all their needs. His words ﴿reclining﴾ indicate the posture most indicative of strength and leisure, for one who stands may stand for a task, and one who sits may sit for a task, but one who reclines does not recline except in leisure and ability, since the sick cannot recline; rather he lies down or lies on his back.

"Arā'ik" is the plural of "arīka", which is a couch on which there is bedding, and it is beneath canopies, so it and what is above it are visible.

His words ﴿for them therein is fruit﴾ indicate that there is no hunger there, and eating is not to ward off the pain of hunger; rather their food is fruit, even if it were fresh meat. It may be said: His words ﴿and the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:21] indicate difference and genuine desire, which is hunger. We answer: His words ﴿of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:21] confirm the meaning of the absence of pain, because eating something may be for treatment without desire. So He said ﴿of what they desire﴾, because the flesh of birds in this world is eaten in two situations:

One: the state of luxury.

The second: the state of weakness of the stomach.

In that state one does not eat bird meat that he desires; rather he eats what suits him and what the physician orders. As for the claim that it indicates difference, we say: we grant that, because the specific differs from the general. Moreover, that does not harm our purpose, because we say: He chose fruit from among the kinds of food in this place, because it is more indicative of luxury, delight, and absence of hunger. The indefinite form is for indicating perfection, and we have mentioned this many times.

His words ﴿for them therein is fruit﴾, without saying "they eat", indicate that the reins of choice are in their hands and that they are owners and capable.

His words ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ have several meanings:

The first: ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ for themselves, that is, their supplication is answered. Then this is an iftiʿāl form with the meaning of the verb, like "iḥtimāl" meaning "carrying" and "irtiḥāl" meaning "departure". On this view, its meaning is not that they make supplication for themselves and their supplication is answered after the request. Rather its meaning is: and for them is what they claim for themselves, that is, that is theirs, so there is no need for them to supplicate and ask. Just as when a king is asked by his slave for something and says, "That is yours," it is understood from this at times that your request is granted and that this is an easy matter, that you will be given what you asked for; and at times it is understood as a refusal and a statement that what you want is already yours, so why do you ask for it? Thus He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and for them is whatever they claim and ask for﴾, so there is no asking for them. Its clarification is that "whatever they claim" means "whatever it is proper to ask for and claim", that is, everything proper to ask for is already theirs before asking. Or we say: the intended meaning is asking and answering, because asking from Allah also has pleasure in it. If Allah cut off the means between them and Him, it would not be pleasant for them; so He left things which He gives them at the time of asking, so that they have pleasure at the time of asking and at the time of giving. For the slave's being in a position to address the king about his needs is a great rank, and the mighty king may fulfil the needs of all his slaves intentionally, so that they will not address him.

The second: ﴿whatever they claim﴾ means "whatever they mutually call for", and on this view it is an iftiʿāl form with the meaning of the reciprocal form, like "iqtitāl" meaning "qitāl" (fighting each other). Its meaning, as we mentioned, is that everything one may call his companion to, or ask of his companion, is theirs.

The third: whatever they wish for.

The fourth: with the meaning of "claim" (da'wā), and on this view its meaning is that in the world they used to claim that Allah is their Lord and their Master, and that the disbelievers have no master. So He says to them in the Garden what they used to claim in the world, so the narration is reported as something said in the world, as if He says: "On this day of ours, for you, O believers, tomorrow is what you claim today." It may be said: His words ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, they and their spouses in shade﴾ indicate that the saying is on the Day of Resurrection. We answer: The reply to this is in two respects:

One: His words ﴿they﴾ are the subject, and ﴿and their spouses﴾ is conjoined to them. So it is possible that this statement is about our present day, informing us that the believer and his spouse will be in shade tomorrow, and for him is what he claims.

The second reply, which is preferable, is that we say: its meaning is "for them is what they claim", that is, what they used to claim. It may be said that this is an implicit ellipsis without necessity, and that it is not permissible. We answer: according to what we have mentioned, the word "claim" remains used in its well-known meaning, because "da'wā" is the bringing of a claim. We said this is preferable because His words ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:58] are in the Abode of the Hereafter, and it is like an explanation of His words ﴿whatever they claim﴾; and because His words ﴿whatever they claim﴾ are mentioned among sentences all of which are in the Hereafter, so "whatever they claim" should also be in the Hereafter, and in the Hereafter no claim or proof remains, because the matters are made manifest and there is a separation between the people of woe and the people of joy.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 36, verse 58:**

Allah's words: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ are the most perfect of things, and it is the last of them, beyond which there is nothing. Let us explain it in several issues.

**The First Issue:** What is the case-marking (raf', nominative) of His words ﴿سَلَامٌ﴾ (salamun, "peace")? We say that it may have several possibilities.

One of them: it is a substitute (badal, apposition) for what they ask for. It is as if Allah, when He said ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾, explained it by its substitute, saying "for them is peace." So in meaning it is like a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is a prepositional phrase, as one says: "In the house there is a man," and "For Zayd there is wealth." Although grammatically this is not the case, it is rather a substitute, and the substitution of an indefinite noun for a definite one is permissible. Thus "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which), which is definite, and "salam" is indefinite. On this view, one may say that "ma" in His words ﴿ما يَدَّعُونَ﴾ (ma yaddda'un, "what they ask for") is neither a qualifying (mawsufah) nor a relative (mawsulah) particle, but rather an indefinite, its implied meaning being: "for them is a thing they ask for," then it was explained by mention of the substitute, saying: ﴿peace﴾. The first view is the correct one.

Another: "salam" is the predicate (khabar) of "ma," and "lahum" (for them) is to specify the direction (li-bayan al-jihah). Its implied meaning is: "what they ask for is pure (salim) for them," meaning unmixed (khalis). The word "salam" has the sense of "salim khalis" (pure, unmixed) or "salim" (sound). One says: "'abd salam," meaning one free from defects. Just as one says: "For Zayd, honour is abundant," where the prepositional phrase indicates who possesses that, honour is the subject and "abundant" is its predicate.

A third: His words ﴿Peace﴾ are disconnected (munqati') from what preceded, and "salam" is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its implied meaning being: "Peace be upon them." Thus this is an information from Allah, Exalted, about our present day, as if He, Exalted, related to us and said: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy with joy﴾. Then, when He had explained the completeness of their state, He said: "Peace be upon them." This is like His words: ﴿Peace upon Noah﴾ [al-Saffat: 79] and ﴿Peace upon the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 181]. So Allah, by this, has been gracious to His believing servants just as He was gracious to His messenger servants. This is an original and fine view, which is supported by transmitted report. Alternatively, we say: its implied meaning is "Peace be upon you," and this would be a kind of iltifat (shift of address), where He spoke to them in a certain manner and then said: "Peace be upon you."

**The Second Issue:** On what is ﴿قَوْلًا﴾ (qawlan, "a word") in the accusative (nasb)? We say it may have several possibilities.

One: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). Its implied meaning, on our view that "the intended meaning for them is peace" is: that it is said to them "peace," which Allah says as a saying (qawlan), or which the angels say as a saying. And on our view that "what they ask for is pure for them," its implied meaning is: Allah said that, as a saying, and promised them that what they ask for is pure for them, as a promise. And on our view of "Peace be upon them," its implied meaning is: "I say it as a saying." His words ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ serve to clarify that the peace is from Him, i.e., "Peace be upon them from a Lord, Most Merciful, I say it as a saying." It may be said on this view that it is a specification (tamyiz), since peace may be a saying and may be an act. For one who enters upon a king and lowers his head says: "I greeted the king," and then it is like the speaker's saying: "The sale exists legally, not physically." This, however, is ruled out definitively, not merely presumed.

**The Third Issue:** Concerning peace He said ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾, and concerning other kinds of honour He said ﴿as a welcome from One Forgiving and Most Merciful﴾ [Fussilat: 32]. Is there a difference between them? We say: Yes. As for there, the welcome (nuzul) is what the guest is provided with first, and although what follows it indicates this, when the guest is honoured first, it indicates that he is honoured, and if he is deprived of honour at first, it indicates that he is always humiliated. However, this is not certain, because it is possible that the king is abundant in provision, so he provides for his guest first, and does not prevent him from food and drink, and then takes him to account for other matters. Therefore He said: "Forgiving," to forgive what proceeded from the servants, so that the servant may be secure, and so that one does not say that feeding may be found from one who is punished afterwards. Peace manifests the excellence of honouring the one greeted, not through forgiveness. Therefore He said: ﴿and a Lord, Forgiving﴾ [Saba': 15], because the lord of a thing is its owner, who, when he looks at the height of his rank, is not expected to turn to him with honour. So when he greets him, he is amazed by it, and it is said: "Look, he is his master, and he greets him."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And separate yourselves today, you criminals.﴾

In this verse there are several interpretations, among them clarifying the aspect of the order (tartib) as well:

The first: separate yourselves within yourselves and disperse, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It almost bursts with rage﴾ [al-Mulk: 8], meaning that some of it separates from some other, except that their separation is from grief and remorse. The aspect of the order in this case is that the criminal sees the station of the believer, his elevation, and the descent of his own rank and lowliness, so he grieves. Then it is said to them: ﴿And separate yourselves today﴾, since there is no remedy for your pain and no cure for your sickness.

The second: separate yourselves from the believers. That is because they will be witnessing what reaches the believer of reward and honor. Then it will be said to them: disperse and enter your dwellings in the Fire. So for you there will be no gathering with them ever again.

The third: separate some of you from others, in contrast to the gathering of the believer with his brethren, to which He pointed with His saying: ﴿they and their spouses﴾. So the people of the Fire will have the painful punishment, and the punishment of separation too, and there is no punishment above separation. Rather, the rational (ʿuqala') have said that every punishment is due to the cause of the separation of connection. For whoever has his hand cut off or his body burned suffers only because of the separation of connected parts from one another. But bodily separation is less than intellectual separation.

The fourth: separate yourselves from your intercessors and your companions: ﴿So you have today no close friend, nor any intercessor﴾.

The fifth: separate yourselves from what you hope for, and withdraw from every good. The criminal is the one who commits the crime. It may be said that what is meant is that God, exalted is He, says "separate", and He manifests upon them a mark by which they are known, as He said: ﴿The criminals are known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. In that case His saying ﴿And separate yourselves﴾ is a command of creation (amr takwin), just as He says: ﴿Be, and it is﴾. Likewise He says: separate, and they separate, being distinguished by their marks, and it appears on their foreheads or on their faces, equally.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 36, verse 60:

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾.

When God, exalted, mentioned the state of the believers and the criminals, someone might say: "Man was indeed wrongdoing and ignorant, and ignorance is an excuse." So God said this when there was no warning. The paths had already been made clear through the messengers' clarification. We charged you, and We recited to you what you should do and what you should not do. There are several issues concerning the verse.

The first issue concerns the dialects (lughat) found in ﴿a'had﴾, which are numerous:

The first: the first letter of ﴿a'had﴾ (the hamza) is pronounced with a kasra (i'hid). All the prefixes of the imperfect (future) are pronounced with a kasra except the yā', so one does not say "yā'lamu" but "yi'lamu".

The second: the kasra on the ha' from the pattern of ḍaraba, yaḍribu.

The third: changing the ʿayn into a jīm, so it becomes "a-lam ajhad". This occurs with every ʿayn followed by a hā'.

The fourth: assimilating the ha' into the ḥā' after the change, so one says "a-lam aḥḥad". Some people have been heard saying "daḥḥā maḥḥā", meaning: leave it with it.

The second issue concerns the meaning of (a'had). There are several interpretations, the closest and strongest of which is: "Did I not enjoin you?"

The third issue concerns this covenant. There are several views:

The first: it is the covenant that was made with our father Adam, in His saying: ﴿We charged Adam﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:115].

The second: it is the covenant made with the descendants of Adam, in His saying, exalted: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes"﴾ [al-A'rāf 7:172]. This requires that we not worship anyone other than God.

The third, and the strongest: this covenant was made with every people through the tongue of a messenger. For this reason, rational people agree that Satan commands evil, although they differ about his reality and his mode.

[p. 85]

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ means: do not obey him. The proof is that what is forbidden is not only prostrating to him, but also submitting to his command and obeying him. Obedience is a form of worship. One may say: then we would be commanded to worship the rulers, since we are commanded to obey them in His saying, exalted: ﴿Obey God, and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:59]. We say: their obedience, when it is by God's command, is nothing but worship of God and obedience to Him. How could it be otherwise, when even prostrating and bowing to another, if it is by God's command, is nothing but worship of God? Do you not see that the angels prostrated to Adam, and that was nothing but worship of God? The worship of rulers is only obedience to them in what God has not permitted. If it is said: how do you know the obedience to Satan from the obedience to the Merciful, since we neither hear anything from Satan nor see any trace of him? We say: the worship of Satan consists in opposing God's command, or in doing what God commanded not because He commanded it. At some times Satan commands you while he is in another, and at other times he commands you while he is in you. So when a person comes to you commanding you to do something, look: if it agrees with God's command, or does not agree. If it does not agree, then that person, together with Satan, commands you to what he commands you. If you obey him, you have worshipped Satan. If your soul calls you to an act, look: is it permitted by the Law or not? If it is not permitted, then your soul is Satan, or Satan is with it calling you. If you follow it, you have worshipped it. Then Satan first commands opposition to God openly. Whoever obeys him has worshipped him, and whoever does not obey him, he does not give up, but says to him: "Worship God so that you may not be humiliated, and so that your standing may rise among people, and your brothers and helpers may benefit from you." If he responds to him, he has worshipped him.

However, the worship of Satan varies in degree. This is because some deeds are done with the agent agreeing with them in his heart, tongue and limbs. Other deeds are done while the heart and tongue oppose the limbs. Among people is one who commits a crime while hating in his heart what he commits of sin, seeking forgiveness from his Lord, acknowledging the evil of what he commits. This is worship of Satan with the outward limbs. Among them is one who commits it while his heart is good and his tongue is moist. Just as you find many people rejoicing in their being frequent at the doors of oppressors for the purpose of informing, and counting it among the good qualities that they accompany kings, and boasting of it with their tongues. You find them rejoicing that they are commanders who make the king command injustice, and the king submits to them, or they rejoice that he commands them to injustice and so they act unjustly, delighted with the command that has come to them. Having understood this, the obedience which is with the outward limbs, while the inner parts are pure, is expiated by illnesses and pains, as reported in the traditions. Among that is his saying (ﷺ): "Fever is from the heat of Hell." And his saying (ﷺ): "The sword erases sins." That is, such sins. This is indicated by what the Prophet (ﷺ) said about the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd): "They are expiations." What happens in the hearts cannot be escaped except by repentance, regret, and the heart turning to the Lord. What happens with the tongue belongs, outwardly, to the category of what happens with the heart.

The example clarifies the situation. We say: if a commander is with the ruler, and he has attendants who are his close companions and distant followers who are among the common people, then if there comes from the commander friendliness and secret dealings with an enemy of the ruler and a bond of friendship between them, the king will not pardon that unless he is in the utmost forgiveness, or the commander has a previous favour with him or a subsequent repentance. If there comes from the commander's close companions an act of disobedience while he knows of it and does not restrain them, the disobedience is considered to be from him. If he dislikes it and shows disapproval, it is good to rebuke him but not to punish him, because the close companions' daring in disobedience is a sign of poor upbringing. If what comes from the distant attendants reaches the commander and he does not restrain them, the commander is rebuked. If he restrains them, the commander deserves honour because of that restraint, and it is good for the king to bestow kindness and favour upon the one restrained, if he knows that his restraint has been achieved. Having understood this, the heart is the commander, the tongue is his close companion, and the limbs are his servants. What comes from the heart is the greatest of sins. If it turns to loving other than God, that is the great woe and the clear error, which entails the painful punishment and the humiliating torment. What comes from the tongue is counted against the heart, and its statement is not accepted if it does not deny its act. What comes from the limbs, while the heart has openly denounced it and been restrained, is the sin about which the Prophet (ﷺ) related from his Lord that He said: "If you did not sin, I would create a people who would sin and seek forgiveness, and I would forgive them."

[p. 86]

Here is a subtle point: Satan may turn away from one of God's servants rejoicing, thinking that he has achieved his goal of seduction, when he sees that servant committing a sin openly, and that this lowers the servant's rank. By sin the servant's heart is broken, and he is freed from self-admiration and from admiring his worship, and becomes closer to those brought near. For one who sins is brought near to God, as He, exalted, said: ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:4]. The sinner who repents and regrets has a broken heart, and God is with him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord: "I am with those whose hearts are broken." There is a difference between one who is with God and one with whom God is. Perhaps what is related of the sins committed by the prophets is of this kind, so that they attain virtue over the angels, since the angels boasted of themselves when they said: ﴿While we glorify You with praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:30]. Satan may also turn away from another whom he had commanded to do something, but the person did not do it, and that person thinks that he has overcome Satan and repelled him disappointed, so he boasts within himself, while he does not know that Satan turned away from him having achieved his goal, accepted and not rejected.

From this a fundamental (uṣūlī) matter becomes clear: people have differed over whether the sinner leaves faith or not. The source of the dispute is that the two disputants look at two different matters. The sin which is of the body and not of the heart does not take one out of faith; rather, it may even increase faith. The sin which is of the heart is feared to lead one out of the bond of faith. For this reason they differed over the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of the prophets from sins. The more likely view is that bodily sins are possible for them, and the Qur'an is evidence of this, while sins of the heart are not possible for them. Then, when He, exalted, forbade His servants from worshipping Satan, He mentioned what would move them to accept what they were commanded and to refrain from what they were forbidden, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾. There are issues concerning it:

The first issue: From where did the enmity between Satan and man arise? We say: its beginning is from Satan, and its cause is God's honouring of the children of Adam. When Iblīs saw that his Lord honoured Adam and his offspring, he became hostile to them, so God, exalted, became hostile to him. The first (Satan's enmity) is baseness, and the second (God's) is generosity. As for the first, it is because when a king honours one person without diminishing anything from another, since there is no shortage in the treasury, then the enmity of one who opposes that honoured person is nothing but baseness. As for the second, it is because when the king knows that his honouring of him is nothing except from him, for the weak one could not reach some of that rank were it not for the king's honouring, he knows that whoever hates him denies the king's act or attributes a shortage to his treasury, and both of these make punishment for it fitting. So he becomes hostile to him, completing the honour and perfecting the bounty. Moreover, many people, following the way of Iblīs, when they see someone honoured near a king, hate him and strive against him, establishing the practice of Iblīs. The king, if he is not characterised by the character of God, does not distance the one who informs against him, and listens to his words, and abandons honouring and esteeming that person.

The second issue: From where does the manifestation of Iblīs's enmity come? We say: when God honoured Adam, Iblīs became hostile to him, and thought that he would remain in his rank and Adam in his rank, like two mutual enemies near a king. God knew the inner thoughts, so He removed him and revealed his matter. He then manifested from himself what he had been hiding, since the reason that had compelled him to hide it was gone. So he said: ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'rāf 7:16], and he said: ﴿I will surely seize his descendants﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:62].

The third issue: If Satan is a clear enemy to man, why does man incline to what pleases him, such as drinking and fornication, and dislike what displeases him, such as striving and worship? We say: the cause of that is Satan's seeking the help of helpers from within man, and man's abandoning seeking God's help. So he seeks help through his desire, which God created in him for the benefits of his survival and the survival of his kind, and makes it a cause for the corruption of his state, and calls him by it to the paths of destruction. Likewise, he seeks help through his anger, which God created to repel harms from him, and makes it a cause of his ruin and the corruption of his condition.

[p. 87]

Man's inclination toward sins is like the sick person's inclination toward harmful things, which happens when the temperament departs from balance. You see the feverish person desiring cold water while it increases his illness. One whose stomach is corrupt does not digest a little food, and inclines to eat a great deal, and is not satisfied with anything, while it increases the corruption of his stomach. The one of sound temperament desires only what benefits him. The world is like polluted air, in which man cannot do without breathing air, and that air corrupts his temperament, and there is no way for him except to purify the air with fragrant odours, pure things, and sprinkling with vinegar and rose water, among the purifying measures. Likewise man in this world cannot do without its affairs, and these are the helpers of Satan. His way is to abandon desire, reduce hope, and turn desire away by good remembrance and asceticism. When the temperament of his intellect is sound, he inclines only to the truth. No burden of obligations remains heavy upon him, and he attains familiarity with divine matters. At that point Satan acknowledges that he has no authority over him.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾

When He forbade the worship of Satan, He urged the worship of the Most Merciful. The Lawgiver is a physician of souls, just as the physician is a physician of bodies. Just as the physician tells the patient, "Do not do this, and do not eat that"—and this is the diet (ḥimya), which is the head of the remedy, so that his illness does not increase—and then tells him, "Take such-and-such medicine to strengthen his power to resist the illness," so too the Lawgiver forbade what corrupts, which is following Satan, and urged what reforms, which is the worship of the Most Merciful. There are several issues here:

The first issue: when forbidding the worship of Satan, He said: ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾, because enmity is the strongest barrier against following. But when commanding the worship of the Most Merciful, He did not say, "Indeed, He is a beloved to you," because love does not necessitate following the beloved; rather, it may produce reliance on love, so that one says, "He loves me, so there is no need to bear hardship in seeking His pleasure." Instead, He mentioned what is most effective in moving one to worship, namely that it is a straight path. This is because a person in the abode of this world is in a desolate, frightening wilderness, heading toward a dwelling of permanence where his brethren are. One who stops in an empty desert fears for his soul and his property, and nothing is dearer to him than a near, safe road. So when God, exalted is He, said, ﴿This is a straight path﴾, this was a cause that urged one to travel it. Within His saying, ﴿This is a path﴾, there is an indication that the human being is a passer-through, for if he were in a dwelling of permanence, His saying, ﴿This is a straight path﴾, would have no meaning, since the one who resides says: "What do I do with a path, when I am among those who reside?"

The second issue: What indicates that it is a straight path? We say: the human being is a traveler, either the traveler returning to his homeland or the traveler of a merchant who has goods to trade. In both cases, God is the destination. As for the homeland: one cannot settle in a place of safety, and there is no safety except under a king whose kingdom does not end, for when the kingdom of kings ends, security and comfort do not remain. God, glory be to Him, is the One whose dominion is everlasting, and everything other than Him is perishing. As for trade: the merchant only heads to a place where he hears or knows that there is demand (rawāj) for his goods. God, exalted is He, says that good deeds are rewarded with Him, repaid with many times what they deserve. God is the destination, and worship of Him is turning toward Him.
